excerpts.author: Justin Martyr
english: Certain men among the Jews became prophets of God, and through them the prophetic Spirit announced beforehand the things that were going to happen before they came to pass. The kings who ruled in Judea at various times, when these prophecies were being spoken, acquired the prophetic books as they were written in the prophets' own Hebrew tongue and preserved them.

When Ptolemy, the king of Egypt, was establishing a library and attempting to gather the writings of all mankind, he learned of these prophecies and sent a request to Herod, who was then king of the Jews, asking that the prophetic books be sent to him. King Herod dispatched them, written in the aforementioned Hebrew language. But since the contents were unknown to the Egyptians, Ptolemy asked him again, this time to send men who could translate the books into Greek. Once this was done, the books remained in Egypt until the present day, and they are now found everywhere among all Jews.

Yet even while reading them, the Jews do not understand what is said; instead they regard us as enemies and adversaries, killing and punishing us whenever they are able, as you yourselves can be persuaded. For even in the recent Jewish war, Barchochebas, the leader of the Jewish revolt, ordered that Christians alone be seized for severe punishments unless they denied Jesus the Christ and blasphemed.

In the books of the prophets we find it proclaimed and foretold that Christ would come, would be born of a virgin, would grow to manhood and heal every disease and every infirmity, and would raise the dead; that he would be envied and unrecognized and crucified, would die and be raised, and would ascend into the heavens; that he is the Son of God and is called so; that certain men would be sent by him to every nation of humanity to proclaim these things; and that the peoples from the nations would believe in him more readily.

These things were prophesied before he appeared — at one time five thousand years beforehand, at another three thousand, at another two thousand, and again one thousand, and yet again eight hundred years — for according to the succession of generations, different prophets arose at different times.

greek: Ἄνθρωποι οὖν τινες ἐν Ἰουδαίοις γεγένηνται θεοῦ προφῆται, δι᾿ ὧν τὸ προφητικὸν πνεῦμα προεκήρυξε τὰ γενήσεσθαι μέλλοντα πρὶν ἢ γενέσθαι· καὶ τούτων οἱ ἐν Ἰουδαίοις κατὰ καιροὺς γενόμενοι βασιλεῖς τὰς προφητείας, ὡς ἐλέχθησαν ὅτε προεφητεύοντο, τῇ ἰδίᾳ αὐτῶν ἑβραΐδι φωνῇ ἐν βιβλίοις ὑπ᾿ αὐτῶν τῶν προφητῶν συντεταγμένας κτώμενοι περιεῖπον. Ὅτε δὲ Πτολεμαῖος, ὁ Αἰγυπτίων βασιλεύς, βιβλιοθήκην κατεσκεύαζε καὶ τὰ πάντων ἀνθρώπων συγγράμματα συνάγειν ἐπειράθη, πυθόμενος καὶ περὶ τῶν προφητειῶν τούτων, προσέπεμψε τῷ τῶν Ἰουδαίων τότε βασιλεύοντι Ἡρώδῃ ἀξιῶν διαπεμφθῆναι αὐτῷ τὰς βίβλους τῶν προφητειῶν. Καὶ ὁ μὲν βασιλεὺς Ἡρώδης τῇ προειρημένῃ ἑβραΐδι αὐτῶν φωνῇ γεγραμμένας διεπέμψατο. Ἐπειδὴ δὲ οὐκ ἦν γνώριμα τὰ ἐν αὐταῖς γεγραμμένα τοῖς Αἰγυπτίοις, πάλιν αὐτὸν ἠξίωσε πέμψας τοὺς μεταβαλοῦντας αὐτὰς εἰς τὴν ἑλλάδα φωνὴν ἀθρώπους ἀποστεῖλαι. Καὶ τούτου γενομένου ἔμειναν αἱ βίβλοι καὶ παρ᾿ Αἰγυπτίοις μέχρι τοῦ δεῦρο, καὶ πανταχοῦ παρὰ πᾶσίν εἰσιν Ἰουδαίοις, οἳ καὶ ἀναγινώσκοντες οὐ συνιᾶσι τὰ εἰρημένα, ἀλλ᾿ ἐχθροὺς ἡμᾶς καὶ πολεμίους ἡγοῦνται, ὁμοίως ὑμῖν ἀναιροῦντες καὶ κολάζοντες ἡμᾶς ὁπόταν δύνωνται, ὡς καὶ πεισθῆναι δύνασθε. Καὶ γὰρ ἐν τῷ νῦν γεγενημένῳ ἰουδαϊκῷ πολέμῳ Βαρχωχέβας, ὁ τῆς Ἰουδαίων ἀποστάσεως ἀρχηγέτης, Χριστιανοὺς μόνους εἰς τιμωρίας δεινάς, εἰ μὴ ἀρνοῖντο Ἰησοῦν τὸν Χριστὸν καὶ βλασφημοῖεν, ἐκέλευεν ἀπάγεσθαι. Ἐν δὴ ταῖς τῶν προφητῶν βίβλοις εὕρομεν προκηρυσσόμενον παραγινόμενον, γεννώμενον διὰ παρθένου, καὶ ἀνδρούμενον καὶ θεραπεύοντα πᾶσαν νόσον καὶ πᾶσαν μαλακίαν καὶ νεκροὺς ἀνεγείροντα, καὶ φθονούμενον καὶ ἀγνοούμενον καὶ σταυρούμενον Ἰησοῦν τὸν ἡμέτερον Χριστόν, καὶ ἀποθνήσκοντα καὶ ἀνεγειρόμενον καὶ εἰς οὐρανοὺς ἀνερχόμενον, καὶ υἱὸν θεοῦ ὄντα καὶ κεκλημένον, καί τινας πεμπομένους ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ εἰς πᾶν γένος ἀνθρώπων κηρύξοντας ταῦτα, καὶ τοὺς ἐξ ἐθνῶν ἀνθρώπους μᾶλλον αὐτᾷ πιστεύειν. Προεφητεύθη δέ, πρὶν ἢ φανῆναι αὐτόν, ἔτεσι ποτὲ μὲν πεντακισχιλίοις, ποτὲ δὲ τρισχιλίοις, ποτὲ δὲ δισχιλίοις, καὶ πάλιν χιλίοις καὶ ἄλλοτε ὀκτακοσίοις· κατὰ γὰρ τὰς διαδοχὰς τῶν γενῶν ἕτεροι καὶ ἕτεροι ἐγένοντο προφῆται.

excerpts.author: Justin Martyr
english: Christ was born to set the rest of humanity free, but only when He had fully become a man; and that has now come to pass, as the earlier passages show. Here they are: "A child has been born to us, and a son has been given to us, whose rule rests upon his shoulders" (Isaiah). This is a sign of the power of the cross, upon which He bore the weight of that rule when He was crucified, as will be made even clearer in the dawning of the Word. Again the same prophet Isaiah, carried by the prophetic Spirit, declares: "I stretched out my hands all day long to a disobedient and contrary people, to those who walk in a way that is not good. They now demand judgment and dare to draw near to God" (Isaiah). And once more, through another prophet, He says: "They pierced my hands and my feet, and cast lots for my clothing" (Isaiah). David, the king and prophet who spoke these words, suffered none of them; but Jesus Christ was put to the test regarding His hands, crucified by the Jews who denied Him and claimed He was not the Christ. Just as the prophet foretold, they dragged Him before the judgment seat and said, "Judge us" (Isaiah). The words "They pierced my hands and feet" explain the nails driven through His hands and feet on the cross. After they crucified Him, they cast lots for His clothing and divided it among themselves, the very ones who crucified Him. That these things happened you can verify from the official records made under Pontius Pilate. And since it was explicitly prophesied that He would mount a donkey's colt and enter Jerusalem, we will cite the words of another prophet, Zechariah: "Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; shout aloud, daughter of Jerusalem! Look, your king comes to you, gentle and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a beast of burden" (Zechariah).

greek: Ὡς δὲ καὶ λήσειν ἔμελλε τοὺς ἄλλους ἀνθρώπους γεννηθεὶς ὁ Χριστὸς ἄχρις ἀνδρωθῇ. ὅπερ καὶ γέγονεν, ἀκούσατε τῶν προειρημένων εἰς τοῦτο. Ἔστι δὲ ταῦτα· „Παιδίον ἐγεννήθη ἡμῖν, καὶ νεανίσκος ἡμῖν ἀπεδόθη, οὗ ἡ ἀρχ(??) ἐπὶ τῶν ὤμων“· μηνυτικὸν τῆς δυνάμεως τοῦ σταυροῦ, ᾧ προσέθηκε τοὺς ὤμους σταυρωθείς, ὡς πρωϊόντος τοῦ λόγον σαφέστερον δειχθήσεται. Καὶ πάλιν ὁ αὐτὸς προφήτης Ἡσαΐας θεοφορούμενος τῷ πνεύματι τῷ προφητικῷ ἔφη· ,Ἐγώ ἐξεπέτασα τὰς χεῖράς μου ἐπὶ λαὸν ἀπειθοῦντα καὶ ἀντιλέγοντα, ἐπὶ τοὺς πορευομένους ἐν ὁδῷ οὐ καλῇ. Αἰτοῦσί με νῦν κρίσιν καὶ ἐγγίζειν θεῷ τολμῶσιν“. Καὶ πάλιν ἐν ἄλλοις λόγοις δι᾿ ἑτέρου προφήτου λέγει· „Αὐιοὶ ὤρυξάν μου πόδας καὶ χεῖρας, καὶ ἔβαλον κλῆρον ἐπὶ τὸν ἱματισμόν μου“. Καὶ ὁ μὲν Δαυῒδ ὁ βασιλεὺς καὶ προφήτης, ὁ εἰπὼν ταῦτα, οὐδὲν τούτων ἔπαθεν· Ἰησοῦς δὲ Χριστὸς ἐξετάθη τὰς χεῖρας, σταυρωθεὶς ὑπὸ τῶν Ἰουδαίων ἀντιλεγόντων αὐτῷ καὶ φασκόντων μὴ εἶναι αὐτὸν Χριστόν· καὶ γάρ, ὡς εἶπεν ὁ προφήτης, διασύροντες αὐτὸν ἐκάθισαν ἐπὶ βήματος καὶ εἶπον· Κρῖνον ἡμῖν. Τὸ δὲ „Ὤρυξάν μου χεῖρας καὶ πόδας‘· ἐξήγησις τῶν ἐν τῷ σταυρῷ παγέντων ἐν ταῖς χερσὶ καὶ τοῖς ποσὶν αὐτοῦ ἥλων ἦν. Καὶ μετὰ τὸ σταυρῶσαι αὐτὸν ἔβαλον κλῆρον ἐπὶ τὸν ἱματισμὸν αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐμερίσαντο ἑαυτοῖς οἱ σταυρώσαντες αὐτόν. Καὶ ταῦτα ὅτι γέγονε, δύνασθε μαθεῖν ἐκ τῶν ἐπὶ Ποντίου Πιλάτου γενομένων ἄκτων. Καὶ ὅτι ῥητῶς καθεσθησόμενος ἐπὶ πῶλον ὄνου καὶ εἰσελευσόμενος εἰς τὰ Ἱεροσόλυμα προεπεφήτευτο, ἑτέρου προφήτου τοῦ Σοφονίου τας τῆς προφητείας λέξεις ἐροῦμεν. Εἰσὶ δὲ αὗται· „Χαῖρε σφόδρα, θύγατερ Σιών, κήρυσσε, θύγατερ Ἱερουσαλήμ· ἰδοὺ ὁ βασιλεύς σου ἔρχεται σοι πρᾶος, ἐπιβεβηκὼς ἐπὶ ὄνον καὶ πῶλον υἱὸν ὑποζυγίου“.

excerpts.author: Justin Martyr
english: The holy prophetic Spirit taught us these things, declaring through Moses to the first man created by God: "Behold, before you lie the good and the evil; choose the good." Again, through Isaiah, another prophet, the word came from the Father of all and the Master, God, saying: "Wash yourselves, become clean, remove your evil deeds from my sight; learn to do good, seek justice, defend the orphan, plead for the widow. Come now, let us reason together, says the Lord: though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be white as wool; though they are red like crimson, they shall become like snow. If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land; but if you refuse and rebel, the sword shall devour you; for the mouth of the Lord has spoken" (Isaiah 1:16-20). The earlier statement "the sword shall devour you" does not mean that the disobedient will be killed by physical swords; rather, the sword of God is fire, and its fuel is those who choose to do evil. Therefore it says: "The sword shall devour you; for the mouth of the Lord has spoken." If it were speaking of a sword that cuts and destroys at once, it would not have said "devour." So also Plato, when he said, "The cause lies with the one who chooses; God is blameless," took this from Moses the prophet, for Moses is older than all the writers among the Greeks. And all that philosophers and poets have said about the immortality of the soul, or punishments after death, or the contemplation of heavenly things, or similar doctrines—they received their starting points from the prophets, and were able to understand and explain them. Hence there appear to be seeds of truth among all people; yet they are convicted of not having understood accurately whenever they contradict themselves. When we say that future events were prophesied, we do not say this because they happen by the necessity of fate; but because God is foreknowing, knowing what all human beings will do, and because there is a decree with Him to repay each person according to their deeds. Through the prophetic Spirit He foretells what will befall each according to their works, ever leading the human race to knowledge and remembrance, showing that He cares for them and provides for them. By the operation of evil demons, death was appointed against those who read the books of Hystaspes, or the Sibyl, or the prophets, so that through fear they might turn away from the knowledge of good things those who approach these writings, and hold in bondage those who serve the demons; yet they were not able to accomplish this in the end. For we approach these writings without fear, and we bring them to you, as you see, for examination, knowing they will prove pleasing to all; and even if we persuade only a few, we shall have gained the greatest things, for as good farmers we shall receive the reward from the Master.

greek: Ἐδίδαξε δὲ ἡμᾶς ταῦτα τὸ ἅγιον προφητικὸν πνεῦμα, διὰ Μωϋσέως φῆσαν τῷ πρώτῳ πλασθέντι ἀνθρώπῳ εἰρῆσθαι ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ οὕτως· „Ἰδοὺ πρὸ προσώπου σου τὸ ἀγαθὸν καὶ τὸ κακόν, ἔκλεξαι τὸ ἀγαθόν“. Καὶ πάλιν διὰ Ἡσαΐου, τοῦ ἑτέρου προφήτου, ὡς ἀπὸ προσώπου τοῦ πατρὸς τῶν ὅλων καὶ δεσπότου θεοῦ εἰς τοῦτο λεχθῆναι οὕτως· „Λούσασθε, καθαροὶ γένεσθε, ἀφέλετε τὰς πονηρίας ἀπὸ τῶν ψυχῶν ὑμῶν, μάθετε καλὸν ποιεῖν, κρίνατε ὀρφανῷ καὶ δικαιώσατε χήραν, καὶ δεῦτε καὶ διαλεχθῶμεν, λέγει κύριος· καὶ ἐὰν ὦσιν αἱ ἁμαρτίαι ὑμῶν ὡς φοινικοῦν, ὡσεὶ ἔριον λευκανῶ, καὶ ἐὰν ὦσιν ὡς κόκκινον, ὡς χιόνα λευκανῶ. Καὶ ἐὰν θέλητε καὶ εἰσακούσητέ μου, τὰ ἀγαθὰ τῆς γῆς φάγεσθε, ἐὼν δὲ μὴ εἰσακούσητέ μου, μόχαιρα ὑμᾶς κατέδεται· τὸ γὰρ στόμα κυρίου ἐλάλησε ταῦτα“. Τὸ δὲ προειρημένον „Μάχαιρα ὑμᾶς κατέδεται“ οὐ λέγει διὰ μαχαιρῶν φονενθήσεσθαι τοὺς παρακούσαντας, ἀλλ᾿ ἡ μάχαιρα τοῦ θεοῖ ἐστι τὸ πῦρ. οὗ βορὰ γίνονται οἱ τὰ φαῦλα πράττειν αἱρούμενοι. Διὰ τοῦτο λέγει· „Μάχαιρα ὑμᾶς κατέδεται· τὸ γὰρ στόμα κυρίου ἐλάλησεν“. Εἰ δὲ καὶ περὶ τεμνούσης καὶ αὐτίκα ἀπαλλασσούσης μαχαίρας ἔλεγεν, οὐκ ἂν εἶπε „Κατέδεται“. Ὥστε καὶ Πλάτων εἰπών. „Αἰτία ἑλομένου, θεὸς δ᾿ ἀναίτιος“ παρὰ Μωϋσέως τοῦ προφήτου λαβὼν εἶπε· πρεσβύτερος γὰρ Μωϋσῆς καὶ πάντων τῶν ἐν Ἕλλησι συγγραφέων. Καὶ πάντα. ὅσα περὶ ἀθανασίας ψυχῆς ἢ τιμωριῶν τῶν μετὰ θάνατον ἢ θεωρίας οὐρανίων ἢ τῶν ὁμοίων δογμάτων καὶ φιλόσοφοι καὶ ποιηταὶ ἔφασαν, παρὰ τῶν προφητῶν τὰς ἀφορμὰς λαβόντες καὶ νοῆσαι δεδύνηνται καὶ ἐξηγήσαντο. Ὅθεν παρὰ πᾶσι σπέρματα ἀληθείας δοκεῖ εἶναι· ἐλέγχονται δὲ μὴ ἀκριβῶς νοήσαντες. ὅταν ἐναντία αὐτοὶ ἑαυτοῖς λέγωσιν. Ὥστε ὅ φαμεν, πεπροφητεῦσθαι τὰ μέλλοντα γίνεσθαι, οὐ διὰ τὸ εἱμαρμένης ἀνάγκῃ πράττεσθαι λέγομεν· ἀλλὰ προγνώστου τοῦ θεοῦ ὄντος τῶν μελλόντων ὑπὸ πάντων ἀνθρώπων πραχθήσεσθαι, καὶ δόγματος ὄντος παρ᾿ αὐτόν κατ᾿ ἀξίαν τῶν πράξεων ἕκαστον ἀμείψεσθαι μέλλοντα τῶν ἀνθρώπων. καὶ τὰ παρ᾿ αὐτοῦ κατ᾿ ἀξίαν τῶν πραττομένων ἀπαντήσεσθαι διὰ τοῦ προφητικοῦ πνεύματος προλέγει, εἰς ἐπίστασιν καὶ ἀνάμνησιν ἀεὶ ἄγων τὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων γένος, δεικνύς, ὅτι καὶ μέλον ἐστιν αὐτῷ καὶ προνοεῖται αἰτῶν. Κατ᾿ ἐνέργειαν δὲ τῶν φαύλων δαιμόνων θάνατος ὡρίσθη κατὰ τῶν τὰς Ὑστάσπου ἢ Σιβύλλης ἢ τῶν προφητῶν βίβλους ἀναγινωσκόντων, ὅπως διὰ τοῖ φόβου ἀποστρέψωσιν ἐντυγχάνοντας τοὺς ἀνθρώπους τῶν καλῶν γνῶσιν λαβεῖν, αἰτοῖς δὲ δουλεύοντας κατέχωσιν· ὅπερ εἰς τέλος οὐκ ἴσχυσαν πρᾶξαι. Ἀφόβως μὲν γὰρ οὐ μόνον ἐντυγχάνομεν αὐταῖς, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὑμῖν, ὡς ὁρᾶτε, εἰς ἐπίσκεψιν φέρομεν, ἐπιστάμενοι πᾶσιν εὐάρεστα φανήσεσθαι· κἂν ὀλίγους δὲ πείσωμεν, τὰ μέγιστα κερδήσαντες ἐσόμεθα· ὡς γεωργοὶ γὰρ ἀγαθοὶ παρὰ τοῖ δεσπόζοντος τὴν ἀμοιβὴν ἕξομεν.

excerpts.author: Justin Martyr
english: What need, then, is there for a teacher from whom anyone could benefit, if the truth is not found in these matters? Long before any of the so‑called philosophers there lived certain men—older, blessed, righteous, and beloved by God—who spoke by the divine Spirit and foretold events that are now occurring; they are called prophets. These alone both saw and declared the truth to humanity, neither intimidated nor swayed by anyone, nor overcome by a desire for glory. Filled with the Holy Spirit, they spoke only what they had heard and seen. Their writings survive to this day, and anyone who reads them can gain great benefit concerning first principles, the end, and all that a philosopher ought to know, provided he believes them. They did not support their words with proof at the time, because they were trustworthy witnesses to the truth, standing above every proof. The events that have happened and continue to happen compel agreement with what was spoken through them. Moreover, they were also worthy of belief because of the powers they performed, since they glorified the Creator of all things, God the Father, and proclaimed the Christ, His Son. False prophets, filled with a deceitful and unclean spirit, have never done this and never do; instead they dare to work certain wonders to astonish people and they glorify the spirits of deceit and demons. I pray that, above all, the gates of light may be opened to you, for these things are not understood or perceived by everyone unless God grants understanding together with His Christ.

greek: Τίνι οὖν, φημί, ἔτι τις χρήσαιτο διδασκάλῳ (??) πόθεν ὠφεληθείη τις. εἰ μηδὲ ἐν τούτοις τὸ ἀληθές ἐστιν; Ἐγένοντό τινες πρὸ πολλοῦ χρόνου πάντων τούτων τῶν νομιζομένων φιλοσόφων παλαιότεροι, μακάριοι καὶ δίκαιοι καὶ θεοφιλεῖς, θείῳ πνεύματι λαλήσαντες καὶ τὰ μέλλοντα θεσπίσαντες, ἃ δὴ νῦν γίνεται· προφήτας δὲ αὐτοὺς καλοῦσιν. Οὗτοι μόνοι τὸ ἀληθὲς καὶ εἶδον καὶ ἐξεῖπον ἀνθρώποις, μήτ᾿ εὐλαβηθέντες μήτε δυσωπηθέντες τινά. μὴ ἡττημένοι δόξης. ἀλλὰ μόνα ταῦτα εἰπόντες ἃ ἤκουσαν καὶ ἃ εἶδον ἁγίῳ πληρωθέντες πνεύματι. Συγγράμματα δὲ αὐτῶν ἔτι καὶ νῦν διαμένει, καὶ ἔστιν ἐντυχόντα τούτοις πλεῖστον ὠφεληθῆναι καὶ περὶ ἀρχῶν καὶ περὶ τέλους καὶ ὧν χρὴ εἰδέναι τὸν φιλόσοφον, πιστεύσαντα ἐκείνοις. Οὐ γὰρ μετὰ ἀποδείξεως πεποίηνται τότε τοὺς λόγους, ἃτε ἀνωτέρω πάσης ἀποδείξεως ὄντες ἀξιόπιστοι μάρτυρες τῆς ἀληθείας· τὰ δὲ ἀποβάντα καὶ ἀποβαίνοντα ἐξαναγκάζει συντίθεσθαι τοῖς λελαλημένοις δι᾿ αὐτῶν. Καίτοι γε καὶ διὰ τὰς δυνάμεις, ἃς ἐπετέλουν, πιστεύεσθαι δίκαιοι ἦσαν, ἐπειδὴ καὶ τὸν ποιητὴν τῶν ὅλων θεὸν καὶ πατέρα ἐδόξαζον καὶ τὸν παρ᾿ αὐτοῦ Χριστὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ κατήγγελλον· ὅπερ οἱ ἀπὸ τοῦ πλάνου καὶ ἀκαθάρτου πνεύματος ἐμπιπλάμενοι ψευδοπροφῆται οὕτε ἐποίησαν οὔτε ποιοῦσιν, ἀλλὰ δυνάμεις τινὰς ἐνεργεῖν εἰς κατάπληξιν τῶν ἀνθρώπων τολμῶσι καὶ τὰ τῆς πλάνης πνεύματα καὶ δαιμόνια δοξολογοῦσιν. Εὔχου δέ σοι πρὸ πάντων φωτὸς ἀνοιχθῆναι πύλας· οὐ γὰρ συνοπτὰ οὐδὲ συννοητὰ πᾶσίν ἐστιν, εἰ μή τῳ θεὸς δῷ συνιέναι καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς αὐτοῦ.

excerpts.author: Athenagoras
english: Since, therefore, the unity of the Deity is confessed by almost all, even against their will, when they come to treat of the first principles of the universe , and we in our turn likewise assert that He who arranged this universe is God — why is it that they can say and write with impunity what they please concerning the Deity, but that against us a law lies in force, though we are able to demonstrate what we apprehend and justly believe , namely that there is one God , with proofs and reason accordant with truth ?

For poets and philosophers , as to other subjects so also to this, have applied themselves in the way of conjecture, moved, by reason of their affinity with the afflatus from God , each one by his own soul , to try whether he could find out and apprehend the truth ; but they have not been found competent fully to apprehend it, because they thought fit to learn, not from God concerning God , but each one from himself; hence they came each to his own conclusion respecting God , and matter, and forms, and the world. But we have for witnesses of the things we apprehend and believe , prophets , men who have pronounced concerning God and the things of God , guided by the Spirit of God .

And you too will admit, excelling all others as you do in intelligence and in piety towards the true God ( τὸ ὄντως θεῖον ), that it would be irrational for us to cease to believe in the Spirit from God , who moved the mouths of the prophets like musical instruments, and to give heed to mere human opinions.

excerpts.author: Athenagoras
english: If we satisfied ourselves with advancing such considerations as these, our doctrines might by some be looked upon as human . But, since the voices of the prophets confirm our arguments — for I think that you also, with your great zeal for knowledge , and your great attainments in learning, cannot be ignorant of the writings either of Moses or of Isaiah and Jeremiah, and the other prophets , who, lifted in ecstasy above the natural operations of their minds by the impulses of the Divine Spirit, uttered the things with which they were inspired, the Spirit making use of them as a flute-player breathes into a flute — what, then, do these men say? The Lord is our God ; no other can be compared with Him. And again: I am God , the first and the last, and besides Me there is no God.

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: We have come to know the plan of our salvation through others — through those, that is, by whom the Gospel first reached us. They proclaimed it beforehand; then, by God's will, they committed it to Scripture so that it would become the foundation and pillar of our faith. It is not permissible to claim that they preached before they possessed perfect knowledge, yet some have the audacity to say exactly that, boasting that they are the correctors of the Apostles.

For after our Lord rose from the dead, and they were clothed with the power of the Holy Spirit descending from on high, they were filled with all things and attained perfect knowledge. They went out to the ends of the earth, preaching the good things God has prepared for us and announcing heavenly peace to humanity — each and all of them bearing the Gospel of God.

Thus Matthew, writing in the Hebrews' own tongue, published his Gospel while Peter and Paul were evangelizing in Rome and founding the Church. After their departure, Mark, disciple and interpreter of Peter, handed down to us in writing what Peter had proclaimed. Luke, a follower of Paul, set down in a book the Gospel that Paul preached. Later, John, the Lord's disciple who had reclined on His breast, published his Gospel while living in Ephesus of Asia.

All these men delivered to us one God, the Maker of heaven and earth, announced by the Law and the Prophets, and one Christ, the Son of God. If anyone refuses to assent to this testimony, he despises the companions of the Lord; he despises Christ the Lord Himself; he despises the Father; and he stands self-condemned, resisting and opposing his own salvation — which is precisely what all heretics do.

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: We have come to know the plan of our salvation through others — through those, that is, through whom the Gospel reached us. At first the Apostles preached it publicly; later, by God's will, they handed it down to us in the Scriptures, which were to become the foundation and pillar of our faith (1 Timothy 3:15). It is not right to claim that they preached before they possessed full knowledge, as certain people dare to assert, boasting that they are correctors of the Apostles. For after the Lord Jesus rose from the dead, and they were clothed with power from on high when the Holy Spirit came upon them (Luke 24:49; Acts 1:8), they were filled with all things and attained perfect knowledge. They went out to the ends of the earth, proclaiming the good things that come to us from God and announcing heavenly peace to humanity (Luke 2:14; Acts 10:36), each of them equally possessing the Gospel of God. Accordingly, Matthew composed a written Gospel in the Hebrew language while Peter and Paul were evangelizing in Rome and founding the Church. After their departure, Mark, the disciple and interpreter of Peter, handed down in writing what Peter had proclaimed. Luke, a follower of Paul, set down in a book the Gospel that Paul preached. Afterwards, John, the disciple of the Lord who had leaned on His breast (John 13:23), published his Gospel while living in Ephesus in Asia. All these witnesses proclaimed to us one God, the Maker of heaven and earth, announced by the Law and the Prophets, and one Christ, the Son of God. If anyone refuses to assent to them, he despises the Lord's own associates, he despises Christ the Lord, he despises the Father, and he condemns himself by resisting and opposing his own salvation — which is exactly what all heretics do (John 15:23; 1 John 2:22-23).

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: The Lord's disciple John proclaims this faith, writing his Gospel to uproot the error that Cerinthus had sown among men, and even earlier, the Nicolaitans, a false offshoot that sought to confuse them. He aims to convince them that there is one God who made all things through His Word—not one creator and another Father of the Lord, as the heretics claim, nor one son of the creator and another Christ from above who remained impassible, descended into Jesus the creator's son, and then returned to his Pleroma. They also teach that the Trinity is the Monogenes, the Logos is the true son of the Monogenes, and that our material condition was not made by the first God but by a far lower power, severed from the invisible and ineffable realm above (John 1:1-14).

Therefore the Lord's disciple, determined to fence off all such teachings and establish the rule of truth in the Church, grounds everything in the confession that there is one almighty God who made all things, visible and invisible, through His Word. He also shows that through the same Word by which God perfected the creation, He provided salvation for those who live in it. So John opens his Gospel doctrine with the words: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; He was with God in the beginning. All things were made through Him, and without Him nothing was made. In Him was life, and that life was the light of men; the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it (John 1:1-5).

All things, John says, were made through Him; therefore this creation of ours is included in that all. The heretics cannot claim that everything belongs to their Pleroma and then exclude this world. If their Pleroma contains these things, then this world is not outside it, as we showed in the previous book; but if these things are outside the Pleroma—an impossibility—then their Pleroma is not all things. So this creation is not outside it either. John removes every dissension by declaring: He was in the world, and the world was made through Him, yet the world did not know Him. He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him (John 1:10-11).

According to Marcion and his followers, the world was not made through Him, nor did He come to His own but to another's. According to certain Gnostics, angels made this world, not the Word of God. According to the Valentinians, the Demiurge made the world, not the Word; they say he fashioned it by copying the things above. Yet the Gospel plainly states that all things were made through the Word who was in the beginning with God, and that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). The heretics deny that the Word became flesh, that Christ became flesh, or that the Savior from all things came. They refuse to let the Word and Christ enter this world; they say the Savior did not become incarnate or suffer, but descended like a dove into Jesus, who came from the condition, announced the unknown Father, and then returned to the Pleroma.

Some claim Jesus from the condition was incarnate and suffered, passing through Mary like water through a pipe. Others say the Demiurge's son received the Jesus from the condition. Still others say Jesus was born of Joseph and Mary, and the impassible, fleshless Christ from above descended into him. By no heretical opinion did the Word of God become flesh. Examine all their systems and you will find that every one presents the Word of God and the Christ from above as without flesh and impassible. Some think He merely appeared as a transfigured man, denying He was born or became incarnate; others say He did not assume human form at all but descended like a dove into the Jesus born of Mary.

The Lord's disciple exposes all these as false witnesses and declares: The Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). So that we need not ask whose Word became flesh, John himself teaches: There was a man sent from God, whose name was John; he came as a witness to testify about the light. He was not the light, but came to testify about the light (John 1:6-8). John the forerunner, who testifies to the light, was sent by which God? Surely by the God whose angel is Gabriel, who also announced John's birth; the God who promised through the prophets to send His messenger before the face of His Son to prepare His way—to testify to the light in the spirit and power of Elijah. Elijah was the servant and prophet of which God? Of the God who made heaven and earth, as Elijah himself confesses. Therefore John was sent by the founder and creator of this world; how else could he testify to a light that, on the heretics' view, descended from the ineffable and invisible realms? All heretics decree that the Demiurge is ignorant of the power above him, yet John is found to be that power's witness and revealer. For this reason the Lord said John was more than a prophet (Luke 7:26).

All the other prophets announced the coming of the Father's light and longed to see the one they preached; John not only announced Him but saw Him come, pointed Him out, and persuaded many to believe in Him, so that he holds the place of both prophet and apostle. He is indeed more than a prophet: first an apostle, second a prophet; yet all things are from one and the same God.

Incarnatum autem et passum quidam quidem eum qui ex dispositione sit dicunt Jesum, quem per Mariam dicunt pertransisse, quasi aquam per tubum: alii vero ° Demiurgi filium, in quem descendisse eum Jesum qui ex dispositione sit: alii rursum Jesum quidem ex Joseph et Maria natum dicunt, et in hune descendisse Christum qui de superioribus sit, sine carne et impassibilem exsistentem. Secundum autem nullam sententiam heereticorum, Verbum Dei caro factum est. Si enim quis regulas ipsorum omnium perscrutetur, inveniet quoniam sine carne et impassibilis ab omnibus illis inducitur Dei Verbum, et qui est in superioribus Christus. Alii enim putant manifestatum eum, quemadmodum hominem transfiguratum; neque autem natum, neque incarnatum dicunt illum: alii vero neque figuram eum assumsisse hominis; sed quemadmodum columbam descendisse in eum Jesum, qui natus est ex Maria. Omnes igitur illos falsos testes ostendens discipulus Domini, ait: Ht Verbum caro factum est, et habitavit in nobis. Et ut non inquiramus, cujus Dei Verbum caro factum est, ipse insuper docet, dicens : Fuit homo missus a Deo, erat ei nomen Johannes: hic venit in testimonium, ut testaretur de lumine. Non erat ipse lumen, sed ut testaretur de lumine. Preecursor igitur Johannes, qui testatur de lumine, a quo Deo missus est? Helias autem rursus cujus Dei servus et propheta fuit? Ejus qui fecit coelum et terram, quemadmodum et ipse confitetur. A conditore igitur et fabricatore hujus mundi missus Johannes, quemadmodum poterat testificari de eo lumine, quod ex his que sunt innominabilia et invisibilia descenderit ? Omnes enim heeretici decreverunt, Demiurgum ignorare eam que sit super eum virtutem, cujus testis et ostensor invenitur Johannes. Propter hoc Dominus plus quam prophetam dixit eum habuisse. excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: Knowing God by measuring His magnitude is impossible, for no one can measure the Father. But His love leads us to God through His Word, and as we obey Him we always learn how great God truly is. He Himself establishes, chooses, and adorns all things through Himself—He who relates to us—and so we, together with everything He contains, have been made.

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: The spiritual disciple is the one who truly receives the Spirit of God. This Spirit was present from the beginning in all God's arrangements with humanity; he announced future events, revealed present realities, and explained the past. He judges all things, yet is himself judged by no one. For he judges the nations—creatures who serve the created order rather than the Creator (Rom 1:25), consuming their entire effort in vain with depraved minds. He also judges the Jews, who failed to perceive the word of liberty and refused to go out free, even though their Liberator was present with them. Instead, they pretended to serve God outside the Law at the wrong time, acting as if He needed nothing, and they refused to know or understand the advent of Christ, which He accomplished for human salvation. All the prophets foretold two advents of His. The first: He became man and knew weakness; He rode on a donkey's colt; He was the stone rejected by the builders; He was led like a sheep to the slaughter; by the stretching out of His hands He overthrew Amalek; He gathered the scattered children from the ends of the earth into the Father's fold; He remembered His own dead who had fallen asleep and descended to them to bring them up. The second: He will come on the clouds, bringing a day that burns like a furnace; He will strike the earth with the word of His mouth and slay the wicked with the breath of His lips; He will hold a winnowing fork in His hand, clear His threshing floor, gather the wheat into His barn, and burn the chaff with unquenchable fire (Isa 11:4; Matt 3:12; 2 Thess 2:8; Mal 4:1).

Now let us examine the teaching of Marcion: how does he accept that there are two gods, separated by infinite distance? How can the one he calls 'good' be good, when he lures away strangers from the God who made them and summons them into his own kingdom? Why does his goodness fail by not saving everyone? Why does he appear good toward human beings, yet prove most unjust toward the One who made them, by stripping that Maker of what belongs to Him? How can the Lord be just if He springs from another Father, yet assumes this human condition, declaring the bread to be His body and the cup's mixture to be His blood? Why did He confess Himself to be the Son of Man if He did not undergo the generation that comes from man? How could He forgive us the sins we owe to our Maker and God? How could He be crucified when He was not flesh, but was born only in appearance as a man—and from His pierced side blood and water flowed out? What was that body the buriers buried? And what was it that rose from the dead?

latin: Ta is discipulus spiritalis vere recipiens Spiritum Dei, qui ab initio in universis dispositionibus Dei adfuit hominibus, et futura annuntiavit et preesentia ostendit et preeterita enarrat, judicat quidem omnes, ipse autem a nemine judicatur. Nam judicat gentes, creature magis quam Oreatori servientes, et reprobabili mente universam suam operationem in vanum consumentes. Judicat autem etiam Judos, non percipientes verbum libertatis, neque volentes abire liberos, cum habeant preesentem liberatorem ; sed intempestive extra legem servire simulantes nihil indigenti Deo, et Christi adventum, quem propter salutem hominum fecit, non cognoseentes, neque intelligere volentes, quoniam duos adventus ejus omnes annuntiaverunt prophetee: unum quidem, in homo in plaga factus est, sciens ferre imbecillitatem, et in pullo asinee sedens, et reprobatus lapis ab eedificantibus, et sicut ovis ad victimam adductus, et per extensionem manuum dissolvens quidem Amalech; congregans autem dispersos filios a terminis terre in ovile Patris, et recommemoratus mortuorum suorum qui dormierant, et descendens ad eos, uti erueret eos®; secundum autem, in quo super nubes veniet, superducens diem que est sicut clibanus ardens, et percutiens terram verbo oris sui, et spiritu per labia sua interficiens impios, et ventilabrum in manu habens, et’ emundans aream suam, et triticum quidem in horreum comburens autem paleas igne inexstinguibili. 1. Examrnasir autem et doctrinam Marcionis, quomodo accipiat duos deos esse, infinita distantia separatos ab invicem? Vel quemadmodum bonus erit, qui alienos homines abstrahit ab eo qui fecit, et ad suum advocat regnum? et quare bonitas ejus deficit, non omnes salyans? et quare circa homines quidem bonus videtur, in ipsum autem qui fecit homines injustissimus, auferens ab eo quee sunt ejus? Quomodo autem juste Dominus, si alterius patris exsistit, hujus conditionis que est secundum nos, accipiens panem suum corpus esse confitebatur, et temperamentum calicis suum sanguinem confirmavit? Et quare se Filium Hominis confitebatur, si non eam que ex homine est generationem sustinuisset? Quemadmodum autem et peccata nobis dimittere poterat, quee nostro debeamus factori et Deo? 4Quomodo autem et cum caro non esset, sed cum pareret quasi homo, crucifixus est, et e Jatere ejus puncto sanguis exiit et aqua? Quod autem corpus sepelierunt sepultores? et quid illud erat quod surrexit a mortuis ?

excerpts.author: Theophilus of Antioch
english: Cain also fathered a son named Enoch, and he built a city which he named after his son Enoch (Genesis 4:17). From that point onward the building of cities began, and this occurred before the flood; not as Homer falsely says, 'For not yet had a city been built for mortal men.'

To Enoch was born a son named Gaidad; Gaidad fathered Meel, Meel fathered Mathusala, and Mathusala fathered Lamech. Lamech took two wives, Ada and Sella, and from that time the practice of bigamy and the origin of music began. Lamech had three sons: Obel, Jubal, and Tubel. Obel became a man who lived in tents and raised livestock; Jubal was the one who introduced the psaltery and the harp; and Tubel became a metalworker, forging copper and iron.

Thus the line of Cain had a recorded catalog up to this point, but afterward his genealogy fell into oblivion because he had murdered his brother. In place of Abel, God gave Eve to conceive and bear a son named Seth, from whom the rest of humanity descends to this day. For anyone who wishes and loves to learn, it is easy to demonstrate every generation through the holy scriptures. A partial account has already been given in another work, as we noted above, outlining the genealogy in the first book of histories. The Holy Spirit teaches us all these things through Moses and the other prophets, so that our sacred writings are shown to be more ancient and also more true than those of any other writers and poets.

Some have foolishly claimed that Apollo invented music, while others say Orpheus discovered it from the sweet song of birds. Their claims are empty and vain, for these figures lived many years after the flood.
The account of Noah, who is also called Deucalion by some, has been presented in the book mentioned earlier; if you wish, you may examine it as well.

greek: Ὁ οὖν Κάϊν καὶ αὐτὸς ἔσχεν υἱόν, ᾧ ὄνομα Ἐνώχ. Καὶ ᾠκοδόμησεν πόλιν, ἣν ἐπωνόμασεν ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνόματι τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ Ἐνώχ. Ἀπὸ τότε ἀρχὴ ἐγένετο τοῦ οἰκοδομεῖσθαι πόλεις, καὶ τοῦτο πρὸ κατακλυσμοῦ· οὐχ ὡς Ὅμηρος ψεύδεται λέγων· Οὐ γάρ πω πεπόλιστο πόλις μερόπων ἀνθρώπων. Τῷ δὲ Ἐνὼχ ἐγενήθη υἱὸς ὀνόματι Γαϊδάδ· ἐγέννησεν τὸν καλούμενον Μεήλ, καὶ Μεὴλ τὸν Μαθουσάλα, καὶ Μαθουσάλα τὸν Λάμεχ. Ὁ δὲ Λάμεχ ἔλαβεν ἑαυτῷ δύο γυναῖκας, αἷς ὀνόματα Ἀδᾶ καὶ Σελᾶ. Ἔκτοτε ἀρχὴ ἐγένετο τῆς πολυμιξίας, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῆς μουσικῆς. Τῷ γὰρ Λάμεχ ἐγένοντο τρεῖς υἱοί, Ὠβὴλ Ἰουβὰλ Θοβέλ. Καὶ ὁ μὲν Ὠβὴλ ἐγένετο ἀνὴρ ἐν σκηναῖς κτηνοτροφῶν, Ἰουβὰλ δέ ἐστιν ὁ καταδείξας ψαλτήριον καὶ κιθάραν, Θοβὲλ δὲ ἐγένετο σφυροκόπος χαλκεὺς χαλκοῦ καὶ σιδήρου. Ἕως μὲν οὖν τούτου ἔσχεν τὸν κατάλογον τὸ σπέρμα τοῦ Κάϊν· καὶ τὸ λοιπὸν εἰς λήθην αὐτοῦ γέγονεν τὸ σπέρμα τῆς γενεαλογίας, διὰ τὸ ἀδελφοκτονῆσαι αὐτὸν τὸν ἀδελφόν. Εἰς τὸν τόπον δὲ τοῦ Ἄβελ ἔδωκεν ὁ θεὸς συλλαβεῖν τὴν Εὔαν καὶ τεκεῖν υἱὸν, ὃς κέκληται Σήθ· ἀφ᾿ οὗ τὸ λοιπὸν γένος τῶν ἀνθρώπων ὁδεύει μέχρι τοῦ δεῦρο. Τοῖς δὲ βουλομένοις καὶ φιλομαθέσιν καὶ περὶ πασῶν τῶν γενεῶν εὔκολόν ἐστιν ἐπιδεῖξαι διὰ τῶν ἁγίων γραφῶν. Καὶ γὰρ ἐκ μέρους ἡμῖν γεγένηται ἤδη λόγος ἐν ἑτέρῳ λόγῳ, ὡς ἐπάνω προειρήκαμεν, τῆς γενεαλογίας ἡ τάξις ἐν τῇ πρώτῃ βίβλῳ τῇ περὶ ἱστοριῶν. Ταῦτα δὲ πάντα ἡμᾶς διδάσκει τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον, τὸ διὰ Μωσέως καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν προφητῶν, ὥστε τὰ καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς τοὺς θεοσεβεῖς ἀρχαιότερα γράμματα τυγχάνει, οὐ μὴν ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀληθέστερα πάντων συγγραφέων καὶ ποιητῶν δείκνυται ὄντα.Ἀλλὰ μὴν καὶ τὰ περὶ τῆς μουσικῆς ἐφλυάρησάν τινες εὑρετὴν Ἀπόλλωνα γεγενῆσθαι· ἄλλοι δὲ Ὄρφεα ἀπὸ τῆς τῶν ὀρνέων ἡδυφωνίας φασὶν ἐξευρηκέναι τὴν μουσικήν. Κενὸς δὲ καὶ μάταιος ὁ λόγος αὐτῶν δείκνυται· μετὰ γὰρ πολλὰ ἔτη τοῦ κατακλυσμοῦ οὗτοι ἐγένοντο. Τὰ δὲ περὶ τοῦ Νῶε, ὅς κέκληται ὑπὸ ἐνίων Δευκαλίων, ἐν τῇ βίβλῳ ᾗ προειρήκαμεν ἡ διήγησις ἡμῖν γεγένηται· ᾗ, εἰ βούλει, καὶ σὺ δύνασαι ἐντυχεῖν.

excerpts.author: Theophilus of Antioch
english: Why should I go on listing the countless names and genealogies of such figures? In every respect the writers, poets, and philosophers — and even those who follow them — are deceived. They have fabricated myths and sheer foolishness about the gods they describe, failing to prove those beings are divine; instead they portray them as mere humans, some drunkards, others fornicators and murderers.

They also speak discordantly and vilely about the origin of the world. First, some declared the world uncreated, as we have already shown. Those who claim it is uncreated and eternal by nature do not speak consistently with those who assert it was created; they rely on conjecture and human reasoning, not on truth. Others, on the other hand, maintain that providence exists and then analyze their own teachings. Aratus, for instance, says: “We begin with Zeus, whom men never leave unspoken; all streets, marketplaces, seas, and harbors are full of him, and we all need him, for we are his offspring. He is gentle to humanity, extending his right hand, rousing people to work and reminding them of their livelihood, telling when the soil is best for plowing and for sowing every seed.” So whom should we trust — Aratus or Sophocles, who declares, “There is no clear providence; it is best to live as one can”? Homer disagrees, saying, “Zeus gives virtue to men and increases it.” Simonides adds, “No one obtains virtue without the gods, neither city nor mortal.” God is all‑wise; nothing exists apart from him. Euripides echoes, “There is nothing without God for men.” Menander states, “No one cares for us except God alone.” Euripides again: “When it seems good to God, he saves, providing many pretexts for salvation.” And Thesius: “If God wills, you will be saved, even if you sail on a raft.” Yet having said all this, they contradict themselves. Sophocles, speaking of divine neglect, says, “No mortal can escape the blow of God.” Moreover they have introduced a multitude of deities or even a single monarchy, and those who affirm providence have simultaneously asserted its opposite, neglect. Consequently Euripides confesses, “We strive for many things in vain, enduring troubles while knowing nothing.” Reluctantly they admit they do not know the truth, for they have been inspired and possessed by demons, and they spoke through those spirits.

The poets Homer and Hesiod, as they claim, were inspired by the Muses, yet they spoke in fantasy and error, not by a pure spirit but by deception. From this it is clearly shown that even those who are possessed by demons are sometimes exorcised in the name of the true God, and the errant spirits themselves confess they are demons who were active in those individuals at that time. Nevertheless, at times certain people, awakened in their souls, have spoken in agreement with the prophets, so that they may serve as a testimony to the prophets and to all humanity concerning the monarchy of God, his judgment, and the other matters the prophets declared.

greek: Καὶ τί μοι τὸ λοιπὸν τὸ πλῆθος τῶν τοιούτων ὀνομασιῶν καὶ γενεαλογιῶν καταλέγειν; Ὥστε κατὰ πάντα τρόπον ἐμπαίζονται οἱ συγγραφεῖς πάντες καὶ ποιηταὶ καὶ φιλόσοφοι λεγόμενοι, ἔτι μὴν καὶ οἱ προσέχοντες αὐτοῖς, Μύθους γὰρ μᾶλλον καὶ μωρίας συνέταξαν περὶ τῶν κατ᾿ αὐτοὺς θεῶν· οὐ γὰρ ἀπέδειξαν αὐτοὺς θεοὺς ἀλλὰ ἀνθρώπους, οὓς μὲν μεθύσους, ἑτέρους πόρνους καὶ φονεῖς. Ἀλλὰ καὶ περὶ τῆς κοσμογονίας ἀσύμφωνα ἀλλήλοις καὶ φαῦλα ἐξεῖπον. Πρῶτον μὲν ὅτι τινὲς ἀγένητον τὸν κόσμον ἀπεφήναντο, καθὼς καὶ ἔμπροσθεν ἐδηλώσαμεν. Καὶ οἱ μὲν ἀγένητον αὐτὸν καὶ ἀΐδιον φύσιν φάσκοντες οὐκ ἀκόλουθα εἶπον τοῖς γενητὸν αὐτὸν δογματίσασιν. Εἰκασμῷ γὰρ ταῦτα καὶ ἀνθρωπίνῃ ἐννοίᾳ ἐφθέγξαντο, καὶ οὐ κατὰ ἀλήθειαν. Ἕτεροι δ᾿ αὖ εἶπον πρόνοιαν εἶναι, καὶ τὰ τούτων δόγματα ἀνέλυσαν. Ἄρατος μὲν οὖν φησιν· Ἐκ Διὸς ἀρχώμεσθα, τὸν οὐδέποτ᾿ ἄνδρες ἐῶμεν Ἄῤῥητον· μεσταὶ δὲ Διὸς πᾶσαι μὲν ἀγυιαί, Πᾶσαι δ᾿ ἀνθρώπων ἀγοραί, μεστὴ δὲ θάλασσα Καὶ λιμένες· πάντη δὲ Διὸς κεχρήμεθα πάντες. Τοῦ γὰρ καὶ γένος ἐσμέν· ὁ δ᾿ ἤπιος ἀνθρώποισιν Δεξιὰ σημαίνει, λαοὺς δ᾿ ἐπὶ ἔργον ἐγείρει Μιμνήσκων βιότοιο· λέγει δ᾿ ὅτε βῶλος ἀρίστη Βουσί τε καὶ μακέλῃσι, λέγει δ᾿ ὅτε δεξιαὶ ὧραι Καὶ φυτὰ γυρῶσαι καὶ σπέρματα πάντα βαλέσθαι. Τίνι οὖν πιστεύσωμεν, πότερον Ἀράτῳ ἢ Σοφοκλεῖ λέγοντι Πρόνοια δ᾿ ἐστὶν οὐδενὸς [σαφής], Εἰκῆ κράτιστον ζῆν ὅπως δύναιτό τις; Ὅμηρος δὲ πάλιν τούτῳ οὐ συνᾴδει. Λέγει γάρ· Ζεὺς δ᾿ ἀρετὴν ἄνδρεσσιν ὀφέλλει τε μινύθει τε. Καὶ Σιμωνίδης· Οὔτις ἄνευ θεῶν Ἀρετὰν λάβεν, οὐ πόλις, οὐ βροτός. Θεὸς ὁ παμμῆτις· ἀπήμαντον δ᾿ οὐδὲν Ἔστιν ἐν αὐτοῖς. Ὁμοίως καὶ Εὐριπίδης· Οὐκ ἔστιν οὐδὲν χωρὶς ἀνθρώποις θεοῦ. Καὶ Μένανδρος· Οὐκ ἄρα φροντίζει τις ἡμῶν ἢ μόνος θεός. Καὶ πάλιν Εὐριπίδης· Σῶσαι γὰρ ὁπόταν τῷ θεῷ δοκῇ, Πολλὰς προφάσεις δίδωσιν εἰς σωτηρίαν. Καὶ [Θέστιος]· Θεοῦ θέλοντος σώζῃ, κἂν ἐπὶ ῥιπὸς πλέῃς. Καὶ τὰ τοιαῦτα μυρία εἰπόντες ἀσύμφωνα ἑαυτοῖς ἐξεῖπον. Ὁ γοῦν Σοφοκλῆς ἀπρονοησίαν ἐν ἑτέρῳ λέγων· Θεοῦ δὲ πληγὴν οὐχ ὑπερπηδᾷ βροτός. Πλὴν καὶ πληθὺν εἰσήγαγον ἢ καὶ μοναρχίαν εἷπον, καὶ πρόνοιαν εἶναι τοῖς λέγουσιν ἀπρονοησίαν τἀναντία εἰρήκασιν. Ὁθεν Εὐριπίδης ὁμολογεῖ λέγων· Σπουδάζομεν δὲ πολλ᾿ ὑπ᾿ ἐλπίδων, μάτην Πόνους ἔχοντες, οὐδὲν εἰδότες. Καὶ μὴ θέλοντες ὁμολογοῦσιν τὸ ἀληθὲς μὴ ἐπίστασθαι· ὑπὸ δαιμόνων δὲ ἐμπνευσθέντες καὶ ὑπ᾿ αὐτῶν φυσιωθέντες ἃ εἶπον δι᾿ αὐτῶν εἶπον. Ἤτοι γὰρ οἱ ποιηταί, Ὅμηρος δὴ καὶ Ἡσίοδος, ὥς φασιν ὑπὸ Μουσῶν ἐμπνευσθέντες, φαντασίᾳ καὶ πλάνῃ ἐλάλησαν, καὶ οὐ καθαρῷ πνεύματι ἀλλὰ πλάνῳ. Ἐκ τούτου δὲ σαφῶς δείκνυται, εἰ καὶ οἱ δαιμονῶντες ἐνίοτε καὶ μέχρι τοῦ δεῦρο ἐξορκίζονται κατὰ τοῦ ὀνόματος τοῦ ὄντως θεοῦ, καὶ ὁμολογεῖ αὐτὰ τὰ πλάνα πνεύματα εἶναι δαίμονες, οἱ καὶ τότε εἰς ἐκείνους ἐνεργήσαντες· πλὴν ἐνίοτέ τινες τῇ ψυχῇ ἐκνήψαντες ἐξ αὐτῶν εἶπον ἀκόλουθα τοῖς προφήταις, ὅπως εἰς μαρτύριον αὐτοῖς τε καὶ πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις, περί τε θεοῦ μοναρχίας καὶ κρίσεως καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν ὧν ἔφασαν.

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: It is entirely reasonable that the divinely inspired apostle declares the mystery was made known to him by revelation, just as he wrote briefly, so that when you read it you may grasp his insight into the mystery of Christ (Ephesians 3:3-4). That mystery was not disclosed to the sons of men in earlier generations, but it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets (Ephesians 3:5). There is indeed a perfection of knowledge, and concerning it he writes to the Colossians: "We have not ceased praying for you and asking that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding, so that you may walk worthily of the Lord, fully pleasing to him, bearing fruit in every good work and growing in the knowledge of God, being strengthened with all power according to the might of his glory" (Colossians 1:9-10). Again, in line with the stewardship of God entrusted to me for your sake, he says he became a minister to fulfill the word of God — the mystery hidden from the ages and from generations, but now made manifest to his saints, to whom God chose to make known the riches of the glory of this mystery among the nations (Colossians 1:25-27).

Thus other mysteries that were concealed until the apostles and then handed down by them as received from the Lord — hidden in the Old Covenant — have now been revealed to the saints; but the riches of the glory of the mystery among the nations is something different: it is the faith and hope that rest on Christ, whom he elsewhere calls the foundation (1 Corinthians 3:11). Once more, as if eager to display this knowledge, he writes: "We admonish everyone with all wisdom, that we may present everyone mature in Christ" (Colossians 1:28). He does not mean every person without distinction, for then no one would be an unbeliever; nor does he mean that every believer is already mature in Christ. Rather, by "every person" he means, so to speak, the whole person — purified in body and soul. Since not everyone possesses this knowledge, he adds explicitly that they are "knit together in love, and to all the riches of the full assurance of understanding, to the knowledge of the mystery of God, namely Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Colossians 2:2-3).

"Continue steadfastly in prayer, being watchful in it with thanksgiving" (Colossians 4:2); and thanksgiving is offered not only for the soul and spiritual blessings, but also for the body and the goods of the body. He makes it even clearer that not everyone possesses this knowledge when he adds: "At the same time, pray also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, to declare the mystery of Christ, on account of which I am in prison — that I may make it clear, as I ought to speak" (Colossians 4:3-4). For there were certain things handed down without writing. At once, to the Hebrews he says: since they ought to be teachers by reason of time, they have become, as it were, aged in the Old Covenant; yet you have need again for someone to teach you the elementary principles of the oracles of God, and you have become those who need milk and not solid food (Hebrews 5:12).

greek: Εἰκότως ἄρα ὁ θεσπέσιος ἀπόστολος κατὰ ἀποκάλυψιν φησὶν ἐγνωρίσθη μοι τὸ μυστήριον, καθὼς προέγραψα ἐν ὀλίγῳ, πρὸς ὃ δύνασθε ἀναγινώσκοντες νοῆσαι τὴν σύνεσίν μου ἐν τῷ μυστηρίῳ τοῦ Χριστοῦ, ὃ ἑτέραις γενεαῖς οὐκ ἐγνωρίσθη τοῖς υἱοῖς τῶν ἀνθρώπων, ὡς νῦν ἀπεκαλύφθη τοῖς ἁγίοις ἀποστόλοις αὐτοῦ καὶ προφήταις. ἔστιν γάρ τις καὶ τελείων μάθησις, περὶ ἧς πρὸς τοὺς Κολοσσαεῖς γράφων φησίν· οὐ παυόμεθα ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν προσευχόμενοι καὶ αἰτούμενοι, ἵνα πληρωθῆτε τὴν ἐπίγνωσιν τοῦ θελήματος αὐτοῦ ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ καὶ συνέσει πνευματικῇ, περιπατῆσαι ἀξίως τοῦ κυρίου εἰς πᾶσαν ἀρέσκειαν, παντὶ ἔργῳ ἀγαθῷ καρποφοροῦντες καὶ αὐξανόμενοι τῇ ἐπιγνώσει τοῦ θεοῦ, ἐν πάσῃ δυνάμει ἐνδυναμούμενοι κατὰ τὸ κράτος τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ. καὶ πάλιν κατὰ τὴν οἰκονομίαν τοῦ θεοῦ τὴν δοθεῖσάν μοι φησὶν εἰς ὑμᾶς πληρῶσαι τὸν λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ, τὸ μυστήριον τὸ ἀποκεκρυμμένον ἀπὸ τῶν αἰώνων καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν γενεῶν, ὃ νῦν ἐφανερώθη τοῖς ἁγίοις αὐτοῦ, οἷς ἠθέλησεν ὁ θεὸς γνωρίσαι, τί τὸ πλοῦτος τῆς δόξης τοῦ μυστηρίου τούτου ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν. ὥστε ἄλλα μὲν τὰ μυστήρια τὰ ἀποκεκρυμμένα ἄχρι τῶν ἀποστόλων καὶ ὑπ’ αὐτῶν παραδοθέντα ὡς ἀπὸ τοῦ κυρίου παρειλήφασιν (ἀποκεκρυμμένα δὲ ἐν τῇ παλαιᾷ διαθήκῃ), ἃ νῦν ἐφανερώθη τοῖς ἁγίοις, ἄλλο δὲ τὸ πλοῦτος τῆς δόξης τοῦ μυστηρίου τοῦ ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν, ὅ ἐστιν ἡ πίστις καὶ ἡ ἐλπὶς ἡ εἰς Χριστόν, ὃν ἀλλαχῇ θεμέλιον εἴρηκεν. καὶ πάλιν οἷον φιλοτιμούμενος ἐμφῆναι τὴν γνῶσιν ὧδέ πως γράφει· νουθετοῦντες πάντα ἄνθρωπον ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ, ἵνα παραστήσωμεν πάντα ἄνθρωπον τέλειον ἐν Χριστῷ· οὐ πάντα ἁπλῶς ἄνθρωπον, ἐπεὶ οὐδεὶς ἂν ἦν ἄπιστος, οὐδὲ μὴν πάντα τὸν πιστεύοντα τέλειον ἐν Χριστῷ, ἀλλὰ πάντα ἄνθρωπον λέγει, ὡς εἰπεῖν ὅλον τὸν ἄνθρωπον, οἷον σώματι καὶ ψυχῇ ἡγνισμένον, ἐπεί, ὅτι οὐ πάντων ἡ γνῶσις, διαρρήδην ἐπιφέρει· συμβιβασθέντες ἐν ἀγάπῃ καὶ εἰς πᾶν πλοῦτος τῆς πληροφορίας τῆς συνέσεως, εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν τοῦ μυστηρίου τοῦ θεοῦ ἐν Χριστῷ, ἐν ᾧ εἰσι πάντες οἱ θησαυροὶ τῆς σοφίας καὶ τῆς γνώσεως ἀπόκρυφοι. τῇ προσευχῇ προσκαρτερεῖτε, γρηγοροῦντες ἐν αὐτῇ ἐν εὐχαριστίᾳ· ἡ εὐχαριστία δὲ οὐκ ἐπὶ ψυχῆς μόνον καὶ τῶν πνευματικῶν ἀγαθῶν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ σώματος γίνεται καὶ τῶν τοῦ σώματος ἀγαθῶν. καὶ ἔτι σαφέστερον ἐκκαλύπτει τὸ μὴ πάντων εἶναι τὴν γνῶσιν, ἐπιλέγων· προσευχόμενοι ἅμα καὶ περὶ ἡμῶν, ἵνα ὁ θεὸς ἀνοίξῃ ἡμῖν θύραν τοῦ λαλῆσαι τὸ μυστήριον τοῦ Χριστοῦ, δἰ ὃ καὶ δέδεμαι, ἵνα φανερώσω αὐτὸ ὡς δεῖ με λαλῆσαι. ἦν γάρ τινα ἀγράφως παραδιδόμενα. αὐτίκα τοῖς Ἑβραίοις καὶ γὰρ ὀφείλοντες εἶναι διδάσκαλοι διὰ τὸν χρόνον φησίν, ὡς ἂν ἐγγηράσαντες τῇ διαθήκῃ τῇ παλαιᾷ, πάλιν χρείαν ἔχετε τοῦ διδάσκειν ὑμᾶς, τίνα τὰ στοιχεῖα τῆς ἀρχῆς τῶν λογίων τοῦ θεοῦ, καὶ γεγόνατε χρείαν ἔχοντες γάλακτος καὶ οὐ στερεᾶς τροφῆς·

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: Everything, then, which falls under a name, is originated, whether they will or not. Whether, then, the Father Himself draws to Himself everyone who has led a pure life, and has reached the conception of the blessed and incorruptible nature; or whether the free-will which is in us, by reaching the knowledge of the good , leaps and bounds over the barriers, as the gymnasts say; yet it is not without eminent grace that the soul is winged, and soars, and is raised above the higher spheres, laying aside all that is heavy, and surrendering itself to its kindred element. Plato , too, in Meno , says that virtue is God-given, as the following expressions show: From this argument then, O Meno, virtue is shown to come to those, in whom it is found, by divine providence .

Does it not then appear that the gnostic disposition which has come to all is enigmatically called divine providence ? And he adds more explicitly: If, then, in this whole treatise we have investigated well, it results that virtue is neither by nature, nor is it taught, but is produced by divine providence , not without intelligence, in those in whom it is found. Wisdom which is God-given, as being the power of the Father , rouses indeed our free-will , and admits faith , and repays the application of the elect with its crowning fellowship. And now I will adduce Plato himself, who clearly deems it fit to believe the children of God . For, discoursing on gods that are visible and born, in Timæus , he says: But to speak of the other demons , and to know their birth, is too much for us.

But we must credit those who have formerly spoken, they being the offspring of the gods, as they said, and knowing well their progenitors, although they speak without probable and necessary proofs . I do not think it possible that clearer testimony could be borne by the Greeks, that our Saviour, and those anointed to prophesy (the latter being called the sons of God , and the Lord being His own Son), are the true witnesses respecting divine things. Wherefore also they ought to be believed , being inspired, he added. And were one to say in a more tragic vein, that we ought not to believe , For it was not Zeus that told me these things, yet let him know that it was God Himself that promulgated the Scriptures by His Son . And he, who announces what is his own, is to be believed .

No one, says the Lord, has known the Father but the Son , and he to whom the Son shall reveal Him. Matthew 11:27 ; Luke 10:22 This, then, is to be believed , according to Plato , though it is announced and spoken without probable and necessary proofs , but in the Old and New Testament . For unless you believe , says the Lord, you shall die in your sins . John 8:24 And again: He that believes has everlasting life. Blessed are all they that put their trust in Him. For trusting is more than faith . For when one has believed that the Son of God is our teacher, he trusts that his teaching is true . And as instruction, according to Empedocles, makes the mind grow, so trust in the Lord makes faith grow.

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: The next step is to return what is owed and to expose more clearly the Greek appropriation of barbarian philosophy. The Stoics declare that God is a body and spirit in essence, just as they regard the soul. You will find all these points stated plainly in the scriptures. Do not mistake their allegories for the truth that the gnosis now delivers; if they indicate something else, they do so in the way ancient sages hint at one thing while meaning another. The Stoics claim that God permeates every essence, but we call Him only the Creator — the Creator by His Word. They were led astray by the saying in Wisdom: "He permeates and extends through all things because of purity," since they did not understand that these words refer to the primal Wisdom created by God. "Yes," they object, "but the philosophers posit matter among the first principles — Stoics, Plato, Pythagoras, and even Aristotle the Peripatetic — not a single principle." Let them recognize, then, that this so-called matter is described by them as unqualified and unformed, and that Plato goes even further and says it does not exist. And in the Timaeus, knowing the one truly existing principle, he speaks of it in those very words. For now, let our position stand thus: whether there is one first principle or many, or whatever one supposes about them, we must not discuss it now — not for any other reason than that it is difficult to set forth the apparent truths in our present mode of exposition. Besides, the prophetic word, "the earth was invisible and unformed" (Genesis 1:2), supplied them with the raw material for a doctrine of material substance. Epicurus, failing to follow the text, slipped in the notion of the automatic and so arrived at "vanity of vanities, all is vanity." Aristotle, drawing from the psalm, "Lord, your mercy is in the heavens, and your truth reaches to the clouds" (Psalm 36:5), brought providence down only as far as the moon. For the revelation of the prophetic mysteries had not yet been unveiled before the Lord's coming. And the punishments after death, the punishment by fire, the whole poetic tradition of the Muses, and indeed Greek philosophy itself, all drew their origin from barbarian philosophy.

greek: τὰ δ’ ἑξῆς προςαποδοτέον καὶ τὴν ἐκ τῆς βαρβάρου φιλοσοφίας Ελληνικὴν κλοπὴν σαφέστερον ἤδη παραστατέον. Φασὶ γὰρ σῶμα εἶναι τὸν θεὸν οἱ Στωϊκοὶ καὶ πνεῦμα κατ’ οὐσίαν, ὥσπερ ἀμέλει καὶ τὴν ψυχήν. πάντα ταῦτα ἄντικρυς εὑρήσεις ἐν ταῖς γραφαῖς. μὴ γάρ μοι τὰς ἀλληγορίας αὐτῶν ἐννοήσῃς τὰ νῦν ὡς ἡ γνωστικὴ παραδίδωσιν ἀλήθεια, εἰ ἄλλο τι δεικνύουσαι, καθάπερ οἱ σοφοὶ παλαισταί, ἄλλο μηνύουσιν. ἀλλ’ οἳ μὲν διήκειν διὰ πάσης τῆς οὐσίας τὸν θεόν φασιν, ἡμεῖς δὲ ποιητὴν μόνον αὐτὸν καλοῦμεν καὶ λόγῳ ποιητήν. παρήγαγεν δὲ αὐτοὺς τὸ ἐν τῇ Σοφίᾳ εἰρημένον διήκει δὲ καὶ χωρεῖ διὰ πάντων διὰ τὴν καθαριότητα, ἐπεὶ μὴ συνῆκαν λέγεσθαι ταῦτα ἐπὶ τῆς σοφίας τῆς πρωτοκτίστου τῷ θεῷ. ναί, φασίν, ἀλλὰ ὕλην ὑποτίθενται οἱ φιλόσοφοι ἐν ταῖς ἀρχαῖς, οἵ τε Στωϊκοὶ καὶ Πλάτων καὶ Πυθαγόρας, ἀλλὰ καὶ Ἀριστοτέλης ὁ Περιπατητικός, οὐχὶ δὲ μίαν ἀρχήν. ἴστωσαν οὖν τὴν καλουμένην ὕλην ἄποιον καὶ ἀσχημάτιστον λεγομένην πρὸς αὐτῶν, καὶ τολμηρότερον ἤδη μὴ ὂν πρὸς τοῦ Πλάτωνος εἰρῆσθαι. καὶ μή τι μυστικώτατα μίαν τὴν ὄντως οὖσαν ἀρχὴν εἰδὼς ἐν τῷ Τιμαίῳ αὐταῖς φησι λέξεσιν· νῦν δ’ οὖν τὸ παρ’ ἡμῶν ὧδε ἐχέτω· τὴν μὲν περὶ πάντων εἴτε ἀρχὴν εἴτε ἀρχὰς εἴτε ὅπῃ δοκεῖ τούτων πέρι, τὸ νῦν οὐ ῥητέον, δἰ ἄλλο μὲν οὐδέν, διὰ δὲ τὸ χαλεπὸν εἶναι κατὰ τὸν παρόντα τρόπον τῆς διεξόδου δηλῶσαι τὰ δοκοῦντα. ἄλλως τε ἡ λέξις ἡ προφητικὴ ἐκείνη ἡ δὲ γῆ ἦν ἀόρατος καὶ ἀκατασκεύαστος ἀφορμὰς αὐτοῖς ὑλικῆς οὐσίας παρέσχηται. Ναὶ μὴν Ἐπικούρῳ μὲν ἡ τοῦ αὐτομάτου παρείσδυσις οὐ παρακολουθήσαντι τῷ ῥητῷ γέγονεν ἐντεῦθεν ματαιότης ματαιοτήτων, τὰ πάντα ματαιότης. Ἀριστοτέλει δὲ μέχρι σελήνης ἐπῆλθε καταγαγεῖν τὴν πρόνοιαν ἐκ τοῦδε τοῦ ψαλμοῦ· κύριε, ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ τὸ ἔλεός σου καὶ ἡ ἀλήθειά σου ἕως τῶν νεφελῶν. οὐδέπω γὰρ ἀποκεκάλυπτο ἡ τῶν προφητικῶν δήλωσις μυστηρίων πρὸ τῆς τοῦ κυρίου παρουσίας. Τάς τε αὖ μετὰ θάνατον κολάσεις καὶ τὴν διὰ πυρὸς τιμωρίαν ἀπὸ τῆς βαρβάρου φιλοσοφίας ἥ τε ποιητικὴ πᾶσα μοῦσα, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡ Ἑλληνικὴ φιλοσοφία ὑφείλετο.

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: Barbarians are the discoverers not only of philosophy but of almost every art. The Egyptians, for instance, were the first to bring astrology to humankind, and the Chaldeans did the same. They also showed how to burn lamps, divided the year into twelve months, forbade women from having intercourse in temples, and legislated that no one who had lain with a woman could enter a temple without first being purified. The Egyptians discovered geometry as well. Some claim the Carians were the first to conceive knowledge of the stars; the Phrygians first observed the flights of birds, and the Tyrrhenians, neighbors of Italy, refined sacrificial divination. The Isaurians and Arabs worked on divination by birds, just as the Telmisseans did by dreams. The Tyrrhenians invented the trumpet, the Phrygians the aulos—for Olympus and Marsyas were Phrygians. Cadmus the Phoenician discovered letters for the Greeks, as Ephorus says; from this Herodotus writes that the letters are called Phoenician, though others say the Phoenicians and Syrians invented them first. Concerning medicine, they say Apis, an Egyptian native, practiced it before Io arrived in Egypt, and afterwards Asclepius developed the art. Atlas the Libyan first built a ship and sailed the sea. Celmis and Damnameneus, Idaean Dactyls, first found iron in Cyprus, and another Idaean, Delas, discovered the mixture of copper—Hesiod says a Scythian did. The Thracians first discovered the so-called harpe (a curved sword) and first used peltae on horseback; similarly, the Illyrians invented the parma. The Tuscans are said to have invented modeling, and Itanos the Saunite first constructed a shield. Cadmus the Phoenician discovered stoneworking and conceived the gold mines around Mount Pangaion. The Cappadocians first discovered the nabla, just as the Assyrians the dichord. The Carthaginians built the first quadrireme, and Bosporus constructed it without a model. Medea, daughter of Aeetes of Colchis, first conceived hair dye. The Noropes, a Paeonian nation now called Noricans, first worked copper and refined iron. Amycus, king of the Bebrycians, first discovered boxing gloves. In music, Olympus the Mysian developed the Lydian harmony; the Troglodytes discovered the sambuca, a musical instrument. They say the Phrygian Satyr found the plagal syrinx, and Agnis, also a Phrygian, the trichord and diatonic harmony. Olympus the Phrygian discovered the croumata, as did Marsyas from the same region the Phrygian, mixophrygian, and mixolydian harmonies. Thamyris the Thracian first conceived the Dorian harmony. We have heard the Persians first made the wagon, bed, and footstool, and the Sidonians first built the trireme. The Sicilians near Italy first discovered the phorminx (not far from the cithara) and invented crotala. They record that fine linen garments were discovered under the Egyptian queen Semiramis; Hellanicus says Atossa, queen of the Persians, first composed letters. Scamon of Mytilene, Theophrastus of Eresus, Cydippus of Mantinea, Antiphones, Aristodemus, Aristotle, Philostephanus, and Strato the Peripatetic recorded these things in their works on inventions. I have cited a few of their discoveries to demonstrate the inventive and beneficial character of barbarian culture, from which Greeks have profited in their pursuits. If anyone maligns the barbarian tongue, Anacharsis says to me, "All Greeks speak Scythian." He was the man admired among Greeks for saying his cloak was a sheepskin, his dinner milk, his dessert cheese. You see that barbarian philosophy promises deeds, not words. The apostle likewise says: "If you do not speak intelligible words with your tongue, how will what is spoken be known? For you will be speaking into the air" (1 Corinthians 14:9). There are so many kinds of voices in the world, and none is without sound; if I do not know the force of a voice, I shall be a barbarian to the speaker and the speaker a barbarian to me. Let the one who speaks in a tongue pray that he may interpret. The teaching of discourse and writing came to the Greeks late. Alcmaeon son of Perithous of Croton first wrote a treatise on nature; they say Anaxagoras son of Hegesibulus of Clazomenae first published a book in writing. Terpander of Antissa first set poems to melody and put the Spartan laws into song; Lasus of Hermione invented the dithyramb; Stesichorus of Himera the hymn; Alcman of Sparta choral song; Anacreon of Teos erotic song. Pindar of Thebes first composed a nomos; Timotheus of Miletus first sang a nomos with chorus and cithara. Archilochus of Paros invented the iambic, Hipponax of Ephesus the limping iambic; Thespis of Athens tragedy; Susarion of Icaria comedy. Grammarians' pupils hand down the dates of these men, but to list them accurately would be long—especially since Dionysus, through whom the Dionysian festivals arose, is later than Moses. Some say Phanotea wife of Icarus discovered the hexameter; others say Themis, one of the Titanides. Didymus, in his work on Pythagorean philosophy, records that Theano of Croton was the first woman to philosophize and write poems. Greek philosophy, as some hold, follows truth but only in part and dimly; others say it derives its impulse from the devil; some suppose certain inspired powers gave rise to all philosophy. Yet even if Greek philosophy does not grasp the full magnitude of truth and still fails in keeping the Lord's commandments, it nevertheless prepares the way for the most royal teaching, in some measure making men sober, shaping their character, and fitting them to receive the truth—those who glorify providence.

greek: Οὐ μόνης δὲ φιλοσοφίας, ἀλλὰ καὶ πάσης σχεδὸν τέχνης εὑρεταὶ βάρβαροι. Αἰγύπτιοι γοῦν πρῶτοι ἀστρολογίαν εἰς ἀνθρώπους ἐξήνεγκαν, ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ Χαλδαῖοι. Αἰγύπτιοι λύχνους τε αὖ καίειν πρῶτοι κατέδειξαν καὶ τὸν ἐνιαυτὸν εἰς δώδεκα μῆνας διεῖλον καὶ ἐν ἱεροῖς μίσγεσθαι γυναιξὶν ἐκώλυσαν μηδ’ εἰς ἱερὰ εἰσιέναι ἀπὸ γυναικὸς ἀλούτους ἐνομοθέτησαν γεωμετρίας τε αὖ εὑρεταὶ οἱ αὐτοὶ γεγόνασιν. εἰσὶν δὲ οἳ Κᾶρας οἳ τὴν δἰ ἀστέρων πρόγνωσιν ἐπινενοηκέναι λέγουσιν. πτήσεις δὲ ὀρνίθων παρεφυλάξαντο πρῶτοι Φρύγες, καὶ θυτικὴν ἠκρίβωσαν Τοῦσκοι, Ἰταλίας γείτονες. Ἴσαυροι δὲ καὶ Ἄραβες ἐξεπόνησαν τὴν οἰωνιστικήν, ὥσπερ ἀμέλει Τελμισεῖς τὴν δἰ ὀνείρων μαντικήν. Τυρρηνοὶ δὲ σάλπιγγα ἐπενόησαν καὶ Φρύγες αὐλόν· Φρύγες γὰρ ἤστην Ὄλυμπός τε καὶ Μαρσύας. Κάδμος δὲ Φοῖνιξ ἦν ὁ τῶν γραμμάτων Ἕλλησιν εὑρετής, ὥς φησιν Ἔφορος, ὅθεν καὶ Φοινικήια τὰ γράμματα Ἡρόδοτος κεκλῆσθαι γράφει· οἳ δὲ Φοίνικας καὶ Σύρους γράμματα ἐπινοῆσαι πρώτους λέγουσιν. ἰατρικὴν δὲ Ἆπιν Αἰγύπτιον αὐτόχθονα πρὶν εἰς Αἴγυπτον ἀφικέσθαι τὴν Ἰώ, μετὰ δὲ ταῦτα Ἀσκληπιὸν τὴν τέχνην αὐξῆσαι λέγουσιν. Ἄτλας δὲ ὁ Λίβυς πρῶτος ναῦν ἐναυπηγήσατο καὶ τὴν θάλασσαν ἔπλευσεν. Κέλμις τε αὖ καὶ Δαμναμενεὺς οἱ τῶν Ἰδαίων δάκτυλοι πρῶτοι σίδηρον εὗρον ἐν Κύπρῳ, Δέλας δὲ ἄλλος Ἰδαῖος εὗρε χαλκοῦ κρᾶσιν, ὡς δὲ Ἡσίοδος, Σκύθης. ναὶ μὴν Θρᾷκες πρῶτοι τὴν καλουμένην ἅρπην εὗρον (ἔστι δὲ μάχαιρα καρπύλη) καὶ πρῶτοι πέλταις ἐπὶ τῶν ἵππων ἐχρήσαντο. ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ Ἰλλυριοὶ τὴν καλουμένην πάρμην ἐξεῦρον. ἔτι φασὶ Τουσκανοὺς πλαστικὴν ἐπινοῆσαι, Ἴτανόν τε ̔Σαυνίτης οὗτος ἦν’ πρῶτον θυρεὸν κατασκευάσαι. Κάδμος γὰρ ὁ Φοῖνιξ λιθοτομίαν ἐξεῦρεν καὶ μέταλλα χρυσοῦ τὰ περὶ τὸ Πάγγαιον ἐπενόησεν ὄρος. ἤδη δὲ καὶ ἄλλο ἔθνος Καππάδοκες πρῶτοι εὗρον τὸν νάβλαν καλούμενον, ὅν τρόπον καὶ τὸ δίχορδον Ἀσσύριοι. Καρχηδόνιοι γὰρ πρῶτοι τετρήρη κατεσκεύασαν, ἐναυπήγησε δὲ αὐτὴν Βόσπορος αὐτοσχέδιον. Μήδειά τε ἡ Αἰήτου ἡ Κολχὶς πρώτη βαφὴν τριχῶν ἐπενόησεν. ἀλλὰ καὶ Νώροπες (ἔθνος ἐστὶ Παιονικόν, νῦν δὲ Νωρικὸν καλοῦνται) κατειργάσαντο χαλκὸν καὶ σίδηρον ἐκάθηραν πρῶτοι. Ἄμυκός τε ὁ Βεβρύκων βασιλεὺς ἱμάντας πυκτικοὺς πρῶτος εὗρεν. περί τε μουσικὴν Ὄλυμπος ὁ Μυσὸς τὴν Λύδιον ἁρμονίαν ἐφιλοτέχνησεν· οἵ τε Τρωγλοδύται καλούμενοι σαμβύκην εὗρον, ὄργανον μουσικόν. φασὶ δὲ καὶ τὴν πλαγίαν σύριγγα Σάτυρον εὑρεῖν τὸν Φρύγα· τρίχορδον δὲ ὁμοίως καὶ τὴν διάτονον ἁρμονίαν Ἄγνιν τὸν καὶ αὐτὸν Φρύγα· κρούματα δὲ Ὄλυμπον ὁμοίως τὸν Φρύγα, καθάπερ Φρύγιον ἁρμονίαν καὶ μιξοφρύγιον καὶ μιξολύδιον Μαρσύαν, τῆς αὐτῆς ὄντα τοῖς προειρημένοις χώρας, καὶ τὴν Δώριον Θάμυριν ἐπινοῆσαι τὸν Θρᾷκα. Πέρσας τε πρώτους ἀκηκόαμεν ἀπήνην καὶ κλίνην καὶ ὑποπόδιον ἐργάσασθαι τούς τε Σιδονίους τρίκροτον ναῦν κατασκευάσαι. Σικελοί τε οἱ πρὸς τῇ Ἰταλίᾳ πρῶτοι φόρμιγγα εὗρον οὐ πολὺ τῆς κιθάρας λειπομένην καὶ κρόταλα ἐπενόησαν. ἐπί τε † Σεμιράμεως βασιλέως Αἰγυπτίων τὰ βύσσινα ἱμάτια εὑρῆσθαι ἱστοροῦσιν. καὶ πρώτην ἐπιστολὰς συντάξαι Ἄτοσσαν τὴν Περσῶν βασιλεύσασάν φησιν Ἑλλάνικος. Σκάμων μὲν οὖν ὁ Μιτυληναῖος καὶ Θεόφραστος ὁ Ἐρέσιος Κύδιππός τε ὁ Μαντινεύς, ἔτι τε Ἀντιφάνης καὶ Ἀριστόδημος καὶ Ἀριστοτέλης, πρὸς τούτοις δὲ Φιλοστέφανος, ἀλλὰ καὶ Στράτων ὁ περιπατητικὸς ἐν τοῖς Περὶ εὑρημάτων ταῦτα ἱστόρησαν. παρεθέμην δὲ αὐτῶν ὀλίγα εἰς σύστασιν τῆς παρὰ βαρβάροις εὑρετικῆς καὶ βιωφελοῦς φύσεως, παρ’ ὧν Ἕλληνες τὰ ἐπιτηδεύματα ὠφέληνται. Εἰ δέ τις τὴν φωνὴν διαβάλλει τὴν βάρβαρον, ἐμοὶ δέ, φησὶν ὁ Ἀνάχαρσις, πάντες Ἕλληνες σκυθίζουσιν. οὗτος ἦν ὁ παρ’ Ἕλλησι θαυμασθεὶς ὁ φήσας ἐμοὶ περίβλημα χλαῖνα, δεῖπνον γάλα, τυρός. ὁρᾷς φιλοσοφίαν βάρβαρον ἔργα ἐπαγγελλομένην, οὐ λόγους. ὁ δὲ ἀπόστολος οὕτω φησὶν καὶ ὑμεῖς διὰ τῆς γλώσσης ἐὰν μὴ εὔσημον λόγον δῶτε, πῶς γνωσθήσεται τὸ λαλούμενον; ἔσεσθε γὰρ εἰς ἀέρα λαλοῦντες. τοσαῦτα, εἰ τύχοι, γένη φωνῶν εἰσιν ἐν κόσμῳ, καὶ οὐδὲν ἄφωνον· ἐὰν οὖν μὴ εἰδῶ τὴν δύναμιν τῆς φωνῆς, ἔσομαι τῷ λαλοῦντι βάρβαρος καὶ ὁ λαλῶν ἐμοὶ βάρβαρος. καὶ ὁ λαλῶν γλώσσῃ προσευχέσθω, ἵνα διερμηνεύῃ. Ναὶ μὴν ὀψέ ποτε εἰς Ἕλληνας ἡ τῶν λόγων παρῆλθε διδασκαλία τε καὶ γραφή. Ἀλκμαίων γοῦν Περίθου Κροτωνιάτης πρῶτος φυσικὸν λόγον συνέταξεν. οἳ δὲ Ἀναξαγόραν Ἡγησιβούλου Κλαζομένιον πρῶτον διὰ γραφῆς ἐκδοῦναι βιβλίον ἱστοροῦσιν. μέλος τε αὖ πρῶτος περιέθηκε τοῖς ποιήμασι καὶ τοὺς Λακεδαιμονίων νόμους ἐμελοποίησε Τέρπανδρος ὁ Ἀντισσαῖος, διθύραμβον δὲ ἐπενόησεν Λᾶσος Ἑρμιονεύς, ὕμνον Στησίχορος Ἱμεραῖος, χορείαν Ἀλκμὰν Λακεδαιμόνιος, τὰ ἐρωτικὰ Ἀνακρέων Τήιος. ὑπόρχησιν Πίνδαρος Θηβαῖος νόμους τε πρῶτος ᾖσεν ἐν χορῷ καὶ κιθάρᾳ Τιμόθεος ὁ Μιλήσιος. ναὶ μὴν ἴαμβον μὲν ἐπενόησεν Ἀρχίλοχος ὁ Πάριος, χωλὸν δὲ ἴαμβον Ἱππῶναξ ὁ Ἐφέσιος, καὶ τραγῳδίαν μὲν Θέσπις ὁ Ἀθηναῖος, κωμῳδίαν δὲ Σουσαρίων ὁ Ἰκαριεύς. τοὺς χρόνους τούτων παῖδες παραδιδόασι γραμματικῶν, μακρὸν δ’ ἂν εἴη τούτους ἀκριβολογούμενον παραθέσθαι αὐτοῦ δεικνυμένου τοῦ Διονύσου, δἰ ὃν καὶ Διονυσιακαὶ θέαι, μεταγενεστέρου Μωυσέως ἢ αὐτίκα μάλα. φασὶ δὲ καὶ τοὺς κατὰ διατριβὴν λόγους καὶ τὰ ῥητορικὰ ἰδιώματα εὑρεῖν καὶ μισθοῦ συνηγορῆσαι πρῶτον δικανικὸν λόγου εἰς ἔκδοσιν γραψάμενον Ἀντιφῶντα Σωφίλον Ῥαμνούσιον, ὥς φησι Διόδωρος, Ἀπολλόδωρος δὲ ὁ Κυμαῖος πρῶτος τοῦ γραμματικοῦ ἀντὶ τοῦ κριτικοῦ εἰσηγήσατο τοὔνομα καὶ γραμματικὸς προσηγορεύθη, ἔνιοι δὲ Ἐρατοσθένη τὸν Κυρηναῖόν φασιν, ἐπειδὴ ἐξέδωκεν οὗτος βιβλία δύο γραμματικὰ ἐπιγράψας. ὠνομάσθη δὲ γραμματικός, ὡς νῦν ὀνομάζομεν, πρῶτος Πραξιφάνης Διονυσοφάνους Μιτυληναῖος. Ζάλευκός τε ὁ Λοκρὸς πρῶτος ἱστόρηται νόμους θέσθαι, οἳ δὲ Μίνω τὸν Διὸς ἐπὶ Λυγκέως. οὗτος μετὰ Δαναὸν γίνεται ἑνδεκάτῃ ἄνωθεν ἀπὸ Ἰνάχου καὶ Μωσέως γενεᾷ, ὡς ὀλίγον ὑποβάντες δείξομεν. Λυκοῦργος δὲ μετὰ πολλὰ τῆς Ἰλίου ἁλώσεως γεγονὼς ἔτη πρὸ τῶν ὀλυμπιάδων ἔτεσιν ἑκατὸν πεντήκοντα νομοθετεῖ Λακεδαιμονίοις· Σόλωνος γὰρ τοὺς χρόνους προειρήκαμεν. Δράκων δὲ ὁ καὶ αὐτὸς νομοθέτης περὶ τὴν τριακοστὴν καὶ ἐνάτην ὀλυμπιάδα γεγονὼς εὑρίσκεται. Ἀντίλοχος δὲ αὖ ὁ τοὺς ἵστορας πραγματευσάμενος ἀπὸ τῆς Πυθαγόρου ἡλικίας ἐπὶ τὴν Ἐπικούρου τελευτήν, γαμηλιῶνος δὲ δεκάτῃ ἱσταμένου γενομένην. ἔτη φέρει τὰ πάντα τριακόσια δώδεκα. ἔτι φασὶ τὸ ἡρῷον τὸ ἑξάμετρον Φανοθέαν τὴν γυναῖκα Ἰκαρίου, οἳ δὲ Θέμιν μίαν τῶν Τιτανίδων εὑρεῖν. Δίδυμος δ’ ἐν τῷ περὶ Πυθαγορικῆς φιλοσοφίας Θεανὼ τὴν Κροτωνιᾶτιν πρώτην γυναικῶν φιλοσοφῆσαι καὶ ποιήματα γράψαι ἱστορεῖ. Ἡ μὲν οὖν Ἑλληνικὴ φιλοσοφία, ὡς μέν τινες, κατὰ περίπτωσιν ἐπήβολος τῆς ἀληθείας ἁμῇ γέ πῃ, ἀμυδρῶς δὲ καὶ οὐ πάσης, γίνεται· ὡς δὲ ἄλλοι βούλονται, ἐκ τοῦ διαβόλου τὴν κίνησιν ἴσχει. ἔνιοι δὲ δυνάμεις τινὰς ὑποβεβηκυίας ἐμπνεῦσαι τὴν πᾶσαν φιλοσοφίαν ὑπειλήφασιν. ἀλλ’ εἰ καὶ μὴ καταλαμβάνει ἡ Ἑλληνικὴ φιλοσοφία τὸ μέγεθος τῆς ἀληθείας, ἔτι δὲ ἐξασθενεῖ πράττειν τὰς κυριακὰς ἐντολάς, ἀλλ’ οὖν γε προκατασκευάζει τὴν ὁδὸν τῇ βασιλικωτάτῃ διδασκαλίᾳ, ἁμῇ γέ πῃ σωφρονίζουσα καὶ τὸ ἦθος προτυποῦσα καὶ προστύφουσα εἰς παραδοχὴν τῆς ἀληθείας τὸν τὴν πρόνοιαν δοξάζοντα.

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: After showing a little peep-hole to those who love to contemplate the Church from the law of sacrifices respecting clean and unclean animals (inasmuch as thus the common Jews and the heretics are distinguished mystically from the divine Church), let us bring the discourse to a close. For such of the sacrifices as part the hoof, and ruminate, the Scripture represents as clean and acceptable to God ; since the just obtain access to the Father and to the Son by faith . For this is the stability of those who part the hoof, those who study the oracles of God night and day, and ruminate them in the soul's receptacle for instructions; which gnostic exercise the Law expresses under the figure of the rumination of the clean animal. But such as have neither the one nor the other of those qualities it separates as unclean.

Now those that ruminate, but do not part the hoof, indicate the majority of the Jews , who have indeed the oracles of God , but have not faith , and the step which, resting on the truth , conveys to the Father by the Son. Whence also this kind of cattle are apt to slip, not having a division in the foot, and not resting on the twofold support of faith . For no man, it is said, knows the Father , but he to whom the Son shall reveal Him. Luke 10:22 And again, those also are likewise unclean that part the hoof, but do not ruminate. For these point out the heretics , who indeed go upon the name of the Father and the Son , but are incapable of triturating and grinding down the clear declaration of the oracles, and who, besides, perform the works of righteousness coarsely and not with precision, if they perform them at all.

To such the Lord says, Why will you call me Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say? Luke 6:46 And those that neither part the hoof nor chew the cud are entirely unclean. But you Megareans, says Theognis, are neither third, nor fourth, Nor twelfth, neither in reckoning nor in number, but as chaff which the wind drives away from the face of the earth, and as a drop from a vessel. Isaiah 40:15 These points, then, having been formerly thoroughly treated, and the department of ethics having been sketched summarily in a fragmentary way, as we promised; and having here and there interspersed the dogmas which are the germs of true knowledge , so that the discovery of the sacred traditions may not be easy to any one of the uninitiated, let us proceed to what we promised.

Now the Miscellanies are not like parts laid out, planted in regular order for the delight of the eye, but rather like an umbrageous and shaggy hill, planted with laurel, and ivy, and apples, and olives, and figs; the planting being purposely a mixture of fruit-bearing and fruitless trees, since the composition aims at concealment, on account of those that have the daring to pilfer and steal the ripe fruits; from which, however, the husbandmen, transplanting shoots and plants, will adorn a beautiful park and a delightful grove. The Miscellanies, then, study neither arrangement nor diction; since there are even cases in which the Greeks on purpose wish that ornate diction should be absent, and imperceptibly cast in the seed of dogmas , not according to the truth , rendering such as may read laborious and quick at discovery.

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: We shall shortly examine how the doctrines of the philosophers were seen among the Hebrews; first, however, as is fitting, we must speak of the times of Moses, through which it will be shown beyond dispute that the Hebrew philosophy is the most ancient of all wisdom. Tatian has already treated these matters precisely in his *Address to the Greeks*, and Cassian has done so in the first book of his *Exegetical Works*; nevertheless, the present memorandum also requires us to run through what has been said on the topic.

Apion the grammarian, surnamed Plistonicus, in the fourth book of his *Egyptian Histories* — although he is hostile toward the Hebrews, being Egyptian by birth, and has even composed a work against the Jews — mentions Amosis, king of the Egyptians, and the events of his reign, and cites Ptolemy of Mendes as a witness. Ptolemy's words run thus: Amosis, having become king in the time of Argive Inachus, demolished the city of Avaris, as Ptolemy of Mendes recorded in his *Chronicles*. This Ptolemy was a priest, and in three books he set forth the deeds of the Egyptian kings; he states that during the reign of Amosis, king of Egypt, the Jews, led by Moses, made their journey out of Egypt, from which it follows that Moses flourished in the time of Inachus.

The most ancient of Greek history is the Argolic — that is, the history reckoned from Inachus — as Dionysius of Halicarnassus teaches in his *Chronicles*. The Attic history, reckoned from Cecrops the two-natured and autochthonous, is, as Tatian says word for word, forty generations younger; the Arcadian history, reckoned from Pelasgus, is nine generations younger, and Pelasgus too is said to be autochthonous. The Phthiotic history, reckoned from Deucalion, is younger still by two generations. From Inachus to the time of the Trojan War, twenty or a few more generations are counted, amounting, so to speak, to about four hundred years.

If the Assyrian history is far older than the Greek, as Ctesias says, it will appear that in the four hundred and second year of the Assyrian empire, and in the thirty-second year of the eighth dynasty of Belochus, the migration of Moses out of Egypt took place under Amosis the Egyptian and Inachus the Argive. In Greece, during the time of Phoroneus, who came after Inachus, there occurred the flood of Ogygus and the kingdom in Sicyon — first of Aegialeus, then of Eurypus, then of Telchin — and the kingdom of Crete in Crete. Acusilaus declares that Phoroneus was the first man born; hence the poet of the *Phoroneis* calls him the father of mortal men. Following Acusilaus, Plato writes in the *Timaeus* that, wishing to draw his interlocutors into discourse about ancient things, he undertakes to speak of the most ancient traditions of the city: of Phoroneus, said to be the first, of Niobe, and of the events after the flood.

Under Phorbas came Actaeus, from whom the Attic Actaea takes its name. Under Triopas came Prometheus, Atlas, Epimetheus, the two-natured Cecrops, and Io. Under Crotopus occurred the conflagration in the time of Phaethon and the flood in the time of Deucalion. Under Sthenelus came the kingdom of Amphictyon, the arrival of Danaus in the Peloponnese, and the foundation of Dardania by Dardanus, whom Homer says was the firstborn of cloud-gathering Zeus, together with the carrying off of Europa from Phoenicia to Crete.
