Omnia per ipsum facta sunt, et sine ipso factum est nihil. Quod factum est, in ipso vita erat, et vita erat lua hominum, et lux in tenebris lucet, et tenebre eam non comprehenderunt. Omnia, inquit, per ipsum facta sunt ; in omnibus ergo est et hzee quae secundum nos est conditio: non enim concedetur eis, omnia dici ea que sunt infra Pleroma ipsorum. Si enim et hee Pleroma ipsorum continet, non extra est tanta ista conditio, quemadmodum ostendimus in eo libro qui ante hune est ; si autem extra Pleroma sunt heec, quod quidem impossibile visum est, jam non est omnia Pleroma ipsorum: non est ergo extra heee tanta conditio. Abstulit autem a nobis dissensiones omnes ipse Johannes, dicens: In hoc mundo erat, et mundus per ipsum factus est, et mundus eum non cognovit. In sua propria venit, et sui eum non receperunt. Secundum autem Marcionem et eos qui similes sunt ei, neque mundus per eum factus est ; neque in sua venit, sed in aliena, Secundum autem quosdam Gnosticorum, ¢ab angelis factus est iste mundus, et non per Verbum Dei. Secundum autem eos qui sunt a Valentino, iterum non per eum factus est, sed per Demiurgum. Hic enim operabatur similitudines tales fieri, ad imitationem eorum que sunt sursum, quemadmodum dicunt: Demiurgus autem perficiebat fabricationem conditionis. Emissum enim dicunt eum a matre Dominum et Demiurgum ejus dispositionis quee est secundum conditionem, per quem hune mundum factum volunt: cum Evangelium manifeste dicat, quoniam per Verbum, quod in principio erat apud Deum, omnia sunt facta: quod Verbum, inquit, caro factum est, et habitavit in nobis. 8. Secundum autem illos, neque Verbum caro factum est, neque Christus, neque qui ex omnibus factus est Salvator. Htenim Verbum et Christum nec advenisse in hune mundum volunt: Salvatorem vero non incarnatum neque passum; descendisse autem quasi columbam in eum Jesum qui factus est ex dispositione, et cum annuntiasset incognitum Patrem, iterum ascendisse in Pleroma. Incarnatum autem et passum quidam quidem eum qui ex dispositione sit dicunt Jesum, quem per Mariam dicunt pertransisse, quasi aquam per tubum: alii vero ° Demiurgi filium, in quem descendisse eum Jesum qui ex dispositione sit: alii rursum Jesum quidem ex Joseph et Maria natum dicunt, et in hune descendisse Christum qui de superioribus sit, sine carne et impassibilem exsistentem. Secundum autem nullam sententiam heereticorum, Verbum Dei caro factum est. Si enim quis regulas ipsorum omnium perscrutetur, inveniet quoniam sine carne et impassibilis ab omnibus illis inducitur Dei Verbum, et qui est in superioribus Christus. Alii enim putant manifestatum eum, quemadmodum hominem transfiguratum; neque autem natum, neque incarnatum dicunt illum: alii vero neque figuram eum assumsisse hominis; sed quemadmodum columbam descendisse in eum Jesum, qui natus est ex Maria.

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english:
When they are confronted with Scripture, they turn their attack against Scripture itself, claiming it is not rightly preserved, lacks authority, contradicts itself in its varied expressions, and cannot yield truth to those who lack the tradition. For that tradition was not handed down in writing but by living voice — which is why Paul declared, "We speak wisdom among the perfect, but not the wisdom of this world" (1 Corinthians 2:6). Each of these teachers claims that this wisdom is his own private discovery, a mere invention, so that truth might be whatever suits him: one moment it appears in Valentinus, another in Marcion, then in Cerinthus, later in Basilides, even in the one who argues against the rest yet could speak nothing that saves. Every single one of them is thoroughly perverted; without shame each makes himself the rule of truth, distorting it as he preaches.

But when we appeal to the tradition that comes from the Apostles — the tradition guarded through the succession of presbyters in the churches — they reject it, boasting that they have found the pure truth and are wiser not only than the presbyters but than the Apostles themselves. They allege that the Apostles mixed legal ordinances with the Savior's words, and that even the Lord Himself spoke sometimes from the Demiurge, sometimes from the middle realm, sometimes from the highest summit. Meanwhile they claim to know the hidden mystery without doubt, without stain, purely — which is nothing less than the most brazen blasphemy against their own Maker. Consequently they agree with neither Scripture nor tradition. Our struggle, dear friend, is against such men, who like slippery serpents try to wriggle free on every side. Therefore they must be resisted on every front, so that by refuting them we may confound some and lead them to the conversion of truth. For though it is not easy for a soul seized by error to recover, it is not utterly impossible to escape error when truth is applied.

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: The Church has been spread throughout the whole world to the ends of the earth, and she received this faith from the Apostles and their disciples. It is faith in one God, the Father Almighty, who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them; in one Christ Jesus, the Son of God, who became incarnate for our salvation; and in the Holy Spirit, who through the prophets proclaimed the dispositions of God, the advent, the virgin birth, the passion, the resurrection from the dead, and the bodily ascension into heaven of the beloved Jesus Christ our Lord. The Spirit also proclaimed His coming from heaven in the glory of the Father to recapitulate all things and to raise every flesh of the human race, so that every knee of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings may bow to Christ Jesus our Lord and God and Savior and King, according to the will of the invisible Father (Romans 14:11; Philippians 2:10-11), and that He may execute just judgment upon all: He will send spiritual wickedness, the angels who transgressed and became apostates, and impious, unjust, iniquitous, and blasphemous men into eternal fire; but to the just, to those who keep His commandments and persevere in His love — whether from the beginning or through repentance — He will give incorruptible life as a reward and surround them with eternal glory.

Having received this preaching and this faith, as we said before, the Church, though scattered throughout the whole world, guards it carefully, as if dwelling in one house. She believes these things with one soul and one heart, and she preaches, teaches, and hands them down in perfect harmony, as if she had but one mouth. Although the languages of the world differ, the power of the tradition is one and the same. The churches in Germany, Spain, Gaul, the East, Libya, and the center of the world — none of them believe or hand down anything different. Just as the sun, God's creature, is one and the same across the whole world, so the preaching of the truth shines everywhere and enlightens all who desire to come to the knowledge of the truth.

No one who is powerful in speech among those who preside over the churches will say anything other than these things, for no one is above the Master. Nor will the one who is weak in speaking diminish the tradition. Since the faith is one and the same, neither does the one who can say much increase it, nor does the one who can say less diminish it.

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: We have come to know the plan of our salvation through others, through those by whom the Gospel reached us; indeed, they first preached it, and afterward, by the will of God, handed it down to us in the Scriptures, to serve as the foundation and pillar of our faith (1 Tim 3:15). It is not right to claim that they preached before they possessed perfect knowledge, as some dare to assert, boasting that they are correctors of the Apostles. For after our Lord rose from the dead, and they were clothed with power from on high when the Holy Spirit came upon them, they were filled with all things and gained perfect knowledge (Luke 24:49; Acts 1:8; John 16:13). They went out to the ends of the earth, proclaiming the good things that come to us from God and announcing heavenly peace to humanity, each of them possessing the Gospel of God (Mark 16:15; Acts 1:8; Rom 10:15; Eph 2:17). Thus Matthew published a written Gospel in the Hebrews' own language, while Peter and Paul were evangelizing at Rome and founding the Church. After their departure, Mark, the disciple and interpreter of Peter, handed down to us in writing the things Peter had proclaimed. Luke, a follower of Paul, set down in a book the Gospel that Paul preached. Afterwards John, the disciple of the Lord who had also reclined on His breast, published the Gospel while living at Ephesus in Asia (John 13:23; 21:20). All of these announced to us one God, the Maker of heaven and earth, proclaimed by the Law and the Prophets, and one Christ, the Son of God (Acts 4:24; 14:15; Rom 1:2-3). If anyone does not assent to them, he despises the partakers of the Lord, he despises Christ the Lord, he despises the Father as well, and he stands self-condemned, resisting and opposing his own salvation; this is what all heretics do (Luke 10:16; 1 John 5:10-12; John 12:48).

latin: 1. Now enim per alios dispositionem salutis nostree cognovimus, quam per eos per quos Evangelium pervenit ad nos: quod quidem tune preeconayerunt, postea vero per Dei voluntatem in Seripturis nobis tradiderunt, fundamentum et columnam fidei nostree futurum. Nec enim fas est dicere, quoniam ante preedicaverunt quam perfectam haberent agnitionem; sicut quidam audent dicere, gloriantes emendatores se esse Apostolorum. Postea enim quam surrexit Dominus noster a mortuis, et induti sunt supervenientis Spiritus sancti virtutem ex alto, de omnibus adimpleti sunt, et habuerunt perfectam agnitionem; exierunt in fines terree, ea quee a Deo nobis bona sunt evangelizantes, et ccelestem pacem hominibus annuntiantes, qui quidem et omnes pariter et singuli eorum habentes Evangelium Dei*. Ita Mattheus in Hebreis ipsorum lingua scripturam y. edidit Evangelii, cum Petrus et Paulus Rome evangelizarent, et ecxdyoiav. Mera de trav fundarent Ecclesiam. Post vero horum excessum, Marcus discipulus et interpres Petri, et ipse quee a Petro annuntiata erant, per ———— seripta nobis tradidit. Et Lucas autem sectator Pauli, quod ab illo preedicabatur Evangelium, in libro condidit. Postea et Johannes discipulus Domini, qui et supra pectus ejus recumbebat, et ipse edidit Evangelium, Ephesi Asie commorans. Et omnes isti unum Deum factorem cceli et terre a lege et prophetis annuntiatum, et unum Christum filium Dei tradiderunt nobis: quibus si quis non assentit, spernit quidem participes Domini, spernit autem et ipsum Christum Dominum, spernit vero et Patrem, et est a semetipso damnatus, resistens et repugnans saluti suze: quod faciunt omnes heeretici.

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: John the disciple of the Lord proclaims this faith. He wants to strip away the error that Cerinthus planted in people, and much earlier the Nicolaitans planted it — a false offshoot meant to confuse them. He wants to persuade them that one God made all things through his Word. Their teaching is different: they say one being is the creator and another is the Father of the Lord; one is the son of the creator and another is the Christ from above. They say this Christ is impassible and remained above, descended into Jesus the son of the creator, and then returned to his Pleroma. They call the Trinity 'monogenes' and say the Logos is the true son of the monogenes. They say the world we live in was not made by the first God, but by a certain power far below, cut off from the invisible and ineffable realm above. The Lord's disciple wants to draw a boundary around all such ideas and establish the rule of truth in the Church: there is one God, almighty, who made everything visible and invisible through his Word. He also shows that through the Word by which God finished creation, God also provided salvation for those who live in this creation. So he opens his Gospel teaching with these words: 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made. What was made in him was life, and the life was the light of men. The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it' (John 1:1–5).

He says, 'All things were made through him' (John 1:3); therefore this creation of ours is included in that 'all.' It will not be granted to the heretics to claim that 'all things' means only what lies inside their Pleroma. If their Pleroma contains these things, then this creation is not outside it — as we showed in the previous book. But if these things are outside the Pleroma, which is impossible, then their Pleroma is not 'all things.' Therefore this creation is not outside. John himself removes every dissension from us when he says: 'He was in the world, and the world was made through him, yet the world did not know him. He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him' (John 1:10–11). According to Marcion and those like him, the world was not made through him, and he did not come to his own but to another's. According to certain Gnostics, the world was made by angels, not through the Word of God. According to the followers of Valentinus, the world was not made through him but through the Demiurge. They say the Demiurge fashioned this creation by producing copies that imitate the realities above. But the Gospel plainly says that all things were made through the Word who was in the beginning with God, and that this Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). According to them, however, the Word did not become flesh, nor did Christ, nor the Savior assembled from all things. They refuse to let the Word and Christ enter this world. They say the Savior — unincarnate and impassible — descended like a dove into the Jesus who came from the condition, announced the unknown Father, and then ascended back to the Pleroma. Some say the Jesus from the condition was incarnate and suffered, passing through Mary like water through a pipe. Others say he was the Demiurge's son, into whom the Jesus from the condition descended. Others say Jesus was born of Joseph and Mary, and the Christ from above — impassible and without flesh — descended into him. But according to no heretical opinion did the Word of God become flesh. If you examine all their systems, you will find that every one of them presents the Word of God and the Christ from above as without flesh and impassible. Some think he appeared only like a transfigured man; they deny he was born or incarnate. Others say he did not even assume human form, but descended like a dove into the Jesus born of Mary. The Lord's disciple shows all these to be false witnesses when he declares: 'The Word became flesh and dwelt among us' (John 1:14).

So that we do not ask whose Word became flesh, he himself teaches further: 'There was a man sent from God, whose name was John. He came as a witness, to testify about the light. He was not the light, but came to testify about the light' (John 1:6–8). John the forerunner, who testifies to the light — by which God was he sent? Surely by the God whose angel is Gabriel, who also announced John's birth. That same God promised through the prophets to send his angel before the face of his Son to prepare his way — that is, to testify to the light in the spirit and power of Elijah (Luke 1:17). Elijah was the servant and prophet of which God? The God who made heaven and earth, as Elijah himself confesses (1 Kings 18:36–37). Therefore John was sent by the founder and creator of this world. How else could he testify about the light that descended from the invisible and ineffable realm? All heretics have decreed that the Demiurge is ignorant of the power above him, yet John is found to be the witness and revealer of that power. Because of this, the Lord said John was more than a prophet (Luke 7:26). All the other prophets announced the coming of the Father's light; they longed to see the one they preached. But John not only announced him like the others — he saw him coming, pointed him out, and persuaded many to believe in him, so that he held the place of both prophet and apostle. He is more than a prophet: first among apostles, second among prophets; yet all things come from one and the same God.

latin: Hane fidem annuntians Johannes Domini discipulus, volens per Evangelii annuntiationem auferre eum, qui a Cerintho inseminatus erat hominibus errorem, et multo prius ab his qui dicuntur Nicolaite, qui sunt vulsio ejus quee falso cognominatur ut confunderet eos, et suaderet quoniam unus Deus qui omnia fecit per Verbum suum ; et non, quemadmodum illi dicunt, alterum quidem fabricatorem, alium autem Patrem Domini: et alium quidem fabricatoris filium, alterum vero ®de superioribus Christum, quem et impassibilem perseverasse, descendentem in Jesum filium fabricatoris, et iterum revolasse in suum Pleroma: et Tinitium quidem esse monogenem; Logon autem verum filium unigeniti: et eam conditionem quze est secundum nos, non a primo Deo factam, sed a virtute aliqua valde deorsum subjecta, et abscissa ab eorum communicatione quze sunt invisibilia et innominabilia. Omnia igitur talia cireumscribere volens discipulus Domini, et ' regulam veritatis constituere in Ecclesia, quia est unus Deus omnipotens, qui per Verbum suum omnia fecit, et visibilia et invisibilia; significans quoque, quoniam per Verbum, per quod Deus perfecit conditionem, in hoe et salutem his qui in conditione sunt preestitit hominibus; sic inchoavit in ea que est secundum Evangelium doctrina: Jn principio erat Verbum, et Verbum erat apud Deum, et Deus erat Verbum: hoc erat in principio apud Deum. Omnia per ipsum facta sunt, et sine ipso factum est nihil. Quod factum est, in ipso vita erat, et vita erat lua hominum, et lux in tenebris lucet, et tenebre eam non comprehenderunt. Omnia, inquit, per ipsum facta sunt ; in omnibus ergo est et hzee quae secundum nos est conditio: non enim concedetur eis, omnia dici ea que sunt infra Pleroma ipsorum. Si enim et hee Pleroma ipsorum continet, non extra est tanta ista conditio, quemadmodum ostendimus in eo libro qui ante hune est ; si autem extra Pleroma sunt heec, quod quidem impossibile visum est, jam non est omnia Pleroma ipsorum: non est ergo extra heee tanta conditio. Abstulit autem a nobis dissensiones omnes ipse Johannes, dicens: In hoc mundo erat, et mundus per ipsum factus est, et mundus eum non cognovit. In sua propria venit, et sui eum non receperunt. Secundum autem Marcionem et eos qui similes sunt ei, neque mundus per eum factus est ; neque in sua venit, sed in aliena, Secundum autem quosdam Gnosticorum, ¢ab angelis factus est iste mundus, et non per Verbum Dei. Secundum autem eos qui sunt a Valentino, iterum non per eum factus est, sed per Demiurgum. Hic enim operabatur similitudines tales fieri, ad imitationem eorum que sunt sursum, quemadmodum dicunt: Demiurgus autem perficiebat fabricationem conditionis. Emissum enim dicunt eum a matre Dominum et Demiurgum ejus dispositionis quee est secundum conditionem, per quem hune mundum factum volunt: cum Evangelium manifeste dicat, quoniam per Verbum, quod in principio erat apud Deum, omnia sunt facta: quod Verbum, inquit, caro factum est, et habitavit in nobis. 8. Secundum autem illos, neque Verbum caro factum est, neque Christus, neque qui ex omnibus factus est Salvator. Htenim Verbum et Christum nec advenisse in hune mundum volunt: Salvatorem vero non incarnatum neque passum; descendisse autem quasi columbam in eum Jesum qui factus est ex dispositione, et cum annuntiasset incognitum Patrem, iterum ascendisse in Pleroma. Incarnatum autem et passum quidam quidem eum qui ex dispositione sit dicunt Jesum, quem per Mariam dicunt pertransisse, quasi aquam per tubum: alii vero ° Demiurgi filium, in quem descendisse eum Jesum qui ex dispositione sit: alii rursum Jesum quidem ex Joseph et Maria natum dicunt, et in hune descendisse Christum qui de superioribus sit, sine carne et impassibilem exsistentem. Secundum autem nullam sententiam heereticorum, Verbum Dei caro factum est. Si enim quis regulas ipsorum omnium perscrutetur, inveniet quoniam sine carne et impassibilis ab omnibus illis inducitur Dei Verbum, et qui est in superioribus Christus. Alii enim putant manifestatum eum, quemadmodum hominem transfiguratum; neque autem natum, neque incarnatum dicunt illum: alii vero neque figuram eum assumsisse hominis; sed quemadmodum columbam descendisse in eum Jesum, qui natus est ex Maria. Omnes igitur illos falsos testes ostendens discipulus Domini, ait: Ht Verbum caro factum est, et habitavit in nobis. Et ut non inquiramus, cujus Dei Verbum caro factum est, ipse insuper docet, dicens : Fuit homo missus a Deo, erat ei nomen Johannes: hic venit in testimonium, ut testaretur de lumine. Non erat ipse lumen, sed ut testaretur de lumine. Preecursor igitur Johannes, qui testatur de lumine, a quo Deo missus est? Utique ab eo cujus Gabriel est angelus, qui etiam evangelisavit generationem ejus; qui et per prophetas promisit angelum suum missurum ante faciem Filii sui, et preeparaturum viam ejus, hoc est, testificaturum de lumine, i spiritw et virtute Helie. Helias autem rursus cujus Dei servus et propheta fuit? Ejus qui fecit coelum et terram, quemadmodum et ipse confitetur. A conditore igitur et fabricatore hujus mundi missus Johannes, quemadmodum poterat testificari de eo lumine, quod ex his que sunt innominabilia et invisibilia descenderit ? Omnes enim heeretici decreverunt, Demiurgum ignorare eam que sit super eum virtutem, cujus testis et ostensor invenitur Johannes. Propter hoc Dominus plus quam prophetam dixit eum habuisse. Reliqui enim omnes prophetze annuntiaverunt adventum paterni luminis; concupierunt autem digni esse videre eum quem preedicabant: Johannes autem et preenuntiavit similiter sicut alii, et advenientem vidit et demonstravit, et credere in eum suasit multis, ita ut ipse et prophete et apostoli locum habuerit. est enim plus quam propheta: quoniam primo apostoli, secundo prophetw ; omnia autem ex uno et eodem ipso Deo.

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: When they are refuted from the Scriptures, they turn around and accuse those same Scriptures, as if the Scriptures were not in order, lacked authority, were spoken in contradictory ways, and could not yield the truth to anyone who does not know the tradition. That tradition was not handed down in writing, but by living voice; and for this reason Paul declared, "We speak wisdom among the mature, a wisdom not of this age" (1 Corinthians 2:6-7). Each of these heretics claims that this wisdom is his own private discovery — an obvious fiction — so that the truth may appear credible on his terms. Sometimes it appears in Valentinus, sometimes in Marcion, sometimes in Cerinthus, later in Basilides, and even in the one who argues against them but could speak nothing that saves. Every one of them is thoroughly perverted; each makes himself the rule of truth and preaches without shame.

But when we appeal to the tradition that comes from the Apostles and is preserved in the Churches through the succession of Presbyters, they resist it, boasting that they have found the pure truth and are wiser not only than the Presbyters but than the Apostles themselves. They allege that the Apostles mixed legalistic material with the Savior's words, and that the Lord Himself spoke sometimes from the Demiurge, sometimes from the Middle, sometimes from the Top — while they, they claim, know the hidden mystery without doubt, without stain, in perfect purity. This is nothing less than the most impudent blasphemy against their own Maker. Consequently they agree with neither the Scriptures nor the tradition. Our struggle, dear friend, is against such people, who slip away on every side like cunning serpents. Therefore we must oppose them at every point, if by refuting some we may confound them and lead them to the conversion of truth. For although it is not easy for a soul seized by error to recover, it is not utterly impossible to escape error when the truth is set before it.

latin: 1. Cvum enim ex Seripturis arguuntur, in accusationem con-vertuntur ipsarum Seripturarum, quasi non recte habeant, neque sint ex auctoritate, et quia varie sint dictez, et quia non possit ex his inveniri veritas ab his qui nesciant traditionem. Non enim per literas traditam illam, sed per vivam vocem: ob quam causam et Paulum dixisse: Sapientiam autem loquimur inter perfectos: sapientiam autem non mundi hujus. Et hane sapientiam unusquisque eorum esse dicit, quam a semetipso adinvenit, fictionem videlicet, ut digne secundum eos sit veritas, aliquando quidem in Valentino, aliquando autem in Marcione, aliquando in Cerintho, postea deinde in Basilide, fuit aut et in illo qui contra disputat, qui nihil salutare loqui potuit. Unusquisque enim ipsorum omnimodo perversus, semetipsum regulam veritatis depravans preedicare non confunditur, ' 2. Cum autem ad eam iterum traditionem, que est ab Apostolis, quee per successiones Presbyterorum in Ecclesiis. custoditur, provocamus eos, adversantur traditioni, dicentes se non solum Presbyteris, sed etiam A postolis exsistentes sapientiores, sinceram invenisse veritatem. Apostolos enim admiscuisse ea que sunt legalia Salvatoris verbis: et non solum Apostolos, sed etiam ipsum Dominum, modo quidem a Demiurgo, modo autem a medietate, interdum autem a summitate fecisse sermones : se vero indubitate, et intaminate, et sincere absconditum scire mysterium: quod quidem impudentissime est blasphemare suum factorem. Eyenit itaque, neque Scripturis jam, neque traditioni consentire eos. Adversus tales certamen nobis est, o dilectissime, more serpentum lubrici [7. lubrice] undique effugere conantes. Quapropter undique resistendum est illis, si quos ex his retusione confundentes, ad conversionem veritatis adducere possimus. Etenim si non facile est ab errore apprehensam resipiscere animam, sed non omnimodo impossibile est errorem effugere apposita veritate.

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: The plan of the Apostles stands open to view in every church throughout the world, for all who truly desire to see it; we can trace the bishops appointed by the Apostles and their unbroken succession down to our own day, and none of them ever taught the fancies these people now proclaim. If the Apostles had possessed secret mysteries, reserved for a select few and taught in private, they would surely have entrusted them above all to those to whom they also committed the care of the churches. They wanted those successors to be steadfast and blameless in everything, so that their right stewardship of the apostolic office would bring great benefit, while their failure would bring utter disaster. But to list the succession of every church would swell this work beyond measure; therefore we set forth the tradition of that greatest and most ancient church, known to all, which the two most glorious Apostles Peter and Paul founded and established at Rome, and the faith it has handed down to humanity through the succession of its bishops. By this we confound all who, whether from self-will, empty pride, blindness, or perverse judgment, gather apart from the true communion. For every church must agree with this church — that is, with the faithful everywhere — because in it the tradition from the Apostles has been preserved without interruption. (cf. 1 Tim 1:20; Titus 3:10)

Having founded and built the Church, the blessed Apostles entrusted its oversight to Linus; Paul himself mentions Linus in his letters to Timothy. After Linus came Anacletus, and third from the Apostles, Clement received the episcopate — a man who had seen the Apostles, conversed with them, and held their living preaching and tradition before his eyes. He was not alone in this; many who had been taught by the Apostles were still alive. When a serious dispute broke out among the brothers at Corinth, the Church of Rome sent a most powerful letter to restore peace, renew their faith, and proclaim the tradition it had recently received from the Apostles: one God, almighty, maker of heaven and earth, fashioner of man, who sent the flood, called Abraham, led his people out of Egypt, spoke with Moses, gave the law, sent the prophets, and prepared fire for the devil and his angels. This Father of our Lord Jesus Christ is proclaimed by the churches from Scripture itself; those who wish to learn can recognize the apostolic tradition there, for this letter is older than those who now falsely teach and invent another God above the Demiurge and Creator of all things.

After Clement came Evaristus, then Alexander; sixth from the Apostles came Sixtus, then Telesphorus, who gloriously suffered martyrdom; then Hyginus, then Pius, then Anicetus. When Soter succeeded Anicetus, Eleutherius now holds the episcopate in the twelfth place from the Apostles. This ordered succession demonstrates that the tradition from the Apostles in the Church and the proclamation of truth are one and the same, and have come down to us intact — proving that the life-giving faith preserved and handed on in the Church from the Apostles until now is one and the same.

Polycarp, too, was not only taught by the Apostles and familiar with many who had seen the Lord, but was appointed bishop of the church at Smyrna in Asia by the Apostles themselves. We saw him in our early years; he endured to a great age and departed this life by a glorious and noble martyrdom. He always taught what he had learned from the Apostles — teachings that alone are true. All the churches in Asia and those who have succeeded Polycarp to this day bear witness to this; he is a man of far greater authority and a more faithful witness to the truth than Valentinus, Marcion, and the rest of their perverse school. When he came to Rome under Anicetus, he converted many of the heretics we have mentioned to the Church of God, proclaiming the one truth he had received from the Apostles and handed on to the Church. There are those who heard him tell how John, the Lord's disciple, once went to bathe in Ephesus, saw Cerinthus inside, and rushed out unbathed, saying he feared the bathhouse would collapse because the enemy of truth was within. And when Marcion once confronted Polycarp and asked, "Do you recognize us?" he answered, "I recognize you as the firstborn of Satan." Such was the dread the Apostles and their disciples had of any communion, even in word, with those who corrupted the truth — just as Paul commands: "Avoid a divisive person after a first and second warning, knowing that such a one is warped and self-condemned." (Titus 3:10; cf. 1 Tim 1:20) Polycarp also wrote an excellent letter to the Philippians, from which those who desire to learn and care for their salvation can discern the character of his faith and his proclamation of truth. The church at Ephesus, founded by Paul and where John remained until the time of Trajan, stands as a true witness to the tradition of the Apostles.

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: Since these demonstrations exist, it is no longer necessary to seek the truth from others, for it is easy to take it from the Church. The Apostles, as though pouring into a rich repository, have fully deposited all things of truth within it, so that anyone who wishes may draw from it the drink of life. For this is the entrance to life; all the rest, however, are thieves and robbers (John 10:1, 8-9). Therefore it is necessary to avoid them, but with the greatest diligence to love and to seize the tradition of truth that belongs to the Church. For what if there were a dispute about some small question? Would it not be necessary to have recourse to the most ancient churches, in which the Apostles conversed, and from them to take concerning the present question what is certain and clear? And what if even the Apostles had not left us the Scriptures? Would it not then have been necessary to follow the order of tradition, which they handed down to those to whom they entrusted the churches? To this ordinance many barbarian nations who believe in Christ assent, having salvation written in their hearts by the Spirit without paper or ink (2 Corinthians 3:3), and diligently preserving the old tradition. They believe in one God, the Maker of heaven and earth and all things that are in them (Genesis 1:1; Acts 4:24), through Christ Jesus, the Son of God. He, because of His surpassing love for His creature, endured the birth from the Virgin, Himself uniting man to God (Luke 1:31-35; John 1:14). He suffered under Pontius Pilate, rose again, was received up in glory, and will come in glory as the Savior of those who are saved and the Judge of those who are judged (Acts 1:11; 1 Timothy 6:14-15; 2 Timothy 4:1), sending into eternal fire the transgressors of truth and the despisers of His Father and of His advent (Matthew 25:41; 2 Thessalonians 1:8-9).

Those who have believed without letters are, as far as our speech is concerned, barbarians; but as far as judgment, custom, and conduct are concerned, because of faith they are most wise and they please God, living in all justice, chastity, and wisdom. If anyone should announce to them the things invented by heretics, speaking in their own language, they immediately stop their ears and flee far away, not even enduring to hear the blasphemous talk. Thus, through that ancient tradition of the elders, they do not even admit into their mind's conception whatever portentous speech is theirs, for there was no assembly among them, nor any instituted doctrine. For before Valentinus, those who are from Valentinus did not exist; nor before Marcion did those who are from Marcion exist; nor were the remaining malignant teachings, which we enumerated above, present to become the initiators and inventors of their perversity. Valentinus came to Rome under Hyginus, and under Pius he prolonged his time until Anicetus. Cerdo, who preceded Marcion, also came under Hyginus, who was the eighth bishop, often coming into the church and making confession; thus he completed his course, sometimes teaching secretly, sometimes making confession, sometimes being reproved by some for the wicked things he taught, and he kept away from the assembly of religious men. Marcion, succeeding him, grew strong under Anicetus, who held the tenth place of the episcopate. The rest, who are called Gnostics, receiving their beginnings from Menander, the disciple of Simon, as we have shown — each one of them, whose teaching he shared, appeared as his father and his bishop. All these, however, rose up much later, in the midst of the Church's times, into their own apostasy.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: The rule of faith is straightforward: from here on out we profess what we defend. We believe in one God, and no other—only the Creator of the world. He produced everything from nothing through His Word, which He sent forth first of all. That Word, called His Son, was seen in various ways in God's name by the Patriarchs, was always heard in the Prophets, and was finally sent from the Spirit of God the Father and His power into the virgin Mary. He was made flesh in her womb, born from her, and came forth as Jesus Christ. From there He preached a new law and a new promise of the kingdom of heaven; He performed mighty works; He was fixed to the cross and rose on the third day; He was snatched up into the heavens and sat at the right hand of the Father. He sent the vicarious power of the Holy Spirit, who acts on believers. He is to come with clarity to take up the saints into the fruit of eternal life and the heavenly promises, and to judge the profane to perpetual fire, with the resurrection of both parties accomplished and the flesh restored.

latin: Regula est autem fidei, ut jam hinc quid defendamus profiteamur, illa scilicet qua creditur, unum omnino Deum esse, nec alium praeter mundi conditorem; qui universa de nihilo produxerit, per Verbum suum primo omnium emissum; id Verbum, Filium ejus appellatum, in nomine Dei varie visum a Patriarchis, in Prophetis semper auditum, postremo delatum ex Spiritu Patris Dei et virtute in virginem Mariam, carnem factum in utero ejus, et ex ea natum egisse Jesum Christum; exinde praedicasse novam legem, et novam promissionem regni coelorum; virtutes fecisse; fixum cruci, tertia die resurrexisse; in coelos ereptum sedisse ad dexteram Patris; misisse vicariam vim Spiritus Sancti, qui credentes agat, venturum cum claritate, ad sumendos sanctos in vitae aeternae et promissorum coelestium fructum, et ad profanos adjudicandos igni perpetuo, facta utriusque partis resuscitatione cum carnis restitutione.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: But they themselves traffic in the Scriptures and argue from them; obviously they could not speak about the faith from any other source than the letters of faith. So we arrive at the point we aimed for: we steered the discussion here and prefaced our address precisely so that we can now engage the very issue our opponents raise. They flaunt the Scriptures, and their sheer audacity instantly sways some people; yet in the actual confrontation they merely exhaust the strong, ensnare the weak, and dismiss the undecided with a lingering doubt. Consequently we bar this move outright, refusing them any place in a scriptural debate. If these are indeed their strong points, enabling them to claim them, then it must be determined who rightfully possesses the Scriptures, lest anyone who has no claim whatsoever be admitted to them.

latin: Sed ipsi de Scripturis agunt, et de Scripturis suadent. Aliunde scilicet loqui possent de rebus fidei, nisi ex literis fidei? Venimus igitur ad propositum: huc enim dirigebamus, et hoc praestruebamus allocutionis praefatione, ut jam hinc de eo congrediamur, de quo adversarii provocant. Scripturas obtendunt, et hac sua audacia statim quosdam movent; in ipso vero congressu firmos quidem fatigant, infirmos capiunt, medios cum scrupulo dimittunt. Hunc igitur potissimum gradum obstruimus, non admittendos eos ad ullam de Scripturis disputationem. Si hae sunt illae vires eorum, uti eas habere possint, dispici debet cui competat possessio Scripturarum, ne is admittatur ad eas, cui nullo modo competit.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Therefore we must not appeal to the Scriptures, nor set the contest in them, where the outcome is either no victory, an uncertain one, or a tie that is equally uncertain. Even if a comparison of the Scriptures did not end up leveling both sides, the logical order demanded that the primary question be raised first—the only question now at issue: To whom does the faith itself belong? Whose are the Scriptures? From whom, through whom, when, and to whom was the discipline that makes Christians handed down? For wherever the truth of Christian discipline and faith appears, there will be the truth of the Scriptures, of their interpretations, and of all Christian traditions.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Let Christ Jesus our Lord permit me to speak for a moment—whoever he is, the Son of whatever God, a man and God of whatever substance, the teacher of whatever faith, the promiser of whatever reward—to declare what he was, what he had been, what will of the Father he carried out, what he prescribed for humanity to do, as long as he walked the earth, whether he was addressing the crowds openly or his disciples in private. From these he chose twelve chief men to stand at his side, destined to be masters for the nations. Then, after one of them was struck down, he commanded the remaining eleven, as they were departing to the Father after the resurrection, to go and teach the nations, baptizing them in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. Immediately, therefore, the Apostles—this title means 'those sent'—took up Matthias by lot as the twelfth man in place of Judas, acting on the authority of the prophecy in the Psalm of David (Psalm of David). Having received the promised power of the Holy Spirit for miracles and speech, they first testified to the faith in Jesus Christ throughout Judea and established churches. Then they set out into the world and proclaimed the same doctrine of the same faith to the nations, and accordingly founded churches in every city. From these churches, all other churches have borrowed the tradition of the faith and the seeds of doctrine, and continue to borrow them daily so that they may become churches; and by this very fact they themselves are accounted apostolic, as offspring of the apostolic churches. Every kind must be traced back to its own origin; that is a necessity. And so, numerous and great as these churches are, there is one single first church from the Apostles, from which all the rest proceed. Thus all are primitive, and all are apostolic, so long as they prove their unity by maintaining communion of peace, the name of brotherhood, and the bond of hospitality—rights which are governed by no other principle than the one tradition of the same sacrament.

latin: Christus Jesus Dominus noster permittat dicere interim, quisquis est, cujuscumque Dei Filius, cujuscumque materiae homo et Deus, cujuscumque fidei praeceptor, cujuscumque mercedis repromissor, quid esset, quid fuisset, quam Patris voluntatem administraret, quid homini agendum determinaret, quamdiu in terris agebat, ipse pronuntiabat, sive populo palam, sive discentibus seorsum; ex quibus duodecim praecipuos lateri suo adlegerat destinatos nationibus magistros. Itaque, uno eorum decusso, reliquos undecim, digrediens ad Patrem post resurrectionem, jussit ire et docere nationes, intinguendas in Patrem et in Filium et in Spiritum Sanctum. Statim igitur Apostoli (quos haec appellatio missos interpretatur), assumpto per sortem duodecimo Matthia in locum Judae, ex auctoritate prophetiae quae est in psalmo David, consecuti promissam vim Spiritus Sancti ad virtutes et eloquium primo per Judaeam contestata fide in Jesum Christum et ecclesiis institutis, dehinc in orbem profecti, eamdem doctrinam ejusdem fidei nationibus promulgaverunt, et proinde ecclesias apud unamquamque civitatem condiderunt, a quibus traducem fidei et semina doctrinae, caeterae exinde ecclesiae mutuatae sunt, et quotidie mutuantur ut ecclesiae fiant: ac per hoc et ipsae apostolicae deputantur, ut soboles apostolicarum ecclesiarum. Omne genus ad originem suam censeatur necesse est. Itaque tot ac tantae ecclesiae, una est illa ab Apostolis prima, ex qua omnes. Sic omnes prima, et apostolicae, dum una omnes probant unitatem; dum est illis communicatio pacis, et appellatio fraternitatis, et contesseratio hospitalitatis: quae jura non alia ratio regit, quam ejusdem sacramenti una traditio.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: As I said, it is the same foolishness when they admit that the Apostles knew nothing and did not preach contradictory things among themselves, yet they refuse to accept that the Apostles revealed everything to everyone. They claim some things were entrusted openly to all, others secretly to a few, because Paul also used this language with Timothy: "Timothy, guard the deposit" (1 Timothy 6:20). And again: "Guard the good deposit" (1 Timothy 6:20). What is this deposit, kept silent, so that it might be assigned to some other doctrine? Or does it refer to that charge, about which he says: "I entrust this charge to you, my son Timothy" (1 Timothy 1:18)? Likewise, does it refer to that command, about which he says: "I charge you before God, who gives life to all things, and Christ Jesus, who testified the good confession before Pontius Pilate, to keep the commandment" (1 Timothy 6:13)? But what command, and what charge? It will be understood from the passages above and below. I am not hinting at some obscure doctrine with this statement; rather, the point is to inculcate that no teaching other than what Timothy heard from Paul—and, I think, publicly—is to be admitted. "Before many witnesses," he says. If they refuse to understand the Church as those many witnesses, it makes no difference, since nothing was kept secret that was brought forward before many witnesses. Nor does the fact that he wanted to entrust these things to faithful men who are competent to teach others serve as an argument for some hidden Gospel. For when he says "these things," he means the things he was writing about at that moment; about hidden things, as about things absent from the conscience, he would not have said "these things," but "those things."

latin: Sed ut diximus, eadem dementia est, cum confitentur quidem, nihil Apostolos ignorasse, nec diversa inter se praedicasse; non tamen omnia volunt illos omnibus revelasse: quaedam enim palam, et universis; quaedam secreto, et paucis demandasse: quia et hoc verbo usus est Paulus ad Timotheum: O Timothee, depositum custodi. Et rursum: Bonum depositum serva. Quod hoc depositum est tacitum, ut alteri doctrinae deputetur? An illius denuntiationis, de qua ait: Hanc denuntiationem commendo apud te, fili Timothee. Item illius praecepti, de quo ait: Denuntio tibi ante Deum, qui vivificat omnia, et Jesum Christum, qui testatus est sub Pontio Pilato bonam confessionem, custodias praeceptum Quod autem praeceptum, et quae denuntiatio? Ex supra et infra scriptis intelligetur non nescio quid subostendi hoc dicto de remotiore doctrina, sed potius inculcari de non admittenda alia praeter eam, quam audierat ab ipso, et, puto, palam. Coram multis, inquit, testibus. Quos multos testes si nolunt Ecclesiam intelligi, nihil interest, quando nihil tacitum fuerit, quod sub multis testibus proferebatur. Sed nec quia voluit illum haec fidelibus hominibus demandare, qui idonei sint et alios docere id quoque ad argumentum occulti alicujus Evangelii interpretandum est. Nam cum dicit, haec, de eis dicit, de quibus in praesenti scribebat; de occultis autem, ut de absentibus apud conscientiam, non haec, sed illa dixisset.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: It followed necessarily that when Christ entrusted the administration of the Gospel, He attached a condition drawn from His own voice: it must not be dispensed randomly or thoughtlessly, lest they cast a pearl before pigs and throw something holy to dogs (Matt 7:6). The Lord declared this openly, without any hint of a hidden sacrament. He Himself had commanded that whatever they heard in darkness and in secret, they must preach in the light and from the housetops. He Himself had illustrated through a parable that they must not hoard a single mina — that is, a single word of His — without fruit, locked away in secret. He Himself taught that a lamp is not hidden under a bushel but set on a stand, so that it shines for everyone in the house (Mark 4:21-22). The Apostles either ignored these commands or failed utterly to grasp them, if they did not carry them out by concealing something of the light — that is, of God's word and Christ's sacrament.

As far as I know, they feared no one — not the violence of the Jews, not the Gentiles. All the more, then, they preached freely in the Church, precisely because they did not keep silent in synagogues and public places. Indeed, they could never have converted Jews or won over Gentiles unless they set out in order what they wanted people to believe; much more, then, would they not have withheld anything from the believing Churches that they might have entrusted separately to a few. True, they may have discussed certain matters among their own people, so to speak, but it is not to be believed that those discussions introduced another rule of faith, different from and contrary to what the Catholic Church proclaimed openly — so that they would name one God in church and another at home, designate one substance of Christ in public and another in secret, announce one hope of resurrection to all and another to a few. After all, they themselves pleaded in their Epistles that everyone speak the same thing and that there be no schisms or dissensions in the Church, because whether it was Paul or others, they all preached the same message. Otherwise they remembered the command: Let your word be 'yes, yes; no, no'; anything beyond this comes from evil (Matt 5:37) — lest, that is, they treat the Gospel in diversity.

latin: Porro consequens erat, ut cui demandabat Evangelii administrationem, non passim, nec inconsiderate administrandam, adjiceret secundum dominicam vocem, ne margaritam porcis, et sanctum canibus jactaret. Dominus palam edixit, sine ulla significatione alicujus tecti sacramenti. Ipse praeceperat, si quid in tenebris et in abscondito audissent, in luce et in tectis praedicarent. Ipse per similitudinem praefiguraverat, ne unam mnam, id est unum verbum ejus, sine fructu in abdito reservarent. Ipse docebat, lucernam non sub modio abstrudi solere, sed in candelabrum constitui, ut luceat omnibus qui in domo sunt. Haec Apostoli, aut neglexerunt, aut minime intellexerunt, si non adimpleverunt abscondentes aliquid de lumine, id est, de Dei verbo et Christi sacramento. Neminem quod scio verebantur, non Judaeorum vim, non ethnicorum; quo magis utique in Ecclesia libere praedicabant, qui in synagogis et in locis publicis non tacebant. Imo neque Judaeos convertere, neque ethnicos inducere potuissent, nisi quod credi ab eis volebant ordine exponerent: multo magis jam credentibus Ecclesiis nihil subtraxissent, quod aliis paucis seorsum demandarent. Quanquam, etsi quaedam inter domesticos, ut ita dixerim, disserebant, non tamen ea fuisse credendum est, quae aliam regulam fidei superducerent, diversam et contrariam illi, quam Catholicae in medium proferebant; ut alium Deum in ecclesia dicerent, alium in hospitio; aliam Christi substantiam designarent in aperto, aliam in secreto; aliam spem resurrectionis apud omnes annuntiarent, aliam apud paucos: cum ipsi obsecrarent in Epistolis suis, ut idipsum et unum loquerentur omnes, et non essent schismata et dissensiones in Ecclesia, quia sive Paulus, sive alii, eadem praedicarent. Alioquin meminerant: Sit sermo vester, est, est; non, non; quod amplius, hoc a malo est; ne scilicet Evangelium in diversitate tractarent.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Come now — suppose they all erred. Suppose the Apostle was deceived in his testimony to certain people. Suppose the Holy Spirit never glanced back to guide the Church into truth, despite being sent by Christ for that very purpose, requested from the Father for that very purpose, to be the teacher of truth. Suppose the steward of God, the vicar of Christ, neglected his duty, letting the churches meanwhile understand and believe something other than what he himself preached through the apostles. Is it plausible that so many and such great churches would have erred their way into a single faith? Among many events there is not a single outcome: the error of the churches' doctrine should have varied. Yet what is found to be one across many is not error — it is tradition. So let someone dare to claim that those who handed it down were mistaken.

latin: Age nunc, omnes erraverint; deceptus sit Apostolus de testimonio reddendo quibusdam; nullam respexerit Spiritus Sanctus, uti eam in veritatem deduceret, ad hoc missus a Christo, ad hoc postulatus de Patre, ut esset doctor veritatis; neglexerit officium Dei villicus, Christi vicarius, sinens Ecclesias aliter interim intelligere, aliter credere, quam ipse per Apostolos praedicabat: ecquid verisimile est, ut tot ac tantae in unam fidem erraverint? Nullus inter multos eventus unus est exitus: variasse debuerat error doctrinae Ecclesiarum. Caeterum, quod apud multos unum invenitur, non est erratum, sed traditum. Audeat ergo aliquis dicere illos errasse qui tradiderunt?

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Where was Marcion then, the Pontic shipowner and Stoic enthusiast? Where was Valentinus, the Platonist disciple? The record shows they were not around even earlier, back under Antoninus; at first they actually believed the catholic teaching in the Roman church, under Bishop Eleutherius. But their restless curiosity — the kind that made even fellow Christians avoid them — got them thrown out once, then twice. Finally Marcion was cut off for good, taking his two hundred sestertii with him, and the pair scattered the poison of their doctrines. Later Marcion confessed repentance and tried to meet the condition set for his return: he would be readmitted only if he brought back to the church the others he had schooled for destruction. Death beat him to it. Heresies had to exist, yes; but that does not make heresies good, as if evil were not also necessary. The Lord had to be betrayed; still, woe to the betrayer — lest anyone use that as a defense of heresy. Even Apelles' pedigree needs examining: he is no more ancient than Marcion, his founder and forerunner. He fell for a woman, abandoned Marcionite continence, and slipped away from the eyes of the most holy teacher Alexander to Alexandria. Years later he came back no better, except that he was no longer a Marcionite; he stumbled into another woman, the virgin Philumene (mentioned above), who later became a monstrous prostitute. Deceived by her power, he wrote down the revelations he learned from her. People still alive remember them — their own disciples and successors — so they cannot deny being later arrivals. Though they are also refuted by their own works, as the Lord said. If Marcion split the New Testament from the Old, he comes after what he split; he could not split what was not already united. United first, then separated — that proves the splitter is later. Valentinus, explaining differently and 'correcting,' only shows that whatever he corrects was previously flawed. These are the most notorious and frequent adulterers of the truth. And what about Nigidius, whoever he is, and Hermogenes, and the rest still walking around perverting God's ways? Let them show me their authorization. If they preach another God, how do they use that God's own things, letters, and names against the God they preach? If they preach the same God, how do they do it differently? Let them prove they are new apostles: let them say Christ descended again, taught again, was crucified again, died again, rose again — because that is how apostles operate, receiving power to work the same signs he did. I want to see their powers produced; unless I acknowledge their greatest power, by which they perversely imitate the apostles: the apostles made the dead live; these men make the living dead.

latin: Ubi tunc Marcion, ponticus nauclerus, stoicae studiosus? Ubi Valentinus platonicae sectator? Nam constat illos, neque adeo olim fuisse, Antonini fere principatu, et in catholicae primo doctrinam credidisse apud Ecclesiam romanensem, sub episcopatu Eleutherii benedicti, donec ob inquietam semper eorum curiositatem, qua fratres quoque vitabant semel et iterum ejecti, Marcion quidem cum ducentis sestertiis quae Ecclesiae intulerat, novissime in perpetuum discidium relegati, venena doctrinarum suarum disseminaverunt. Postmodum idem Marcion, poenitentiam confessus cum conditioni datae sibi occurrit, ita pacem recepturus, si caeteros quos perditioni erudisset, Ecclesiae restitueret, morte praeventus est. Oportebat enim haereses esse. Nec tamen ideo bonum haereses, quia eas oportebat, quasi non et malum oportuerit esse. Nam et Dominum tradi oportebat; sed vae traditori? ne quis etiam hinc haereses defendat. Si et Apellis stemma retractandum est, tam non vetus et ipse quam Marcion institutor et praeformator ejus: sed lapsus in foeminam desertor continentiae marcionensis, ab oculis sanctissimi magistri Alexandriam secessit; inde post annos regressus non melior, nisi tantum qua jam non marcionites, in alteram foeminam impegit, illam virginem Philumenen, quam supra edidimus, postea vero immane prostibulum et ipsam, cujus energemate circumventus, quas ab ea didicit phaneroseis scripsit. Adhuc in saeculo supersunt qui meminerint eorum, etiam proprii discentes et successores ipsorum, ne se posteriores negare possint. Quanquam et de operibus suis, ut dixit Dominus, revincuntur. Si enim Marcion Novum Testamentum a Vetere separavit, posterior est eo quod separavit; quia separare non posset, nisi quod unitum fuit. Unitum ergo ante quam separaretur, postea separatum, posteriorem ostendit separatorem. Item Valentinus, aliter exponens, et sine dubio emendans, hoc omnino quicquid emendat, ut mendosum retro, anterius fuisse demonstrat. Hos ut insigniores et frequentiores adulteros veritatis nominamus. Caeterum et Nigidius nescio quis, et Hermogenes, et multi alii qui adhuc ambulant pervertentes vias Dei, ostendant mihi ex qua auctoritate prodierunt. Si alium Deum praedicant, quomodo ejus Dei rebus et litteris et nominibus utuntur adversus quem praedicant? si eumdem, quomodo aliter? Probent se novos apostolos esse: dicant Christum iterum descendisse, iterum ipsum docuisse, iterum crucifixum, iterum mortuum, iterum resuscitatum: sic enim Apostolos solet facere, dare illis praeterea virtutem eadem signa edendi, quae et ipse. Volo igitur et virtutes eorum proferri; nisi quod agnosco maximam virtutem eorum, qua Apostolos in perversum aemulantur: illi enim de mortuis vivos faciebant, isti de vivis mortuos faciunt.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Still, if anyone dares to slot themselves into the apostolic age so they can claim the apostles handed them down—since they were 'under the apostles'—we can say: Let them produce the origins of their churches. Let them lay out the succession of their bishops, running unbroken from the start, so that their first bishop can show an apostle, or an apostolic man who stuck with the apostles, as his author and predecessor. That is how apostolic churches present their credentials: the church of Smyrna reports Polycarp was appointed by John; Rome produces Clement, ordained by Peter; likewise every other church exhibits bishops the apostles installed, as bearers of apostolic seed. Let the heretics fabricate a pedigree like that. What is forbidden them after blasphemy? But even if they forge one, they gain nothing. Their own doctrine, set beside the apostolic, will expose by its variety and contradiction that they have no apostolic author and are not apostolic; because just as the apostles never taught conflicting things among themselves, so apostolic men never proclaimed anything contrary to the apostles—unless those who learned from the apostles preached otherwise. Therefore, they will be tested against those churches which, though they cannot name an apostle or apostolic man as their founder because they are much later, indeed established daily, nevertheless conspire in the same faith and are reckoned no less apostolic by reason of doctrinal kinship. Thus all heresies, challenged by our churches to meet either standard, let them prove themselves apostolic as they imagine. But they are not, they cannot prove what they are not, and they are not received into peace and communion by churches that are in any way apostolic—precisely because of a sacramental difference that is in no way apostolic.

latin: Caeterum, si quae audent interserere se aetati apostolicae, ut ideo videantur ab Apostolis traditae, quia sub Apostolis fuerunt, possumus dicere: Edant ergo origines Ecclesiarum suarum: evolvant ordinem episcoporum suorum, ita per successiones ab initio decurrentem, ut primus ille episcopus aliquem ex Apostolis, vel apostolicis viris, qui tamen cum Apostolis perseveraverit, habuerit auctorem et antecessorem. Hoc enim modo Ecclesiae apostolicae census suos deferunt: sicut Smyrnaeorum Ecclesia Polycarpum ab Joanne conlocatum refert: sicut Romanorum, Clementem a Petro ordinatum edit; proinde utique et caeterae exhibent quos ab Apostolis in episcopatum constitutos apostolici seminis traduces habeant. Confingant tale aliquid Haeretici. Quid enim illis post blasphemiam inlicitum est? Sed etsi confinxerint, nihil promovebunt. Ipsa enim doctrina eorum cum apostolica comparata, ex diversitate et contrarietate sua pronuntiabit, neque apostoli alicujus auctoris esse, neque apostolici; quia sicut Apostoli non diversa inter se docuissent, ita et apostolici non contraria Apostolis edidissent, nisi illi qui ab Apostolis didicerunt aliter praedicaverunt. Ad hanc itaque formam probabuntur ab illis ecclesiis, quae licet nullum ex Apostolis, vel apostolicis, auctorem suum proferant, ut multo posteriores, quae denique quotidie instituuntur; tamen in eadem fide conspirantes, non minus apostolicae deputantur, pro consanguinitate doctrinae. Ita omnes haereses ad utramque formam nostris Ecclesiis provocatae, probent se quaqua putant apostolicas. Sed adeo nec sunt, nec probare possunt quod non sunt, nec recipiuntur in pacem et communicationem ab Ecclesiis quoquo modo apostolicis, scilicet ob diversitatem sacramenti nullo modo apostolicae.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Come now, you who would indulge a better curiosity, if you would apply it to the business of your salvation , run over the apostolic churches , in which the very thrones of the apostles are still pre-eminent in their places, in which their own authentic writings are read, uttering the voice and representing the face of each of them severally. Achaia is very near you, (in which) you find Corinth . Since you are not far from Macedonia, you have Philippi; (and there too) you have the Thessalonians. Since you are able to cross to Asia, you get Ephesus. Since, moreover, you are close upon Italy , you have Rome, from which there comes even into our own hands the very authority (of apostles themselves). How happy is its church, on which apostles poured forth all their doctrine along with their blood! Where Peter endures a passion like his Lord's!

Where Paul wins his crown in a death like John's where the Apostle John was first plunged, unhurt, into boiling oil, and thence remitted to his island-exile! See what she has learned, what taught, what fellowship has had with even (our) churches in Africa! One Lord God does she acknowledge, the Creator of the universe , and Christ Jesus (born) of the Virgin Mary , the Son of God the Creator; and the Resurrection of the flesh; the law and the prophets she unites in one volume with the writings of evangelists and apostles , from which she drinks in her faith . This she seals with the water (of baptism ), arrays with the Holy Ghost, feeds with the Eucharist , cheers with martyrdom , and against such a discipline thus (maintained) she admits no gainsayer.

This is the discipline which I no longer say foretold that heresies should come, but from which they proceeded. However, they were not of her, because they were opposed to her. Even the rough wild-olive arises from the germ of the fruitful, rich, and genuine olive; also from the seed of the mellowest and sweetest fig there springs the empty and useless wild-fig. In the same way heresies , too, come from our plant, although not of our kind; (they come) from the grain of truth , but, owing to their falsehood , they have only wild leaves to show.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: If things stand this way—if the truth is awarded to us, who follow the rule that the Church received from the Apostles, the Apostles from Christ, Christ from God—then the logic of our position is settled: heretics must not be admitted to a contest over Scripture, because we prove, even without Scripture, that they have no claim on it. If they are heretics, they cannot be Christians; they possess nothing from Christ, having chosen to follow their own preference and taken the name 'heretic.' Not being Christians, they hold no right to Christian writings. We are therefore justified in demanding: Who are you? When and where did you come from? What are you doing on my property—property that is not yours? By what right, Marcion, do you cut down my forest? By what license, Valentine, do you divert my springs? By what authority, Apelles, do you move my boundary markers? What are the rest of you sowing and grazing here at your own pleasure? This possession is mine; I have held it for a long time. My title is firm, traced back to the very authors to whom the truth belonged. I am the heir of the Apostles. Just as they safeguarded it in their testament, entrusted it to the faith, and bound it with an oath, so I hold it. You, on the other hand, have always been disinherited and renounced—strangers, enemies. And how else could heretics be strangers and enemies to the Apostles except through a divergence in doctrine, which each one either invented or adopted on his own authority against the Apostles?

latin: Si haec ita se habent, ut veritas nobis adjudicetur, quicumque in ea regula incedimus quam Ecclesia ab Apostolis, Apostoli a Christo, Christus a Deo tradidit, constat ratio propositi nostri, definientis non esse admittendos haereticos ad ineundam de Scripturis provocationem, quos sine Scripturis probamus ad Scripturas non pertinere. Si enim haeretici sunt, christiani esse non possunt, non a Christo habendo quod de sua electione sectati haereticorum nomine admittunt. Ita non christiani, nullum jus capiunt christianarum litterarum. Ad quos merito dicendum est: Qui estis? quando, et unde venistis? quid in meo agitis, non mei? quo denique, Marcion, jure sylvam meam caedis? qua licentia, Valentine, fontes meos transvertis? qua potestate, Apelles, limites meos commoves? Quid hic caeteri ad voluntatem vestram seminatis et pascitis? Mea est possessio; olim possideo: habeo origines firmas, ab ipsis auctoribus quorum fuit res. Ego sum haeres Apostolorum. Sicut caverunt testamento suo, sicut fidei commiserunt, sicut adjuraverunt, ita teneo. Vos certe exhaeredaverunt semper et abdicaverunt, ut extraneos, ut inimicos. Unde autem extranei et inimici Apostolis haeretici, nisi ex diversitate doctrinae, quam unusquisque de suo arbitrio adversus Apostolos, aut protulit, aut recepit?

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: So that is where you have to locate the corruption of Scripture and its interpretation -- right where divergent doctrine shows up. People who set out to teach something different were forced to retool the instruments of doctrine, because they could not teach differently unless they had different tools to teach with. Just as their doctrinal corruption could not have succeeded without corrupting its instruments, so our doctrinal integrity would not be possible without the integrity of the means through which doctrine is handled.

What exactly is the case against us in our own writings? What private material have we ever introduced to fix something contrary to Scripture by subtracting, adding, or transposing? The Scriptures are what we are from their very beginning; we come from them, before anything was otherwise, before you interpolated them. Since every interpolation is by definition later, springing from rivalry -- a rivalry that is neither prior nor native to the thing it rivals -- it is absurd to any wise person that we, who are first and derived from Scripture, should be accused of foisting an adulterated style onto it, while they, who are later and opposed, are not.

One man corrupts Scripture with his hand, another corrupts its sense with his explanation. Even if Valentinus appears to use an intact text, he did not lay hands on the truth with any less cunning than Marcion. Marcion wielded a butcher's cleaver openly, not a pen, because he slaughtered Scripture to supply his own material. Valentinus spared the text, but only because he did not devise Scripture for his material; he devised his material for Scripture. Yet he subtracted more and added more, stripping away the proper force of each word and inserting arrangements of things that do not compare.

latin: Illic igitur et Scripturarum et expositionum adulteratio deputanda est, ubi diversitas doctrinae invenitur. Quibus fuit propositum aliter docendi, eos necessitas coegit aliter disponendi instrumenta doctrinae. Alias enim non potuissent aliter docere, nisi aliter haberent per quae docerent. Sicut illis non potuisset succedere corruptela doctrinae sine corruptela instrumentorum ejus; ita et nobis integritas doctrinae non competisset sine integritate eorum, per quae doctrina tractatur. Etenim quid contrarium nobis in nostris? quid de proprio intulimus, ut aliquid contrarium ei quod esset in Scripturis deprehensum, detractione, vel adjectione, vel transmutatione remediaremus? Quod sumus, hoc sunt Scripturae ab initio suo; ex illis sumus, antequam aliter fuit, antequam a vobis interpolarentur. Cum autem omnis interpolatio posterior credenda sit, veniens utique ex caussa aemulationis, quae neque prior, neque domestica unquam est ejus quod aemulatur, tam incredibile est sapienti cuique, ut nos adulterum stylum intulisse videamur Scripturis, qui sumus et primi et ex ipsis, quam illos non intulisse, qui sunt et posteri et adversi. Alius manu Scripturas, alius sensus expositione intervertit. Neque enim si Valentinus integro instrumento uti videtur, non callidiore ingenio, quam Marcion, manus intulit veritati. Marcion enim exerte et palam machaera, non stylo usus est; quoniam ad materiam suam caedem Scripturarum confecit. Valentinus autem pepercit; quoniam non ad materiam Scripturas, sed materiam ad Scripturas excogitavit: et tamen plus abstulit, et plus adjecit, auferens proprietates singulorum quoque verborum, et adjiciens dispositiones non comparentium rerum.

excerpts.author: Origen
english: 1. All who believe and are assured that grace and truth were obtained through Jesus Christ , and who know Christ to be the truth , agreeably to His own declaration, I am the truth , derive the knowledge which incites men to a good and happy life from no other source than from the very words and teaching of Christ . And by the words of Christ we do not mean those only which He spoke when He became man and tabernacled in the flesh; for before that time, Christ, the Word of God , was in Moses and the prophets . For without the Word of God , how could they have been able to prophesy of Christ? And were it not our purpose to confine the present treatise within the limits of all attainable brevity, it would not be difficult to show, in proof of this statement, out of the Holy Scriptures , how Moses or the prophets both spoke and performed all they did through being filled with the Spirit of Christ . And therefore I think it sufficient to quote this one testimony of Paul from the Epistle to the Hebrews, in which he says: By faith Moses , when he had come to years, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter; choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God , than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season; esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of the Egyptians . Moreover, that after His ascension into heaven He spoke in His apostles , is shown by Paul in these words: Or do you seek a proof of Christ who speaks in me?

2. Since many, however, of those who profess to believe in Christ differ from each other, not only in small and trifling matters, but also on subjects of the highest importance, as, e.g., regarding God , or the Lord Jesus Christ , or the Holy Spirit ; and not only regarding these, but also regarding others which are created existences, viz., the powers and the holy virtues ; it seems on that account necessary first of all to fix a definite limit and to lay down an unmistakable rule regarding each one of these, and then to pass to the investigation of other points. For as we ceased to seek for truth (notwithstanding the professions of many among Greeks and Barbarians to make it known ) among all who claimed it for erroneous opinions, after we had come to believe that Christ was the Son of God , and were persuaded that we must learn it from Himself; so, seeing there are many who think they hold the opinions of Christ , and yet some of these think differently from their predecessors, yet as the teaching of the Church , transmitted in orderly succession from the apostles , and remaining in the Churches to the present day, is still preserved, that alone is to be accepted as truth which differs in no respect from ecclesiastical and apostolic tradition.

3. Now it ought to be known that the holy apostles , in preaching the faith of Christ , delivered themselves with the utmost clearness on certain points which they believed to be necessary to every one, even to those who seemed somewhat dull in the investigation of divine knowledge ; leaving, however, the grounds of their statements to be examined into by those who should deserve the excellent gifts of the Spirit , and who, especially by means of the Holy Spirit Himself, should obtain the gift of language, of wisdom, and of knowledge : while on other subjects they merely stated the fact that things were so, keeping silence as to the manner or origin of their existence ; clearly in order that the more zealous of their successors, who should be lovers of wisdom, might have a subject of exercise on which to display the fruit of their talents — those persons , I mean, who should prepare themselves to be fit and worthy receivers of wisdom.

4. The particular points clearly delivered in the teaching of the apostles are as follow:— First , That there is one God , who created and arranged all things, and who, when nothing existed , called all things into being — God from the first creation and foundation of the world — the God of all just men, of Adam, Abel, Seth, Enos, Enoch , Noe, Sere, Abraham , Isaac, Jacob, the twelve patriarchs, Moses , and the prophets ; and that this God in the last days, as He had announced beforehand by His prophets , sent our Lord Jesus Christ to call in the first place Israel to Himself, and in the second place the Gentiles , after the unfaithfulness of the people of Israel . This just and good God , the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ , Himself gave the law and the prophets , and the Gospels , being also the God of the apostles and of the Old and New Testaments. Secondly , That Jesus Christ Himself, who came (into the world), was born of the Father before all creatures; that, after He had been the servant of the Father in the creation of all things — For by Him were all things made — He in the last times, divesting Himself (of His glory ), became a man , and was incarnate although God , and while made a man remained the God which He was; that He assumed a body like to our own, differing in this respect only, that it was born of a virgin and of the Holy Spirit : that this Jesus Christ was truly born, and did truly suffer, and did not endure this death common (to man) in appearance…

excerpts.author: Cyprian
english: Treatise 1 (Cyprian of Carthage) Home > Fathers of the Church > Treatises (Cyprian of Carthage) > Treatise 1 Treatise 1 On the Unity of the Church. Argument.— On the Occasion of the Schism of Novatian , to Keep Back from Him the Carthaginians, Who Already Were Not Averse to Him, on Account of Novatus and Some Other Presbyters of His Church, Who Had Originated the Whole Disturbance, Cyprian Wrote This Treatise. And First of All, Fortifying Them Against the Deceits of These, He Exhorts Them to Constancy, and Instructs Them that Heresies Exist Because Christ, the Head of the Church , is Not Looked To, that the Common Commission First Entrusted to Peter is Contemned, and the One Church and the One Episcopate are Deserted. Then He Proves, as Well by the Scriptures as by the Figures of the Old and New Testament , the Unity of the Church .

1. Since the Lord warns us, saying, You are the salt of the earth, Matthew 5:13 and since He bids us to be simple to harmlessness, and yet with our simplicity to be prudent , what else, beloved brethren, befits us, than to use foresight and watching with an anxious heart, both to perceive and to beware of the wiles of the crafty foe, that we, who have put on Christ the wisdom of God the Father , may not seem to be wanting in wisdom in the matter of providing for our salvation ? For it is not persecution alone that is to be feared; nor those things which advance by open attack to overwhelm and cast down the servants of God . Caution is more easy where danger is manifest, and the mind is prepared beforehand for the contest when the adversary avows himself. The enemy is more to be feared and to be guarded against, when he creeps on us secretly; when, deceiving by the appearance of peace, he steals forward by hidden approaches, whence also he has received the name of the Serpent. That is always his subtlety; that is his dark and stealthy artifice for circumventing man. Thus from the very beginning of the world he deceived; and flattering with lying words, he misled inexperienced souls by an incautious credulity. Thus he endeavoured to tempt the Lord Himself: he secretly approached Him, as if he would creep on Him again, and deceive; yet he was understood, and beaten back, and therefore prostrated, because he was recognised and detected.

2. From which an example is given us to avoid the way of the old man, to stand in the footsteps of a conquering Christ, that we may not again be incautiously turned back into the nets of death, but, foreseeing our danger, may possess the immortality that we have received. But how can we possess immortality , unless we keep those commands of Christ whereby death is driven out and overcome, when He Himself warns us, and says, If you will enter into life, keep the commandments? Matthew 19:17 And again: If you do the things that I command you, henceforth I call you not servants, but friends. excerpts.author: Eusebius of Caesarea
english: 1. This writer has left us a great many monuments of a mind educated and practiced in divine things, which are replete with profitable matter of every kind. To them we shall refer the studious, noting as we proceed those that have come to our knowledge .

2. There is a certain discourse of his in defense of our doctrine addressed to Antoninus surnamed the Pious , and to his sons, and to the Roman senate. Another work contains his second Apology in behalf of our faith , which he offered to him who was the successor of the emperor mentioned and who bore the same name, Antoninus Verus , the one whose times we are now recording.

3. Also another work against the Greeks, in which he discourses at length upon most of the questions at issue between us and the Greek philosophers , and discusses the nature of demons . It is not necessary for me to add any of these things here.

4. And still another work of his against the Greeks has come down to us, to which he gave the title Refutation. And besides these another, On the Sovereignty of God, which he establishes not only from our Scriptures, but also from the books of the Greeks.
