excerpts.author: Eusebius of Caesarea
english: 1. In those days also Melito , bishop of the parish in Sardis , and Apolinarius, bishop of Hierapolis, enjoyed great distinction. Each of them on his own part addressed apologies in behalf of the faith to the above-mentioned emperor of the Romans who was reigning at that time.

2. The following works of these writers have come to our knowledge . Of Melito , the two books On the Passover , and one On the Conduct of Life and the Prophets , the discourse On the Church , and one On the Lord's Day , still further one On the Faith of Man , and one On his Creation , another also On the Obedience of Faith , and one On the Senses ; besides these the work On the Soul and Body , and that On Baptism , and the one On Truth , and On the Creation and Generation of Christ ; his discourse also On Prophecy , and that On Hospitality ; still further, The Key , and the books On the Devil and the Apocalypse of John , and the work On the Corporeality of God , and finally the book addressed to Antoninus .

3. In the books On the Passover he indicates the time at which he wrote, beginning with these words: While Servilius Paulus was proconsul of Asia, at the time when Sagaris suffered martyrdom , there arose in Laodicea a great strife concerning the Passover , which fell according to rule in those days; and these were written.
4. And Clement of Alexandria refers to this work in his own discourse On the Passover , which, he says, he wrote on occasion of Melito's work.

excerpts.author: Barnabas
english: But let us see if this people is the heir, or the former, and if the covenant belongs to us or to them. Hear now what the Scripture says concerning the people. Isaac prayed for Rebecca his wife, because she was barren; and she conceived. Genesis 25:21 Furthermore also, Rebecca went forth to inquire of the Lord; and the Lord said to her, Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples in your belly; and the one people shall surpass the other, and the elder shall serve the younger. Genesis 25:23 You ought to understand who was Isaac, who Rebecca, and concerning what persons He declared that this people should be greater than that. And in another prophecy Jacob speaks more clearly to his son Joseph, saying, Behold, the Lord has not deprived me of your presence; bring your sons to me, that I may bless them.

And he brought Manasseh and Ephraim, desiring that Manasseh should be blessed, because he was the elder. With this view Joseph led him to the right hand of his father Jacob. But Jacob saw in spirit the type of the people to arise afterwards. And what says [the Scripture ]? And Jacob changed the direction of his hands, and laid his right hand upon the head of Ephraim, the second and younger, and blessed him. And Joseph said to Jacob, Transfer your right hand to the head of Manasseh, for he is my first-born son. Genesis 48:18 And Jacob said, I know it, my son, I know it; but the elder shall serve the younger: yet he also shall be blessed. Genesis 48:19 You see on whom he laid [his hands], that this people should be first, and heir of the covenant.

If then, still further, the same thing was intimated through Abraham , we reach the perfection of our knowledge . What, then, says He to Abraham ? Because you have believed , it is imputed to you for righteousness: behold, I have made you the father of those nations who believe in the Lord while in [a state of] uncircumcision.

excerpts.author: Barnabas
english: Yes, but let us see whether the covenant God swore to give the people was actually given. It was given, but the people themselves were not worthy to receive it because of their sins. The prophet says that Moses fasted on Mount Sinai for forty days and forty nights to receive the Lord's covenant for the people. Moses received the two tablets, written by the finger of the Lord's own hand in the Spirit, and brought them down to give to the people. Then the Lord said to Moses, "Moses, Moses, come down quickly, because your people, whom you led out of Egypt, have acted lawlessly" (Exod 32:7). Moses understood they had made molten idols for themselves again, so he threw the tablets from his hands and they shattered. Moses received the covenant, but the people proved unworthy.

So how did we receive it? Learn this: Moses received it as a servant, but the Lord Himself gave it to us as a people of inheritance, having endured suffering for our sake. He was revealed so that they might be completed in their sins, and so that we, through the heir of the Lord's covenant, Jesus, might receive it. He was prepared for this very purpose: that by appearing He might redeem our hearts—hearts already spent on death and handed over to the lawlessness of error—from darkness, and might establish a covenant with us in word. Scripture says this is how the Father commands Him: having redeemed us from darkness, He is to prepare a holy people for Himself (Isaiah 42:6-7). The prophet declares, "I am the Lord your God; I called you in righteousness, I will hold your hand and strengthen you. I gave you as a covenant to the nation, a light to the nations, to open blind eyes and bring out those bound in chains from prison, those sitting in darkness."

We know, then, from what we were redeemed. Again the prophet says: "Behold, I have set you as a light to the nations, to be salvation to the end of the earth," says the Lord who redeemed you, God (Isaiah 49:6). And again the prophet says: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because He anointed me to preach good news to the poor; He sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to proclaim release to captives and sight to the blind, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense, to comfort all who mourn" (Isaiah 61:1-2).

Μωϋσῆ Μωϋσῆ, κατάβηθι τὸ τάχος, ὅτι ὁ λαός σου, ὃν ἐξήγαγες ἐκ γῆς Αἰγύπτου. ἠνόμησεν. καὶ συνῆκεν Μωϋσῆς, ὅτι ἐποίησαν ἑαυτοῖς πάλιν χωνεύματα, καὶ ἔρριψεν ἐκ τῶν χειρῶν, καὶ συνετρίβησαν αἱ πλάκες τῆς διαθήκης κυρίου. Μωϋσῆς μὲν ἔλαβεν, αὐτοὶ δὲ οὐκ ἐγένοντο ἄξιοι. πῶς δὲ ἡμεῖς ἐλάβομεν, μάθετε. Μωϋσῆς θεράπων ὢν ἔλαβεν, αὐτὸς δὲ κύριος ἡμῖν ἔδωκεν εἰς λαὸν κληρονομίας, δἰ ἡμᾶς ὑπομείνας. ἐφανερώθη δέ. ἵνα κἀκεῖνοι τελειωθῶσιν τοῖς ἁμαρτήμασιν, καὶ ἡμεῖς διὰ τοῦ κληρονομοῦντος διαθήκην κυρίου Ἰησοῦ λάβωμεν, ὃς εἰς τοῦτο ἡτοιμάσθη, ἵνα αὐτὸς φανείς, τὰς ἤδη δεδαπανημένας ἡμῶν καρδίας τῷ θανάτῳ καὶ παραδεδομένας τῇ τῆς πλάνης ἀνομίᾳ λυτρωσάμενος ἐκ τοῦ σκότους, διάθηται ἐν ἡμῖν διαθήκην λόγῳ. γέγραπται γάρ, πῶς αὐτῷ ὁ πατὴρ ἐντέλλεται, λυτρωσάμενον ἡμᾶς ἐκ τοῦ σκότους ἑτοιμάσαι ἑαυτῷ λαὸν ἅγιον. λέγει οὖν ὁ προφήτης: Ἐγὼ κύριος, ὁ θεός σου, ἐκάλεσά σε ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ καὶ κρατήσω τῆς χειρός σου καὶ ἐνισχύσω σε, καὶ ἔδωκά σε εἰς διαθήκην γένους, εἰς φῶς ἐθνῶν ἀνοῖξαι ὀφθαλμοὺς τυφλῶν καὶ ἐξαγαγεῖν ἐκ δεσμῶν πεπεδημένους καὶ ἐξ οἴκου φυλακῆς καθημένους ἐν σκότει. γινώσκομεν οὖν, πόθεν ἐλυτρώθημεν. πάλιν ὁ προφήτης λέγει: Ἰδού, τέθεικά σε εἰς φῶς ἐθνῶν, τοῦ εἶναί σε εἰς σωτηρίαν ἕως ἐσχάτου τῆς γῆς, οὕτως λέγει κύριος ὁ λυτρωσάμενός σε θεός. καὶ πάλιν ὁ προφήτης λέγει: Πνεῦμα κυρίου ἐπ’ ἐμέ, οὖ εἵνεκεν ἔχρισέν με εὐαγγελίσασθαι ταπεινοῖς χάριν, ἀπέσταλκέν με ἰάσασθαι τοὺς συντετριμμένους τὴν καρδίαν, κηρῦξαι αἰχμαλώτοις ἄφεσιν καὶ τυφλοῖς ἀνάβλεψιν, καλέσαι ἐνιαυτὸν κυρίου δεκτὸν καὶ ἡμέραν ἀνταποδόσεως, παρακαλέσαι πάντας τοὺς πενθοῦντας.

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: John, the Lord's disciple, proclaims this faith because he wants to tear out the error that Cerinthus sowed in human hearts — and earlier still, the error that the so-called Nicolaitans planted. They are a counterfeit offshoot, wrongly named, whose purpose is to confuse people and to persuade them that one God made everything through his Word. The heretics deny this. They claim there is one creator and another, different Father of the Lord; one son of the creator, and another Christ from above who, they say, stayed impassible, descended into Jesus the creator's son, and then flew back to his Pleroma. They call the Trinity "the Only-begotten," and the Logos "the true son of the Only-begotten." They insist that our material condition was not made by the first God but by some power far below, cut off from the invisible, ineffable realm above. Therefore the Lord's disciple, wanting to enclose all such teachings and to establish the rule of truth in the Church — because there is one almighty God who made all things, visible and invisible, through his Word — also signals that through the Word, by which God perfected the creation, he has provided salvation for people who live in that creation. So he begins his Gospel teaching: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God (John 1:1). He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made. What was made held life in him, and that life was the light of humanity; the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it. "All things," he says, "were made through him"; therefore this creation of ours is included among those all things. The heretics cannot claim that everything they name exists only below their Pleroma. If their Pleroma contains these things, then this creation is not outside it — as we showed in the previous book. But if these things lie outside the Pleroma, which is impossible, then their Pleroma is not "all things"; so this creation cannot be outside it either. John himself has removed every dissension from us by declaring: He was in the world, and the world was made through him, yet the world did not know him. He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him. But according to Marcion and those like him, the world was not made through him, nor did he come to his own — he came to what is alien. According to certain Gnostics, angels made this world, not the Word of God. According to the Valentinians, the world was not made through him but through the Demiurge. They say the Demiurge fashioned the creation by forming likenesses that imitate the realities above. They claim the Lord and the Demiurge were sent by the Mother, through whom they want the world to have been made — yet the Gospel plainly says that all things were made through the Word who was in the beginning with God, and that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). According to them, neither the Word nor Christ nor the Savior (whom they say was composed from all things) became flesh. They refuse to let the Word and Christ enter this world; they say the Savior did not become incarnate or suffer, but descended like a dove into Jesus — who came from their "disposition" — announced the unknown Father, and then ascended back to the Pleroma. Some say Jesus from the disposition was incarnate and suffered, passing through Mary like water through a pipe. Others say the Demiurge's son received the Jesus from the disposition. Others say Jesus was born of Joseph and Mary, and the impassible, fleshless Christ from above descended into him. By no heretical opinion did the Word of God become flesh. If anyone examines all their systems, he will find that every one of them presents the Word of God and the Christ from above as fleshless and impassible. Some think he merely appeared, like a transfigured man, yet they deny he was born or became incarnate. Others say he did not even assume human form, but descended like a dove into the Jesus born of Mary. Thus the Lord's disciple, exposing all these as false witnesses, declares: The Word became flesh and dwelt among us. And so that we do not ask whose Word became flesh, he himself teaches further: There was a man sent from God, named John; he came as a witness to testify about the light. He was not the light, but came to testify about the light. So John the forerunner, who testifies to the light — by which God was he sent? Surely by the God whose angel is Gabriel, who also announced his birth; who promised through the prophets to send his angel before the face of his Son to prepare his way — that is, to testify about the light — in the spirit and power of Elijah. And Elijah was the servant and prophet of which God? The God who made heaven and earth, as Elijah himself confesses. Therefore John was sent by the founder and creator of this world. How else could he testify about the light that descended from the invisible, ineffable realm? All heretics have decreed that the Demiurge is ignorant of the power above him, yet John is found to be the witness and revealer of that power. That is why the Lord said John was more than a prophet. All the other prophets announced the coming of the Father's light; they longed to see the one they preached. But John not only announced him like the rest — he saw him coming, pointed him out, and persuaded many to believe in him, so that he holds the place of both prophet and apostle.

latin: Hane fidem annuntians Johannes Domini discipulus, volens per Evangelii annuntiationem auferre eum, qui a Cerintho inseminatus erat hominibus errorem, et multo prius ab his qui dicuntur Nicolaite, qui sunt vulsio ejus quee falso cognominatur ut confunderet eos, et suaderet quoniam unus Deus qui omnia fecit per Verbum suum ; et non, quemadmodum illi dicunt, alterum quidem fabricatorem, alium autem Patrem Domini: et alium quidem fabricatoris filium, alterum vero ®de superioribus Christum, quem et impassibilem perseverasse, descendentem in Jesum filium fabricatoris, et iterum revolasse in suum Pleroma: et Tinitium quidem esse monogenem; Logon autem verum filium unigeniti: et eam conditionem quze est secundum nos, non a primo Deo factam, sed a virtute aliqua valde deorsum subjecta, et abscissa ab eorum communicatione quze sunt invisibilia et innominabilia. Omnia igitur talia cireumscribere volens discipulus Domini, et ' regulam veritatis constituere in Ecclesia, quia est unus Deus omnipotens, qui per Verbum suum omnia fecit, et visibilia et invisibilia; significans quoque, quoniam per Verbum, per quod Deus perfecit conditionem, in hoe et salutem his qui in conditione sunt preestitit hominibus; sic inchoavit in ea que est secundum Evangelium doctrina: Jn principio erat Verbum, et Verbum erat apud Deum, et Deus erat Verbum: hoc erat in principio apud Deum. Omnia per ipsum facta sunt, et sine ipso factum est nihil. Quod factum est, in ipso vita erat, et vita erat lua hominum, et lux in tenebris lucet, et tenebre eam non comprehenderunt. Omnia, inquit, per ipsum facta sunt ; in omnibus ergo est et hzee quae secundum nos est conditio: non enim concedetur eis, omnia dici ea que sunt infra Pleroma ipsorum. Si enim et hee Pleroma ipsorum continet, non extra est tanta ista conditio, quemadmodum ostendimus in eo libro qui ante hune est ; si autem extra Pleroma sunt heec, quod quidem impossibile visum est, jam non est omnia Pleroma ipsorum: non est ergo extra heee tanta conditio. Abstulit autem a nobis dissensiones omnes ipse Johannes, dicens: In hoc mundo erat, et mundus per ipsum factus est, et mundus eum non cognovit. In sua propria venit, et sui eum non receperunt. Secundum autem Marcionem et eos qui similes sunt ei, neque mundus per eum factus est ; neque in sua venit, sed in aliena, Secundum autem quosdam Gnosticorum, ¢ab angelis factus est iste mundus, et non per Verbum Dei. Secundum autem eos qui sunt a Valentino, iterum non per eum factus est, sed per Demiurgum. Hic enim operabatur similitudines tales fieri, ad imitationem eorum que sunt sursum, quemadmodum dicunt: Demiurgus autem perficiebat fabricationem conditionis. Emissum enim dicunt eum a matre Dominum et Demiurgum ejus dispositionis quee est secundum conditionem, per quem hune mundum factum volunt: cum Evangelium manifeste dicat, quoniam per Verbum, quod in principio erat apud Deum, omnia sunt facta: quod Verbum, inquit, caro factum est, et habitavit in nobis. 8. Secundum autem illos, neque Verbum caro factum est, neque Christus, neque qui ex omnibus factus est Salvator. Htenim Verbum et Christum nec advenisse in hune mundum volunt: Salvatorem vero non incarnatum neque passum; descendisse autem quasi columbam in eum Jesum qui factus est ex dispositione, et cum annuntiasset incognitum Patrem, iterum ascendisse in Pleroma. Incarnatum autem et passum quidam quidem eum qui ex dispositione sit dicunt Jesum, quem per Mariam dicunt pertransisse, quasi aquam per tubum: alii vero ° Demiurgi filium, in quem descendisse eum Jesum qui ex dispositione sit: alii rursum Jesum quidem ex Joseph et Maria natum dicunt, et in hune descendisse Christum qui de superioribus sit, sine carne et impassibilem exsistentem. Secundum autem nullam sententiam heereticorum, Verbum Dei caro factum est. Si enim quis regulas ipsorum omnium perscrutetur, inveniet quoniam sine carne et impassibilis ab omnibus illis inducitur Dei Verbum, et qui est in superioribus Christus. Alii enim putant manifestatum eum, quemadmodum hominem transfiguratum; neque autem natum, neque incarnatum dicunt illum: alii vero neque figuram eum assumsisse hominis; sed quemadmodum columbam descendisse in eum Jesum, qui natus est ex Maria. Omnes igitur illos falsos testes ostendens discipulus Domini, ait: Ht Verbum caro factum est, et habitavit in nobis. Et ut non inquiramus, cujus Dei Verbum caro factum est, ipse insuper docet, dicens : Fuit homo missus a Deo, erat ei nomen Johannes: hic venit in testimonium, ut testaretur de lumine. Non erat ipse lumen, sed ut testaretur de lumine. Preecursor igitur Johannes, qui testatur de lumine, a quo Deo missus est? Utique ab eo cujus Gabriel est angelus, qui etiam evangelisavit generationem ejus; qui et per prophetas promisit angelum suum missurum ante faciem Filii sui, et preeparaturum viam ejus, hoc est, testificaturum de lumine, i spiritw et virtute Helie. Helias autem rursus cujus Dei servus et propheta fuit? Ejus qui fecit coelum et terram, quemadmodum et ipse confitetur. A conditore igitur et fabricatore hujus mundi missus Johannes, quemadmodum poterat testificari de eo lumine, quod ex his que sunt innominabilia et invisibilia descenderit ? Omnes enim heeretici decreverunt, Demiurgum ignorare eam que sit super eum virtutem, cujus testis et ostensor invenitur Johannes. Propter hoc Dominus plus quam prophetam dixit eum habuisse. Reliqui enim omnes prophetze annuntiaverunt adventum paterni luminis; concupierunt autem digni esse videre eum quem preedicabant: Johannes autem et preenuntiavit similiter sicut alii, et advenientem vidit et demonstravit, et credere in eum suasit multis, ita ut ipse et prophete et apostoli locum habuerit.

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: Therefore, since these demonstrations stand, there is no need to go searching for the truth among others, when it is so easy to receive it from the Church. The Apostles, like men entrusting a treasure to a rich repository, deposited the fullness of truth in her, so that anyone who wishes may draw from her the drink of life. This is the entrance to life; all the rest, however, are thieves and robbers. For this reason we must avoid them, but we must love the things that belong to the Church with the greatest diligence and lay hold of the tradition of truth.

What if a dispute arose over some minor question? Would it not be necessary to turn to the most ancient churches, where the Apostles conversed, and learn from them what is certain and clear regarding the present issue? What if the Apostles had not even left us the Scriptures? Would it not then be necessary to follow the order of tradition, which they handed down to those to whom they entrusted the churches?

Many nations of barbarians who believe in Christ assent to this order. They possess salvation written in their hearts by the Spirit, without paper or ink, carefully preserving the ancient tradition. They believe in one God, the maker of heaven and earth and all that is in them, through Christ Jesus, the Son of God. Because of his surpassing love for his creation, he endured his birth from the Virgin, himself uniting man to God. He suffered under Pontius Pilate, rose again, was received in glory, and will come in glory as the Savior of those who are saved and the Judge of those who are judged. He will send into eternal fire the transgressors of truth and the despisers of his Father and his coming.

Those who have believed this faith without written documents are, in respect to our speech, barbarians; but in respect to judgment, custom, and conduct, they are supremely wise because of their faith, and they please God, living in all justice, chastity, and wisdom. If anyone announces to them the inventions of the heretics, speaking in the heretics' own tongue, they immediately stop their ears and flee far away, refusing even to endure such blasphemous talk. Thus, through that ancient tradition of the elders, they do not admit the heretics' portentous speech even into the conception of their minds, for there was no assembly among them and no instituted doctrine.

Before Valentinus came, those who are from Valentinus did not exist; nor did those who are from Marcion exist before Marcion; nor did any of the other malignant opinions enumerated above exist to become the authors of their perversity. Valentinus came to Rome under Hyginus, flourished under Pius, and remained until Anicetus. Cerdon, Marcion's predecessor, also came to Rome under Hyginus, the eighth bishop, frequently entering the Church and making confession. He ended this way: sometimes teaching secretly, sometimes making confession, sometimes corrected by others for his bad teaching, and he kept away from the gathering of the devout. Marcion succeeded him and grew strong under Anicetus, who held the tenth place in the episcopate. The rest who are called Gnostics received their start from Menander, Simon's disciple, as we have shown; each one, having shared in a particular opinion, became its father and high priest. All these men arose much later, in the midst of the Church's times, to launch their apostasy.

Hee est enim vitze introitus; omnes autem reliqui fures sunt et latrones. Propter quod oportet devitare quidem illos; que autem sunt Ecclesiz, cum summa diligentia diligere, et apprehendere veritatis traditionem. Quid enim? Et si de aliqua modica queestione disceptatio esset, nonne oporteret in antiquissimas recurrere ecclesias, in quibus Apostoli conversati sunt, et ab eis de presenti quastione sumere quod certum et re liquidum est? Quid autem si neque Apostoli quidem Scripturas reliquissent nobis, nonne oportebat ordinem sequi_ traditionis, quam tradiderunt iis quibus committebant ecclesias? Cui ordinationi assentiunt multze gentes barbarorum eorum qui in Christum credunt, sine charta vel atramento scriptam habentes per Spiritum in cordibus suis salutem, et veterem traditionem diligenter custodientes, in unum Deum credentes fabricatorem cceli et terree, et omnium quz in eis sunt, per Christum Jesum Dei Filium. Qui propter eminentissimam erga figmentum suum dilectionem, eam que esset ex Virgine generationem sustinuit, ipse per se hominem adunans Deo, et passus sub Pontio Pilato, et resurgens, et in claritate receptus, in gloria venturus Salvator eorum qui salvantur, et judex eorum qui judicantur, et mittens in ignem sternum transfiguratores veritatis, et contemtores Patris sui et adventus ejus. Hane fidem qui sine literis crediderunt, quantum ad sermonem nostrum, barbari sunt: quantum autem ad sententiam, et consuetudinem, et conversationem, propter fidem perquam sapientissimi sunt, et placent Deo, conversantes in omni justitia et castitate et sapientia. Quibus si aliquis annuntiaverit ea que ab hereticis adinventa sunt, proprio sermone eorum colloquens, statim concludentes aures longo longius fugient, ne audire quidem sustinentes blasphemum colloquium. | Sie per illam veterem stolorum traditionem, ne in conceptionem quidem mentis admittunt, quodcunque eorum portentiloquium est, neque enim congregatio fuit apud eos, neque doctrina instituta. 2. Ante Valentinum enim non fuerunt, qui sunt a Valentino; neque ante Marcionem erant, qui sunt a Marcione; neque omnino erant reliqui sensus maligni, quos supra enumeravimus, initiatores et inventores perversitatis eorum fierent. Valentinus enim venit Romam sub Hygino; Pio, et prorogavit tempus usque ad Anicetum. Oerdon autem qui ante Marcionem, et hic sub Hygino, qui fuit octavus episcopus, seepe in ecclesiam veniens, et exhomologesin faciens, sic consummavit, modo quidem latenter docens, modo vero exhomologesin faciens, modo vero ab aliquibus traductus in his que docebat male, et abstentus est a religiosorum hominum conventu. 3. Marcion autem illi succedens invaluit sub Aniceto, !}decimum locum episcopatus continente. Reliqui vero qui vocantur Gnostici, a Menandro Simonis discipulo, quemadmodum ostendimus, accipientes initia, unusquisque eorum, cujus participatus est sententiz, ejus et pater, et antistes apparuit. Omnes autem hi multo posterius, mediantibus jam Ecclesize temporibus, insurrexerunt in suam apostasiam.

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: 1. But that it was not only the prophets and many righteous men, who, foreseeing through the Holy Spirit His advent, prayed that they might attain to that period in which they should see their Lord face to face, and hear His words, the Lord has made manifest, when He says to His disciples , Many prophets and righteous men have desired to see those things which you see, and have not seen them; and to hear those things which you hear, and have not heard them. Matthew 13:17 In what way, then, did they desire both to hear and to see, unless they had foreknowledge of His future advent? But how could they have foreknown it, unless they had previously received foreknowledge from Himself? And how do the Scriptures testify of Him, unless all things had ever been revealed and shown to believers by one and the same God through the Word; He at one time conferring with His creature, and at another propounding His law; at one time, again, reproving, at another exhorting, and then setting free His servant, and adopting him as a son ( in filium ); and, at the proper time, bestowing an incorruptible inheritance, for the purpose of bringing man to perfection? For He formed him for growth and increase, as the Scripture says: Increase and multiply. Genesis 1:28

2. And in this respect God differs from man, that God indeed makes, but man is made; and truly , He who makes is always the same; but that which is made must receive both beginning, and middle, and addition, and increase. And God does indeed create after a skilful manner, while, [as regards] man, he is created skilfully. God also is truly perfect in all things, Himself equal and similar to Himself, as He is all light, and all mind , and all substance, and the fount of all good; but man receives advancement and increase towards God. For as God is always the same, so also man, when found in God , shall always go on towards God. For neither does God at any time cease to confer benefits upon, or to enrich man; nor does man ever cease from receiving the benefits, and being enriched by God . For the receptacle of His goodness, and the instrument of His glorification, is the man who is grateful to Him that made him; and again, the receptacle of His just judgment is the ungrateful man, who both despises his Maker and is not subject to His Word; who has promised that He will give very much to those always bringing forth fruit, and more [and more] to those who have the Lord's money. Well done, He says, good and faithful servant: because you have been faithful in little, I will appoint you over many things; enter into the joy of your Lord. Matthew 25:21 , etc. The Lord Himself thus promises very much.

3. As, therefore, He has promised to give very much to those who do now bring forth fruit, according to the gift of His grace , but not according to the changeableness of knowledge ; for the Lord remains the same, and the same Father is revealed; thus, therefore, has the one and the same Lord granted, by means of His advent, a greater gift of grace to those of a later period, than what He had granted to those under the Old Testament dispensation. For they indeed used to hear, by means of [His] servants, that the King would come, and they rejoiced to a certain extent, inasmuch as they hoped for His coming; but those who have beheld Him actually present, and have obtained liberty, and been made partakers of His gifts, do possess a greater amount of grace , and a higher degree of exultation, rejoicing because of the King's arrival: as also David says, My soul shall rejoice in the Lord; it shall be glad in His salvation . And for this cause , upon His entrance into Jerusalem, all those who were in the way recognised David their king in His sorrow of soul , and spread their garments for Him, and ornamented the way with green boughs, crying out with great joy and gladness , Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is He that comes in the name of the Lord: hosanna in the highest. Matthew 21:8 But to the envious wicked stewards, who circumvented those under them, and ruled over those that had no great intelligence, and for this reason were unwilling that the king should come, and who…

4. If, therefore, the self-same person is present who was announced by the prophets , our Lord Jesus Christ , and if His advent has brought in a fuller [measure of] grace and greater gifts to those who have received Him, it is plain that the Father also is Himself the same who was proclaimed by the prophets , and that the Son , on His coming, did not spread the knowledge of another Father, but of the same who was preached from the beginning; from whom also He has brought down liberty to those who, in a lawful manner, and with a willing mind , and with all the heart, do Him service; whereas to scoffers, and to those not subject to God , but who follow outward purifications for the praise of men (which observances had been given as a type of future things — the law typifying, as it were, certain things in a shadow, and delineating eternal things by temporal, celestial by terrestrial), and to those who pretend that they do themselves observe more than what has been prescribed, as if preferring their own zeal to God Himself, while within they are full of hypocrisy, and covetousness , and all wickedness — [to such] has He assigned everlasting perdition by cutting them off from life.

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: We do not know God by his magnitude; it is impossible to measure the Father. But we are led to God through his Word by his love, and by obeying him we always learn how great God is. He himself establishes, chooses, and adorns all things through himself — he who is present to us. And so we have been made together with everything he contains. This is what Scripture says: God formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life (Genesis 2:7). Therefore angels did not make us; they did not form us, nor could angels fashion the image of God. No one else could do it except the Word of the Lord — no power far removed from the Father. God did not need such agents to accomplish what he had predetermined, as if he lacked his own hands. The Word and Wisdom, the Son and the Spirit, are always present to him; through them and in them he freely and willingly made all things. To them he speaks, saying, "Let us make man in our image and likeness"; he himself takes from himself the substance of creatures, the pattern of things made, and the design of the world's ornaments.

Et nos igitur cum his que continentur ab eo, factisumus. Et hic est de quo Scriptura ait; Ht plasmavit Deus hominem, limum terre accipiens, et insufflavit in faciem ejus Jjlatum vite. Non ergo angeli fecerunt, nos, nec nos plasmaverunt, nec angeli potuerunt imaginem facere Dei, nec alius quis preter Verbum Domini, nec virtus longe absistens a Patre uniNec enim indigebat horum Deus ad faciendum quie ipse apud se preefinierat fieri, quasi ipse suas non haberet manus. Adest enim ei semper Verbum et Sapientia, Filius et Spiritus, per quos, et in quibus omnia libere et sponte fecit, ad quos et loquitur, dicens: Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram; ipse a semetipso substantiam creaturarum, et exemplum factorum, et figuram in mundo ornamentorum accipiens.

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: All things are of one and the same substance — that is, they come from one and the same God — just as the Lord says to the disciples: "Therefore every scribe who has been trained for the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings out of his treasure what is new and what is old" (Matt 13:52). He did not teach that one person brings out the old and another the new; it is one and the same householder. The Lord is that householder, who rules the whole household of God paternally: to the servants and those still undisciplined he gives a law worthy of them, but to the children, justified by faith, he gives fitting precepts, and to the sons he opens his inheritance. He calls his disciples scribes and teachers of the kingdom of heaven, and of them he also says elsewhere to the Jews: "I send you prophets and wise men and scribes... and you will kill some of them and persecute them from town to town" (Matt 23:34). Thus the new and old brought out of the treasure speak, without contradiction, of the two testaments: the old, which was the former legislation, and the new, which is the way of life according to the Gospel. Of this David says: "Sing to the Lord a new song" (Ps 96:1), and Isaiah: "Sing to the Lord a new hymn" (Isa 42:10). "From the ends of the earth his name is praised; his deeds are proclaimed in the islands" (Isa 24:16; 42:12). And Jeremiah says: "Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord, when I will make a new covenant... not like the covenant I made with their fathers at Mount Horeb" (Jer 31:31). Both testaments, however, are produced by one and the same householder — the Word of God, our Lord Jesus Christ — who spoke with Abraham and Moses, who restored liberty to us in newness and multiplied it, which comes from him.

For he says: "Something greater than the temple is here" (Matt 12:6), and "greater than Solomon... greater than Jonah" (Matt 12:41-42), for he gives to men his presence and resurrection from the dead. But he does not change God, nor does he proclaim another Father; he proclaims the same One who always has more for his household, and as their love for God progresses, he gives more and greater gifts — just as the Lord told the disciples: "You will see greater things than these" (John 1:50), and Paul says: "Not that I have already obtained this or am already perfect... For we know in part and we prophesy in part, but when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away" (1 Cor 13:9-10). So when the perfect comes, we will not see another Father, but this One whom we now long to see, for "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God" (Matt 5:8). We will not wait for another Christ and Son of God, but for this One who was born of the Virgin Mary, who suffered, in whom we believe and whom we love — just as Isaiah says: "They will say in that day: 'Behold, this is our God; we have waited for him, that he might save us. This is the Lord; we have waited for him; let us be glad and rejoice in his salvation'" (Isa 25:9). And Peter says in his epistle: "Though you have not seen him, you love him. Though you do not now see him, you believe in him and rejoice with joy that is inexpressible" (1 Pet 1:8). We will not receive another Holy Spirit, except this One who is with us and cries, "Abba, Father" (Rom 8:15; Gal 4:6). And in these very things we will have increase and progress, so that we may now enjoy the gifts of God not through a mirror and in riddles, but face to face (1 Cor 13:12). Thus also now, perceiving more than Solomon — which is the advent of the Son of God — we have not learned another God besides the Creator and Maker of all things, who was shown to us from the beginning, nor another Christ, Son of God, except the one who was foretold by the prophets.

For with the New Testament known and foretold by the prophets, the One who was to establish it according to the Father's will was also foretold, and he was manifested to men as God willed, so that believers in him may always progress. And through the testaments there is one salvation and one God. The precepts that form a human being are many, and not few are those who lead a human being to God. To an earthly and temporal king, since he is a man, it is permitted to grant greater advancement to those subject to him; but to God, since he is the same and always wills to bestow greater grace on the human race and to honor with more gifts those who please him — is this not progress? To find another Father besides the One announced from the beginning, and then, besides the one thought to have been found a second time, to find a third — and the same progress from a third to a fourth, and from that another and another — so that, always thinking to progress, such a mind will never stand in God. For it is expelled from the One who is, and turning back it seeks but never finds God; it will always swim in the depth of incomprehensibility, unless, converted through repentance, it returns from where it was cast out, confessing and believing in one God, the Father, the Creator, who was announced by the Law and the prophets, who was testified to by Christ — just as he himself says to those who accused his disciples of not keeping the tradition of the elders: "Why do you break the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition? For God commanded, 'Honor your father and your mother,' and, 'Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die.' ... So for the sake of your tradition you have made void the word of God" (Matt 15:3-6). Clearly confessing the Father and God, Christ acknowledges the One who said in the Law: "Honor your father and your mother, that it may go well with you" (Deut 5:16). For the Word of God confessed the precept of the Law; the true God did not call another God except his own Father.

latin: Unius igitur et ejusdem substantize sunt omnia, hoc est, ab uno et eodem Deo, quemadmodum et Dominus ait discipulis: Propterea omnis scriba doctus in regno ceclorum similis est homini patrifamilias, qui profert de thesauro suo nova et vetera. Non alterum quidem vetera, alterum vero proferentem nova docuit; sed unum et eundem. Paterfamilias enim Dominus est, qui universe domui paternee dominatur: et servis quidem et adhuce indisciplinatis condignam tradens legem; liberis autem et fide justificatis congruentia dans precepta, et filiis adaperiens suam heereditatem. Scribas autem et doctores regni ccelorum, suos dicebat discipulos, de quibus et alibi ait Judzis: Hece mitto ad sapientes, et scribas, et doctores, et ex eis occidetis, et effugabitis a civitate in civitatem. Sic itaque que de thesauro proferuntur nova et vetera, sine contradictione duo testamenta dicit: vetus quidem quod ante fuerat legisdatio ; novum autem, que secundum Evangelium est conversatio, ostendit, de qua David ait: Cantate Domino canticum novoum. Et Esaias: Cantate Domino hymmum novum. Initium ejus, glorificatur nomen ejus a summo terre: virtutes ejus in insulis annuntiant. Et Hieremias ait: Ecce disponam, inquit, ¢estamentum nooum, non quemadmodum disposui patribus vestris in monte Oreb. Utraque autem testamenta unus et idem paterfamilias produxit, Verbum Dei, Dominus noster Jesus Christus, qui et Abrahze et Moysi collocutus est, qui nobis in novitate restituit libertatem, et multiplicavit eam, quee ab ipso est, 1. Plus est enim, inquit, templo hic. Plus autem et minus non in his dicitur, quee inter se communionem non habent, et sunt contrarize naturee, et pugnant adversus se; sed in his quee ejusdem sunt substantize, et communicant secum, solum autem multitudine et magnitudine differunt : quemadmodum aqua ab aqua, et lumen a lumine, et gratia a gratia. Major est igitur legisdatio que in libertatem, quam quz data est in servitutem: et ideo non in unam gentem, sed in totum mundum diffusa est. Unus autem et idem Dominus, qui plus quam templum est, et plus quam Salomon, et plus quam Jonas donat hominibus, id est, suam preesentiam et resurrectionem a mortuis: sed non Deum immutans, nec alium spreedicans Patrem, sed eundem ipsum, qui semper habet plura domesticis, et proficiente eorum erga Deum dilectione, plura et majora donans, quemadmodum et Dominus discipulis dicebat: Quoniam et majora horum videbitis, Et Paulus ait: * Non quod jam acceperim, aut quod justificatus sim, aut jam persim: ex parte enim scimus, et ex parte prophetamus. Cum autem venerit quod perfectum est, que sunt ex parte, destruentur. Sicut igitur adveniente perfecto, non alterum Patrem videbimus, sed hune quem nune videre concupimus: Beati enim mundi corde, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt; neque alium Christum et Dei Filium exspectabimus, sed hune qui ex Maria * Virgine, qui et passus est, in quem et credimus, quem et diligimus; quemadmodum Esaias ait: Hé¢ dicent in illa die: Ecce, Dominus Deus noster, in quem speravimus, et exultavimus in salute nostra, Et Petrus ait in epistola sua: Quem non videntes diligitis, inquit, in quem nunc non videntes credidistis, gaudebitis gaudio inenarrabili ; neque alium Spiritum sanctum percipimus, nisi hune qui est nobiscum, et qui clamat, Absa, Pater ; et in iisdem ipsis augmentum habebimus, et proficiemus, ut jam non per speculum, et per eenigmata, sed facie ad faciem fruamur muneribus Dei: sic et nunc plus temet plus Salomone percipientes, quod est adventus Filii Dei, non alterum didicimus Deum, preter fabricatorem et factorem omnium, qui ab initio nobis demonstratus est; neque alterum Christum Dei Filium, preeter eum qui a prophetis preedicatus est. 2. Novo enim Testamento cognito et preedicato per prophetas, et ille qui illud dispositurus erat secundum placitum Patris preedicabatur, manifestatus hominibus quemadmodum voluit Deus; ut possint semper proficere credentes in eum, et per testamenta Una enim salus et unus Deus; quee autem formant hominem, preecepta multa, et non pauci qui adducunt hominem ad Deum. Terreno quidem et temporali regi, cum sit homo, licet aliquoties majores profectus attribuere his qui sunt subjecti: Deo autem non licebit, cum sit idem, et semper majorem gratiam preestare humano generi velit, et pluribus muneribus assidue honorare eos qui placent ei? hoe est proficere, alterum adinvenire Patrem preeter eum qui ab initio annuntiatus est, et rursum, preeter eum qui putatur secundo inyentus esse, alterum tertium adinvenire ; et ejusdem erit profectus et a tertio in quartum, et ab hoc rursum alterum et alterum: et sic semper putans proficere talis sensus, nunquam in stabit Deo. Expulsus enim ab eo qui est, et reversus retrorsum, quzeretquidem semper, inyeniet‘autem nunquam Deum ; sed semper incomprehensibilitatis profundo natabit, nisi per poenitentiam conversus, unde et abjectus erat, revertatur, unum Deum Patrem Demiurgum confitens et credens, qui a Lege et prophetis annuntiatus est, qui a Christo testificatus est, quemadmodum ipse ait ad eos qui accusabant ejus discipulos, quasi non servarent traditionem seniorum: Quare vos frustramini preeceptum Domini propter traditionem vestram? Deus enim dixit: Honora patrem et matrem; et, Qui maledixerit patri aut matri, morte moriatur. Et iterum secundo ait eis: Ht frustrati estis sermonem Dei propter vestram; manifestissime Patrem et Deum confitens Christus eum qui in Lege dixit: Honora patrem et matrem, ut tibi bene sit. Verbum enim Dei confessus est Legis preeceptum verax Deus, et neminem alterum Deum appellavit, quam suum Patrem.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Where was Marcion then, that Pontic shipowner and student of Stoicism? Where was Valentinus, the follower of Platonism? The record shows they were not always what they became; they appeared around the reign of Antoninus, and at first they accepted Catholic teaching in the Roman church under the blessed bishop Eleutherius. Their restless curiosity drove them on, a curiosity that even made their fellow believers avoid them, until they were expelled not once but twice. Marcion, who had brought two hundred sestertii to the church, was finally consigned to permanent separation, and the pair proceeded to spread the poison of their doctrines.

Later Marcion confessed repentance and, meeting the condition imposed on him, was to receive peace if he restored to the church the others he had taught for destruction; but death cut him off first. It was necessary for heresies to exist. That does not make heresies good, as if evil were not also necessary. The Lord had to be betrayed, yet woe to the betrayer; let no one cite this necessity to defend heresy.

If we must trace the line of Apelles, he is no more ancient than Marcion, his founder and forerunner. Apelles fell for a woman, abandoned Marcionite continence, and fled from the eyes of the most holy master Alexander to Alexandria. Years later he returned, no better, except that he was no longer a Marcionite, and he fastened onto another woman, the virgin Philumene, whom I mentioned earlier. She turned out to be a monstrous prostitute, and, caught in her spell, he wrote the phaneroseis he learned from her.

People still alive remember these men, including their own disciples and successors, so they cannot deny being their heirs. Even their own works convict them, as the Lord said. If Marcion separated the New Testament from the Old, he is later than what he separated; he could not separate them unless they had first been united. United before, separated after, the separator is shown to be the later party. Likewise Valentinus, by expounding differently and 'correcting,' proves that whatever he corrects was flawed beforehand. These are the most prominent and frequent adulterers of the truth.

Then there are Nigidius, whoever he is, Hermogenes, and many others still walking about perverting God's ways. Let them show me from what authority they sprang. If they preach another god, how do they use that god's own things, letters, and names against the very one they preach? If they preach the same God, how do they do it differently? Let them prove they are new apostles: let them say Christ descended again, taught again, was crucified again, died again, rose again. That is how the apostles operated, and they received power to work the same signs he did. I want to see their powers produced; unless, of course, you count their supreme power, by which they perversely imitate the apostles: the apostles made the dead live, these men make the living dead.

latin: Ubi tunc Marcion, ponticus nauclerus, stoicae studiosus? Ubi Valentinus platonicae sectator? Nam constat illos, neque adeo olim fuisse, Antonini fere principatu, et in catholicae primo doctrinam credidisse apud Ecclesiam romanensem, sub episcopatu Eleutherii benedicti, donec ob inquietam semper eorum curiositatem, qua fratres quoque vitabant semel et iterum ejecti, Marcion quidem cum ducentis sestertiis quae Ecclesiae intulerat, novissime in perpetuum discidium relegati, venena doctrinarum suarum disseminaverunt. Postmodum idem Marcion, poenitentiam confessus cum conditioni datae sibi occurrit, ita pacem recepturus, si caeteros quos perditioni erudisset, Ecclesiae restitueret, morte praeventus est. Oportebat enim haereses esse. Nec tamen ideo bonum haereses, quia eas oportebat, quasi non et malum oportuerit esse. Nam et Dominum tradi oportebat; sed vae traditori? ne quis etiam hinc haereses defendat. Si et Apellis stemma retractandum est, tam non vetus et ipse quam Marcion institutor et praeformator ejus: sed lapsus in foeminam desertor continentiae marcionensis, ab oculis sanctissimi magistri Alexandriam secessit; inde post annos regressus non melior, nisi tantum qua jam non marcionites, in alteram foeminam impegit, illam virginem Philumenen, quam supra edidimus, postea vero immane prostibulum et ipsam, cujus energemate circumventus, quas ab ea didicit phaneroseis scripsit. Adhuc in saeculo supersunt qui meminerint eorum, etiam proprii discentes et successores ipsorum, ne se posteriores negare possint. Quanquam et de operibus suis, ut dixit Dominus, revincuntur. Si enim Marcion Novum Testamentum a Vetere separavit, posterior est eo quod separavit; quia separare non posset, nisi quod unitum fuit. Unitum ergo ante quam separaretur, postea separatum, posteriorem ostendit separatorem. Item Valentinus, aliter exponens, et sine dubio emendans, hoc omnino quicquid emendat, ut mendosum retro, anterius fuisse demonstrat. Hos ut insigniores et frequentiores adulteros veritatis nominamus. Caeterum et Nigidius nescio quis, et Hermogenes, et multi alii qui adhuc ambulant pervertentes vias Dei, ostendant mihi ex qua auctoritate prodierunt. Si alium Deum praedicant, quomodo ejus Dei rebus et litteris et nominibus utuntur adversus quem praedicant? si eumdem, quomodo aliter? Probent se novos apostolos esse: dicant Christum iterum descendisse, iterum ipsum docuisse, iterum crucifixum, iterum mortuum, iterum resuscitatum: sic enim Apostolos solet facere, dare illis praeterea virtutem eadem signa edendi, quae et ipse. Volo igitur et virtutes eorum proferri; nisi quod agnosco maximam virtutem eorum, qua Apostolos in perversum aemulantur: illi enim de mortuis vivos faciebant, isti de vivis mortuos faciunt.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: If we have done anything against Marcion before, let the record show it from this point on. We are launching a new work from an old foundation. I first withdrew a hasty little treatise, later replacing it with a fuller composition. I lost that one too, before it could be copied, thanks to the fraud of a brother who then turned apostate — he had copied certain passages very badly and circulated them publicly. The need for correction became an opportunity for innovation, and that occasion persuaded me to add more. So this pen, now third after the second, and now first after the third, must preface the outcome of this little work, so that its scattered variety may not confuse anyone.

Pontus, denied by nature the name Euxine, is mocked by it instead. But do not judge hospitable Pontus by its location; it has withdrawn from our more humane shores as if in shame of its own barbarity. The most ferocious nations inhabit it — if you can call it inhabited, given they live in wagons. Their dwellings are uncertain, life is crude, lust promiscuous and mostly naked; even when they hide, they are marked by quivers suspended from their yokes, so that no one may intervene. Thus they do not blush at their own arms. They devour the corpses of their parents alongside slaughtered beasts at a feast. Death is cursed if they do not die so as to be eaten. Women are not softened by their sex according to modesty; they bind their breasts, make a burden for their axes, and prefer to wage war rather than marry.

Harshness comes from heaven as well: the day is never open, the sun never smiles, the air is one unbroken cloud, the whole year is winter, and everything that blows is the north wind. Liquids freeze back into snow, rivers are stopped by ice, mountains are heaped with frost. Everything is numb, everything stiff; nothing there is warm except savagery — the savagery that gave the stage its stories of Tauric sacrifices, Colchian loves, and Caucasian crosses. But nothing in Pontus is as barbarous and sad as the fact that Marcion was born there: worse than a Scythian, more unstable than a Hamaxobian, more inhuman than a Massagete, more daring than an Amazon, darker than a cloud, colder than winter, more fragile than frost, more deceitful than the Hister, more abrupt than the Caucasus. Why not? For with him the true Prometheus, God Almighty, is torn apart by blasphemies.

Now Marcion is even more troublesome to the beasts of that barbarity. For who is as much a castrator of flesh as the man who abolished marriage? Who is as much a devourer of the Pontic mouse as the man who gnawed away the Gospels? Did you, Euxine, produce a more probable beast for philosophers than for Christians? That cynic Diogenes sought to find a human being, carrying a lantern at midday. Marcion, having found God, lost Him with the extinguished light of his faith.

His disciples will not deny that his first faith was with us, as his own letters testify, so that from this point it can already be determined: a heretic is one who, having deserted what he previously was, later chooses for himself what he was not before. For to such an extent will heresy be reckoned as what is introduced later, inasmuch as truth will be held to be what was handed down before and from the beginning.

But another little book will sustain this level against the heretics, even without a re-examination of doctrines, to be overcome. This is what they know about the prescription of novelty. Now, insofar as a confrontation is to be admitted from time to time, lest the summary of the prescription be deemed everywhere to be advocated out of diffidence, I will first weave the rule of the adversary, lest it be hidden from anyone, in which the principal question will be fought.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: For indeed, as the Creator of all things, He was from the beginning discovered equally with them, they having been themselves manifested that He might become known as God . For although Moses , some long while afterwards, seems to have been the first to introduce the knowledge of the God of the universe in the temple of his writings, yet the birthday of that knowledge must not on that account be reckoned from the Pentateuch. For the volume of Moses does not at all initiate the knowledge of the Creator, but from the first gives out that it is to be traced from Paradise and Adam, not from Egypt and Moses .

The greater part, therefore, of the human race , although they knew not even the name of Moses , much less his writings, yet knew the God of Moses ; and even when idolatry overshadowed the world with its extreme prevalence, men still spoke of Him separately by His own name as God , and the God of gods, and said, If God grant, and, As God pleases, and, I commend you to God . Reflect, then, whether they knew Him, of whom they testify that He can do all things. To none of the writings of Moses do they owe this. The soul was before prophecy . From the beginning the knowledge of God is the dowry of the soul , one and the same among the Egyptians , and the Syrians, and the tribes of Pontus . For their souls call the God of the Jews their God. Do not, O barbarian heretic , put Abraham before the world.

Even if the Creator had been the God of one family , He was yet not later than your god; even in Pontus was He known before him. Take then your standard from Him who came first: from the Certain (must be judged) the uncertain; from the Known the unknown. Never shall God be hidden, never shall God be wanting. Always shall He be understood, always be heard, nay even seen, in whatsoever way He shall wish. God has for His witnesses this whole being of ours, and this universe wherein we dwell. He is thus, because not unknown, proved to be both God and the only One, although another still tries hard to make out his claim.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: They say it's justified. After all, who isn't as well known to their own people as to strangers? Nobody. I'll hold to that line of reasoning too. What kind of situation would it be for something to be foreign to God? If anyone existed to whom nothing was foreign — because it's God's nature that all things are His and all things pertain to Him — then He'd immediately hear from us: 'What business does He have with foreigners?' He'll hear that more fully in due course. For now, it's enough that no one is approved when nothing about them is approved. Just as the Creator is God and an undisputed God because all things are His and nothing is foreign to Him, so another is not God because not all things are His and therefore they're foreign. Finally, if the universe belongs to the Creator, I don't even see a place for another God. Everything is full and occupied by its Author. If some space lies vacant in creation for some divinity, it'll be a false vacancy. Truth lies open to falsehood. What great power do idols have that they won't receive Marcion's God somewhere? So I demand this too from the Creator's pattern: God should have been recognized from His works — from His own world, His own man, His own age — since even the world's error has presumed gods, which people sometimes acknowledge, because something from each seems useful and convenient for life's utilities and conveniences. So this too is believed to be divine: to establish or demonstrate what's suitable and necessary for human affairs. So much so that if authority is accommodated to a false divinity from which the true one preceded, Marcion's God ought to have produced at least one little circle of His own, so that some new Triptolemus might be proclaimed. Or produce a reason worthy of God for why He created nothing, if He exists; because He would have created if He had been God, by that very prejudice by which our God is made manifest in no other way than that He created all this. For once the rule stands firm — that they can't confess the Creator as God and also want the other to be believed as God equally without proving Him according to the pattern of Him whom they themselves and everyone acknowledge as God — then, when no one doubts the Creator is God because He created all this, no one ought to believe that the one who created nothing is also God, unless some reason is perhaps brought forward. This necessity appears to be twofold: either He didn't want to create anything, or He wasn't able. The third option is absent, but inability is unworthy of God. Whether unwillingness is worthy, I want to investigate. Tell me, Marcion: did your God want to be recognized at some time or not? Did He come down and preach and suffer and rise again with some other purpose than to be recognized? But without doubt, if He is recognized, He wanted to be. For nothing happens around Him unless He willed it. So He who procured knowledge of Himself so assiduously that He was exhibited in the shame of the flesh — and even greater shame if it's false, for it's more shameful if He also lied about the substance of the body — who also took the Creator's curse upon Himself, hanging on the tree — how much more honestly would He have established knowledge of Himself through some indications of His own creation! Especially against Him, having knowledge, among whom from the beginning He was not recognized by His works. For what kind of thing is it that the Creator, indeed not knowing there is another God above Himself as the Marcionites want — who swore and asserted He is alone — armed knowledge of Himself with such great works, as much as He could not have neglected according to the presumption of His singularity, while the other, more exalted one, knowing the inferior God to be so instructed, provided no preparation for Himself to be recognized? When He ought to have created more remarkable and superior works, so that God might be recognized from His works according to the Creator, and from more honorable works, a more powerful and noble Creator.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Even if we could admit He exists, we would still have to argue that He exists without cause. Anything without cause lacks a thing, because every thing is a cause — it exists so that there is someone whose thing it is. Since nothing ought to be without cause, that is, without a thing — for if it is without cause, it might as well not exist — lacking the cause of a thing means lacking the thing itself. To that extent, I judge it more fitting for God not to exist than to exist without cause. He is without cause who, by not having a thing, has no cause. But God ought not to exist without cause, that is, without a thing. So every time I demonstrate that He exists without cause, as if He exists, I prove He does not exist — because if He had existed, He would not have existed without cause at all.

Thus I also say that faith seizes Him without cause from man. Normally one believes in God shaped by the authority of works. But He foresaw nothing of the kind through which man might learn of God. Even though many believe in Him, they do not believe by reason straightaway. They lack God's pledge, His works worthy of God. And so, under this name of cessation and defection of works, of impudence and malice, He is kin to impudence — which snatches faith not owed to Him, for whom He foresaw nothing to be laid out — and to malice — which made many guilty of unbelief, securing nothing for faith.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: When we push God to this extreme—to the One for whom nothing is more proper or worthy than the testimony that marks Him as Creator—the most shameless Marcionites, recoiling in disgust, turn to demolishing the Creator’s works.

‘Certainly,’ they say, ‘the world is a great work and worthy of God!’ Is the Creator then not God? Clearly He is God. Therefore the world is not unworthy of God: for God would not have made anything unworthy of Himself, even if He made the world for humanity, not for Himself, though every work is inferior to its maker. And yet, if it is unworthy of God to have made something, how much more unworthy is it that He made nothing at all! Or is it unworthy, so that one could even hope for a more worthy author.

So let me speak of something even from this supposedly unworthy world, which even among the Greeks bears the name of ornament and cultivation, not filth. The very substances that the self‑styled professors of wisdom—whose minds animate every heresy—have declared to be gods: Thales called water a god, Heraclitus fire, Anaximenes air, Anaximander all heavenly bodies, Strato heaven and earth, Zeno air and ether, Plato the stars, which he calls the fiery kind of gods. When they considered the world—its magnitude, power, authority, honor, beauty, and the help, faith, and law of the individual elements that conspire to bring forth, nourish, complete, and restore all things—most physicists feared that the world’s substances, so vast, would be deemed less than God, the very substances worshipped by Persian magi, Egyptian hierophants, and Indian gymnosophists.

Even common, vulgar idolatry, ashamed of the names and myths of ancient dead men in its images, flees to a naturalistic interpretation and masks its disgrace with cleverness: it portrays Jupiter as a fiery substance, Juno as an airy one, following the sound of Greek words; Vesta as fire, the Camenae as water, the Great Mother as earth sown with seed, plowed by oxen, watered by baths. Thus Osiris, who is always buried, sought among the living, and found with joy, testifies to the faith of recurring crops, living elements, and the returning year, just as the rites of dry and burning nature philosophize about the lions of Mithras. And indeed, substances that are higher in position or status are more easily regarded as gods than as unworthy of God. Shall I descend to humble things? A single tiny flower from the hedges—not from the meadows—a single shell from any sea—not from the Red Sea—a single feather of a partridge, I say nothing of the peacock—will declare to you a sordid craftsman, the Creator.

plane deus. ergo nec mundus deo indignus: nihil etenim deus indignum se fecisset, etsi mundum homini.\' non sibi fecit, etsi omne opus inferius est suo artifice. et tamen, si quale quid fecisse indignum est deo, quanto indignius deo est nihil eum omnino fecisse! ** uel indignum, quo posset etiam digniorum auctor sperari. ut ergo aliquid + et de isto huius mundi indigno loquar, cui et apud Graecos ornamenti et cultus, non sordium, nomen est, indignas uidelicet substantias ipsi illi sapientiae professores, de quorum ingeniis omnis haeresis animatur. deos pronuntiauerunt, ut Thales aquam, ut Heraclitus ignem, ut Anaximenes aerem. ut Anaximander uniuersa caelestia, ut Strato caelum et terram, ut Zeno aerem et aetherem, ut Plato sidera, quae genus deorum igneum appellat, cum de mundo, considerando scilicet et magnitudinem et uim et potestatem et honorem et decorem, opem fidem legem singulorum elementorum, quae omnibus gignendis alendis conficiendis reficiendisque conspirant, ut plerique physicorum, formidauerint, [initium ac finem mundo constare] ne substantiae eius, tantae scilicet, minus dei haberentur, quas colunt et Persarum magi et Aegyptiorum hierophantae et Indorum gymnosophistae. ipsa quoque uulgaris superstitio communis idolatriae, cum in simulacris de nominibus et fabulis ueterum mortuorum pudet, ad interpretationem naturalium refugit et dedecus suum ingenio obumbrat, figurans Iouem in substantiam feruidam et Iunonem eius in aeream secundum sonum Graecorum uocabulorum. item Vestam in ignem et Camenas in aquam et Magnam Matrem in terram seminalia demessam, lacertis aratam, lauacris rigatam. sic et, Osiris quod semper sepelitur et in uiuido quaeritur et cum gaudio inuenitur, reciprocarum frugum et uiuidorum elementorum et recidiui anni fidem argumentantur, sicut aridae et ardentis naturae sacramenta leones Mithrae philosophantur. et superiores quidem situ aut statu substantias sufficit facilius deos habitas quam deo indignas. ad humilia deficiam? unus, opinor, de sepibus flosculus, non dico de pratis, una cuiuslibet maris conchula, non dico de rubro, una tetraonis pinnula, taceo de pauo, sordidum artificem pronuntiabit tibi creatorem?

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: You mock the smaller animals, too — the ones the greatest Artisan deliberately enlarged through their own talents or strengths — thereby teaching that greatness proves itself in moderation, just as virtue does in weakness, as the apostle says (1 Corinthians 12:22). Imitate the bees' architecture if you can, the ants' dwellings, the spiders' webs, the silkworms' threads; endure the very beasts of your bed and cloak if you can — the beetles' poisons, the flies' stings, the mosquitoes' trumpets and lances. What will the greater things be like, when such tiny things either help or harm you, so that you do not despise the Creator even in the smallest things?

Finally, walk yourself around and examine the human being inside and out: will this work of our God please you, the work your Lord — that better God — admired, for whose sake he labored to descend from the third heaven into these poor elements, for whose sake he was even crucified in this cell of the Creator?

But that God, at any rate, has not rejected up to now the Creator's water, with which he washes his own, nor the oil with which he anoints his own, nor the fellowship of honey and milk, with which he nurtures his infants, nor the bread, with which he represents his own body even in his own sacraments, though he stands in need of the Creator's alms. You, however — a disciple above the master, a servant above the Lord — you presume to be wiser than he, destroying what he desires.

I want to examine whether, at least from faith, you do not also desire what you destroy. You oppose heaven, yet you capture heaven's freedom inside dwellings; you despise the earth — now plainly the mother of your enemy, the flesh — and you wring out all its marrow for food; you reject the sea, but only up to its resources, which you count as holier food. If I offered you a rose, you would not despise the Creator. Hypocrite: so that you may prove yourself a Marcionite — that is, a rejecter of the Creator — for this ought to have been pursued as martyrdom among you, if the world displeased you — into whatever material you resolve, you use the Creator's substance. How great is the obstinacy of your hardness! You devalue the very things in which you both live and die.

latin: At cum et animalia inrides minutiora, quae maximus artifex de industria ingeniis aut uiribus ampliauit, sic magnitu-i dinem in mediocritate probari docens quemadmodum uirtutem ; in infirmitate secundum apostolum, imitare, si potes, apis aedificia, formicae stabula, aranei retia, bombycis stamina, sustine, si potes, illas ipsas lectuli et tegetis tuae bestias,I cantharidis uenena, muscae spicula, culicis et tubam et lanceam. qualia erunt maiora, cum tam modicis aut iuuaris aut laederis, ut nec in modicis despicias creatorem? postremo te tibi circumfer, intus ac foris considera hominem: placebit tibi uel hoc opus dei nostri, quod tuus dominus, ille deus melior, adamauit, propter quem in haec paupertina elementa de tertio caelo descendere laborauit, cuius causa in hac cellula creatoris etiam crucifixus est? sed ille quidem usque nunc nec aquam reprobauit creatoris, qua suos abluit, nec oleum, quo suos ungit, nec mellis et lactis societatem, qua suos infantat, nec panem, quo ipsum corpus suum repraesentat etiam in sacramentis propriis egens mendicitatibus creatoris. at tu, super magistrum discipulus et seruus super dominum. I, sublimius illo sapis, destruens quae ille desiderat. uolo inspicere, si ex fide saltim, ut non et ipse quae destruis adpetas. I aduersaris caelum, et libertatem caeli in habitationibus captas:I despicis terram — plane inimicae iam tuae, carnis, matricem — et, omnes medullas eius uictui extorques; reprobus et mare, sed usque ad copias eius, quas sanctiorem cibum deputas. rosam tibi si obtulero, non fastidies creatorem. hypocrita, ut apocarteresi probes te Marcionitam, id est repudiatorem creatoris, — nam haec apud uos pro martyrio adfectari debuisset, si uobis mundus displiceret — in quamcumque materiam resolueris, substantiam creatoris uteris. quanta obstinatio duritiae tuae! depretias in quibus et uiuis et moreris.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Whether before or after these points, once you claim that Marcion's god has his own condition, his own world, and his own heaven — we will examine that third heaven later, if we ever get around to discussing your apostle — but in the meantime, whatever his substance may be, it ought to have appeared alongside his own god. Yet here we are: the Lord was revealed in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, while the substance remains entirely undiscovered in the fifteenth year of Emperor Severus. This substance, which supposedly outdoes the creator's trivialities, should have stayed hidden — not while its own Lord and author remained hidden. So if the substance itself could not be revealed in this world, how did the Lord obey it in this world? If this world seized the Lord, why could it not seize the substance — unless the Lord is perhaps greater?

Now the question turns to place, and it touches both that upper world and its god. Consider: if that god also has his world beneath him, above the creator, he made it in a place — specifically, the vacant space between his own feet and the creator's head. Therefore the god himself was in a place, and he made the world in a place, and that place will be greater than both god and world. Nothing that contains something else fails to be greater than what it contains. And we must check whether any vacant spaces still remain there, where a third god might station himself with his own world. So start counting gods now. Place will be a god — not only because it surpasses god, but because it is innate, ungenerated, and therefore eternal and equal to god, the place in which god has always existed.

Next, if that god also fashioned the world from some underlying material — innate, ungenerated, and contemporary with god, as Marcion supposes of the creator — you drag this too into the majesty of place, which encloses both god and material: two gods. For material is also a god according to the form of divinity — namely innate, ungenerated, and eternal. Or if he made the world from nothing, this same conclusion will be forced on the creator, to whom material is subjected in the substance of the world. But he, too, ought to have made it from material, since the same reasoning applies to the god opposed to the creator, making him equally god. And so Marcion gives me three gods for now: the maker, the place, and the material.

Accordingly, he also puts the creator in a place, judging by the same condition, and subjects material to him — innate, ungenerated, and eternal by that same name, just like the Lord. Further, by assigning evil to material — innate to the innate, ungenerated to the ungenerated, eternal to the eternal — he has now produced a fourth god. You therefore have, in the upper realm, three substances of divinity; in the lower, four. When their own Christs are added to these — one who appeared under Tiberius, another promised by the creator — Marcion suffers obvious fraud at the hands of those who suppose he introduces two gods, when he actually assigns nine, albeit unknowingly.

quae friuolis creatoris praecellens utique latere desisset, non latente iam domino suo et auctore. et ideo, si ipsa non potuit manifestari in hoc mundo, quomodo dominus paruit eius in hoc mundo? si dominum cepit hic mundus, cur substantiam capere non potuit, nisi domino fortasse maiorem? iam nunc de loco quaestio est, pertinens et ad mundum illum superiorem et ad ipsum deum eius. ecce enim, si et ille habet mundum suum infra se, super creatorem, in loco utique fecit eum, cuius spatium uacabat inter pedes suos et caput creatoris. ergo et deus ipse in loco erat et mundum in loco faciebat, et erit iam locus ille maior et deo et mundo. nihil enim non maius est id quod capit eo quod capitur. et uidendum, ne qua adhuc illic uacent subsiciua. in quibus et tertius aliqui stipare deus se cum mundo suo possit. ergo iam incipe deos computare. erit enim et locus deus, non tantum qua deo maior, sed et qua innatus et infectus ac per hoc aeternus et deo par, in quo semper deus fuerit. dehinc si et ille mundum ex aliqua materia subiacente molitus est innata et infecta et contemporali deo, quemadmodum de creatore Marcion sentit, redigis et hoc ad maiestatem loci, qui et deum et materiam, duos deos, clusit. et materia enim deus secundum formam diuinitatis, innata scilicet et infecta et aeterna, aut si de nihilo molitus est mundum, hoc et de creatore sentire cogetur, cui materiam subicit in substantiam mundi. sed ex, materia et ille fecisse debebit. eadem ratione occurrente illi quoque, [deo] quae opponitur creatori, ut aeque deo. atque ita tres interim mihi deos numera Marcionis, factorem et locum et materiam. proinde et creatorem in loco facit, utique eadem condicione censendo, et materiam ei subicit, utique innatam et infectam et hoc nomine aeternam, ut dominum. amplius; I et malum materiae deputans, innatum innatae, infectum infectae et aeternum aeternae, quartum iam hinc deum fecit. habes igitur in superioribus tres substantias diuinitatis, in inferioribus quat- i tuor. his cum accedunt et sui Christi, alter qui apparuit sub Tiberio alter qui a creatore promittitur. manifestam iam fraudem Marcion patitur ab eis, qui duos illum deos inferre : praesumunt, cum nouem adsignet, licet nesciens,

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Since there is no other world, neither is there another god for it. It follows, then, that they split the two kinds of things—visible and invisible—between two gods as authors, and so they reserve the invisible things for their own god. Who, except a heretical spirit, could even entertain the idea that the invisible things belong to a god who has produced not a single visible thing? They belong far more properly to the one who has actually worked visible things and thereby grounded faith in the invisible as well; it is much more just to trust some exemplars than none at all. We will also see to which author the apostle assigns the invisible things, once we have examined him. For now we are relying on the plainest common sense and sound reasoning, preparing the ground for the appeal to Scripture, confirming that this diversity of visible and invisible things must be credited to the Creator God. His entire operation consists of diversities: corporeal and incorporeal, animate and inanimate, vocal and mute, mobile and stationary, fertile and sterile, dry and moist, hot and cold. That same diversity has tempered man himself, both in body and in senses: some members strong, others weak; some honorable, others dishonorable; some paired, others single; some alike, others unalike. And so also in the inner senses: now joy, now anxiety; now love, now hatred; now anger, now gentleness. If the whole universe is thus modulated as a rivalry of conditions, then the invisible things are owed to the visible things—not to be assigned to a different author than the one to whom their rivals belong. They themselves point out the Creator as diverse: commanding what he forbids and forbidding what he commands, striking and healing. So why do they take him as uniform in this one respect, as only the founder of visible things, when it should be believed that he created both visible and invisible, just as he created both life and death, both evil and peace? And certainly, if those invisible things are greater than the visible things in their own place, then it is also fitting that the greater things belong to him whose are the great things, because neither great things nor, still less, greater things can belong to him to whom not even moderate things are comparable.
