latin: Plane monet Romanos omnibus potestatibus subjici, quia non sit potestas nisi a Deo, quia non sine caussa gladium gestet, et quia ministerium sit Dei; sed et ultrix, inquit, in iram ei qui malum fecerit. Nam et praemiserat: Principes enim non sunt timori bono operi, sed malo. Vis autem non timere potestatem? fac bonum, et laudem ab ea referes. Dei ergo ministra est tibi in bonum. Si vero malum facias, time. Ita, non in occasione frustrandi martyrii jubet te subjici potestatibus, sed in provocatione bene vivendi, etiam sub illarum respectu, quasi adjutricum justitiae, quasi ministrarum divini judicii, hic etiam de nocentibus praejudicantis. Dehinc et exequitur quomodo velit te subjici potestatibus, reddere jubens, cui tributum, tributum; cui vectigal, vectigal; id est quae sunt Caesaris, Caesari, et quae Dei, Deo; solius autem Dei homo. Condixerat scilicet Petrus, regem quidem honorandum; ut tamen tunc rex honoretur, cum suis rebus insistit, cum a divinis honoribus longe est; quia et pater et mater diligentur, cum Deo non comparabuntur. Caeterum, super Deum diligi nec animam licebit.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Are the Apostles' letters also changeable? Are we everywhere simple souls, mere doves, gladly wandering in error? I believe it comes from a desire to live. So let it be, then: let the meanings depart from their letters. What we know the Apostles suffered is a manifest doctrine; I grasp it simply by reading through Acts; I seek nothing else. Prisons, chains, whips, stones, swords, Jewish attacks, mob gatherings, tribunals' speeches, royal audiences, proconsular courts, the very name of Caesar — none of these need an interpreter. That Peter was struck, that Stephen was crushed, that James was slain, that Paul was torn apart — these things were written in their own blood. And if a heretic wants to trust the Commentaries, the instruments of empire will speak, like the stones of Jerusalem. We read the Lives of the Caesars; Nero first bloodied the rising faith at Rome. Then Peter was girded by another when he was bound to the cross. Then Paul obtained the birth of the Roman city when he was reborn there through the nobility of martyrdom. Wherever I read these things now, I learn to suffer; it does not matter which teachers of martyrdom I follow, whether the meanings or the outcomes of the Apostles — except that I also recognize the meanings in the outcomes. For they would not have suffered anything that they had not first sensed was to be suffered. When Agabus also prophesied Paul's chains by a gesture, the disciples wept and prayed that he not commit himself to Jerusalem; they prayed in vain. For he, driven by what he had always taught, said: "Why do you weep and sadden my heart? But I not only wish to suffer chains in Jerusalem, but also to die for the name of my Lord Jesus Christ." And so they yielded, saying: "Let the will of the Lord be done"; certainly trusting that sufferings pertain to the will of God. For they had attempted to restrain him not with the counsel of dissuasion, but with the bond of love, so that they might retain the Apostle — desiring him, not dissuading him from martyrdom. But if Prodicus or Valentinus had been present then, suggesting that one should not confess on earth among men; much less that God thirsts for human blood, nor that Christ, as if He Himself were going to obtain salvation from it, demands the substitute of passion — immediately he would have heard from the servant of God what he had heard from the Lord the devil say: "Depart, Satan, you are a scandal to me; it is written: You shall worship the Lord your God, and serve Him only" (Matthew 4:10). But also now he ought to hear, insofar as he much later poured out those poisons; none of the weak will easily drink them unless they have previously drunk — or even drunk excessively — this our potion of faith.

latin: Num ergo et Apostolorum litterae mobiles? et nos usquequaque simplices animae, et solummodo columbae, libenter errantes? credo vivendi cupiditate. Ita vero sit, ut recedant a litteris suis sensus. Quae tamen passos Apostolos scimus, manifesta doctrina est; hanc intelligo solam Acta decurrens; nihil quaero; carceres illic, et vincula, et flagella, et saxa, et gladii, et impetus Judaeorum, et coetus nationum, et tribunorum elogia, et regum auditoria, et proconsulum tribunalia, et Caesaris nomen interpretem non habent. Quod Petrus caeditur, quod Stephanus opprimitur, quod Jacobus immolatur, quod Paulus distrahitur, ipsorum sanguine scripta sunt. Et si fidem Commentarii voluerit haereticus, instrumenta imperii loquentur, ut lapides Jerusalem. Vitas Caesarum legimus; orientem fidem Romae primus Nero cruentavit. Tunc Petrus ab altero cingitur, cum cruci adstringitur. Tunc Paulus civitatis romanae consequitur nativitatem, cum illic martyrii renascitur generositate. Haec ubicumque jam legero, pati disco; nec mea interest quos sequar martyrii magistros, sensusne an exitus Apostolorum; nisi quod et sensus in exitibus recognosco. Nihil enim passi fuissent, quod non prius patiendum esse sensissent. Cum vincula Paulo Agabus gestu quoque prophetasset, discipuli flentes et orantes ne se Jerosolyma committeret, frustra oraverunt. Ille enim, quod semper docuerat animatus: Quid fletis, inquit, et contristatis cor meum? At ego non modo vincula Jerosolymis pati optaverim, verum etiam mori pro nomine Domini mei Jesu Christi. Atque ita cesserunt, dicendo: Fiat voluntas Domini; fidentes scilicet, passiones ad voluntatem Dei pertinere. Non enim dehortationis consilio, sed dilectionis retinere tantaverant, ut Apostolum desiderantes, non ut martyrium dissuadentes. Quod si jam tunc Prodicus aut Valentinus assisteret, suggerens, non in terris esse confitendum apud homines; minus vero, ne Deus humanum sanguinem sitiat, nec Christus vicem passionis, quasi et ipse de ea salutem consecuturus exposcat; statim audisset a servo Dei, quod audierat a Domino diabolus: Recede, Satana, scandalum mihi es; scriptum est: Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, et illi soli servies. Sed et nunc audire debebit, quatenus multo post, venena ista suffudit; nulli infirmorum facile nisi nocitura, si qui non hanc nostram ex fide praebiberit, vel etiam superbiberit potionem.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: We are not yet discussing the merit of martyrdom — unless it is a debt we owe first — nor its usefulness before we learn its necessity. Divine authority comes first: whether God actually willed and commanded such a thing, so that those who deny the good cannot be coaxed into what fits until they have been subdued. It is not worthy to compel heretics to duty; hardness must be broken, not persuaded. And the decisive point will certainly be this: whatever proves to be established and commanded by God. Let the Gospels wait a moment while I trace their root back to the first Law, and from there draw out God's will — the very source by which I recognize Him. "I am the Lord your God who brought you out of the land of Egypt. You shall have no other gods besides Me. You shall not make for yourself an idol of anything in heaven above, or on the earth beneath, or in the waters under the earth. You shall not bow down to them or serve them, for I am the Lord your God" (Exodus 20:3-5). The same Exodus adds: "You yourselves saw that I spoke to you from heaven. You shall not make gods of silver for yourselves, nor shall you make gods of gold" (Exodus 20:22-23). Deuteronomy repeats the core: "Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one. You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might" (Deuteronomy 6:4-5). Again: "Do not forget the Lord your God who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. You shall fear the Lord your God and serve Him only, and cling to Him, and swear by His name. You shall not go after other gods from among the gods of the peoples around you, for the Lord your God is a jealous God among you, lest His anger burn against you and He destroy you from the face of the earth" (Deuteronomy 6:12-15). He sets out blessings and curses: blessing if you obey the commandments He gives today and do not turn aside to serve unknown gods; but from those gods you must utterly destroy every trace — tear down their altars, smash their pillars, cut down their sacred poles, burn their carved images, and erase their names from the places the nations once held (Deuteronomy 12:2-3). When you enter the land and dispossess the nations, take care not to follow their customs after they are gone, asking, 'How did these nations serve their gods? I will do the same' (Deuteronomy 12:30). If a prophet or dreamer arises among you and gives a sign or wonder that comes true, then says, 'Let us go after other gods you have not known,' do not listen; the Lord your God is testing whether you love Him with all your heart and soul. You shall follow the Lord, fear Him, keep His commandments, obey His voice, serve Him, and cling to Him. But that prophet or dreamer shall die, because he tried to turn you away from the Lord your God (Deuteronomy 13:1-5). Even your closest kin — brother, son, daughter, the wife you cherish, the friend as dear as your own soul — if they secretly entice you to serve other gods, you must not consent or listen. Show no pity, spare no mercy, do not shield them. You must denounce them; your hand shall be first to strike them down, then the hand of all the people, and they shall be stoned to death, because they sought to draw you away from the Lord your God (Deuteronomy 13:6-10). The same ruthless law applies to whole cities that turn to other gods: kill every inhabitant, devote everything to destruction, burn the city and all its spoil before the Lord, and let it remain a ruin forever, never rebuilt, so that the Lord may turn from His fierce anger (Deuteronomy 13:12-17). The curse formula follows the same line: "Cursed is the man who makes a carved or cast metal image, an abomination to the Lord, the work of a craftsman's hands, and sets it up in secret" (Deuteronomy 27:15). Leviticus echoes: "Do not turn to idols or make for yourselves molten gods; I am the Lord your God" (Leviticus 19:4). Again: "The people of Israel are My servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt; I am the Lord your God. You shall not make idols for yourselves, nor set up a carved pillar, nor place a figured stone in your land to worship; I am the Lord your God" (Leviticus 25:55; 26:1). These words first came through Moses, and they apply to anyone the Lord God of Israel delivers from Egypt — the most superstitious age — and from the house of human bondage. Afterward every prophet speaks with the same voice, layering the same law, and their first and principal warning is always the same: beware of every form of making and worshiping idols. As David sings: "The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands. They have mouths, but do not speak; eyes, but do not see; ears, but do not hear; noses, but do not smell; hands, but do not feel; feet, but do not walk. Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them" (Psalm 115:4-8).

latin: Sed nondum de bono Martyrii, nisi debito primum; nec ante de utilitate ejus, quam de necessitate discendum. Auctoritas divina praecedit, an tale quid voluerit atque mandaverit Deus, ut qui negant bonum, non suadeantur accommodum, nisi cum subacti fuerint. Ad officium haereticos compelli, non illici dignum est. Duritia vincenda est, non suadenda. Et utique satis optimum praejudicabitur, quod probabitur a Deo constitutum atque praeceptum. Sustineant Evangelia paulisper, dum radicem eorum ex primo Legem; dum inde elicio Dei voluntatem, unde et ipsum recognosco. Ego sum, inquit, Deus tuus qui te eduxi de terra Aegypti. Non erunt tibi dii alii praeter me. Non facies tibi simulacrum eorum quae in coelo, et quae in terra deorsum, et quae in mari infra terram. Non adorabis ea, neque famulaberis eis. Ego enim sum Dominus Deus tuus. Item in eadem Exodo: Ipsi vidistis quod de coelo locutus ad vos sim. Non facietis vobis deos argenteos, et deos aureos non facietis vobis. Secundum haec et in Deuteronomio: Audi, Israel, Dominus Deus tuus unus est, et: Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, et ex tota anima tua, et ex totis viribus tuis; et rursus: Ne obliviscaris Domini Dei tui, qui te eduxit de terra Aegypti et domo servitutis. Dominum Deum tuum timebis, et illi famulaberis soli, et illi adglutinaberis; et in nomine ejus dejerabis. Non ibitis post deos alienos ex diis nationum quae circum vos, quia aemulatur Deus tuus in te: ne iratus indignetur, et exterminet te a facie terrae. Sed et proponens benedictiones et maledictiones: Benedictiones, inquit, si audieritis praecepta Domini Dei vestri, quaecumque ego praecipio vobis hodie, et non erraveritis de via, quam mandavi vobis, ut abeuntes serviatis diis aliis, quos non scitis. De quibus omnifariam extirpandis: Perditione perdetis, inquit, omnia loca, in quibus servierunt nationes diis suis, quas vos possidebitis haereditate: subter montes et colles, et sub arbores densas quasque effodietis aras earum, evertetis et comminuetis staticula earum, et excidetis lucos earum, et scalptilia ipsorum deorum concremabitis igni, et disperdetis nomen eorum de loco illo. Adhuc ingerit cum introissent terram promissionis, et exterminassent nationes ejus: Cave tibi ne sequaris eas posteaquam exterminatae fuerint a facie tua, ne requisieris deos illarum, dicens: quemadmodum faciunt nationes deis suis, et ego ita faciam. Sed et id: Si prophetes, inquit, exsurrexerit in te, aut somnium somnians, et dederit tibi signum vel ostentum, et evenerit, et dixerit: eamus, et serviamus deis aliis, quos non scitis: ne audiatis sermonem prophetae, aut somniatoris illius; quia tentat vos Dominus Deus vester, an ex toto corde vestro, et ex tota anima vestra timeatis eum. Post Dominum Deum vestrum abibitis, et hunc timebitis, et praecepta ejus custodietis, et vocem ejus audietis, et illi servietis, et illi adjiciemini. Prophetes autem et somniator ille morietur: locutus est enim ad seducendum te a Domino Deo tuo. Sed et alio capitulo: Si autem rogaverit te frater tuus ex patre vel matre, aut filius tuus, aut filia tua, aut mulier, quae in gremio tuo est, aut amicus qui animae tuae pars est, clam dicens: eamus, et serviamus deis aliis, quos non scis, nec patres tui, ex deis nationum quae circum te proxime sunt, aut longe; ne velis ire cum illo, et ne audieris eum. Non parcet oculus tuus super eum, nec misereberis, nec celabis eum: annuntians annuntiabis de eo; manus tuae erunt in eum in primis ad occidendum, et manus omnis populi in novissimis, et lapidabitis illum, et morietur, quoniam quaesivit avertere te a Domino Deo tuo. Subjicit etiam de civitatibus, si quam ex his constitisset suasu iniquorum hominum transiisse ad deos alios. ut interficerentur omnes incolentes eam, et devotamenta fierent universa ejus, et colligerentur omnia spolia ejus in omnes exitus ejus, et igni cremarentur cum omnibus vasis suis, et cum omni populo in conspectu Domini Dei. Et non erit habitabilis, inquit, in aeternum, non reaedificabitur amplius, nec adhaerebit quidquam manibus tuis ex devotamento ejus, uti avertatur Dominus ab indignatione irae suae. Maledictionum quoque ordinem ab idolorum exsecratione commisit: Maledictus homo qui fecerit sculptile aut fusile, aspernamentum Domino, opus manuum artificis, et collocaverit illud in abscondito. In Levitico vero: Non sequemini, inquit, idola, et deos fusiles non facietis vobis. Ego Dominus Deus vester. Et alibi: Filii Israel famuli pueri mei; hi sunt quos eduxi de terra Aegypti. Ego Dominus Deus vester. Non facietis vobis manu facta, nec scalptile staticulum statuetis vobis, nec lapidem scopum ponetis in terra vestra. Ego Dominus Deus vester. Et haec quidem prima per Moysen dicta sunt a Domino, utique pertinentia quoscumque Dominus Deus Israelis perinde de Aegypto superstitiosissimi saeculi, et de domo humanae servitutis eduxerit. Sed et deinceps omne os Prophetarum ejusdem Dei vocibus sonat, eamdem legem suam eorumdem praeceptorum instauratione cumulantis, nec aliud primum tam principaliter denuntiantis, quam ab omni factura atque cultura idolorum cavere; ut per David: Dei nationum argentum et aurum; oculos habent, nec vident; aures habent, nec audiunt; nares habent, nec odorantur; os, nec loquuntur; manus, nec contrectant; pedes, nec ingrediuntur. Similes erunt illis qui faciunt ea, et qui fidunt in illis.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: I do not think it is even debatable whether God is right to forbid His name and honor from being attached to a lie, whether He is right to refuse those He has torn from the error of superstition permission to return to Egypt, or whether He is right to refuse those He has chosen for Himself permission to depart from Him. (Exodus 32:1-6) Consequently, He will not wait for us to re-examine whether He intended to enforce the discipline He chose to establish, and whether He justly punishes the abandonment of that discipline which He intended to be kept. He would have established it in vain if He did not want it kept, and He would have wanted it kept in vain if He did not intend to punish its violation. It follows, then, that I must prove these definitions of God against superstitions—both those already refuted and those already punished—because the entire rationale for martyrdom rests on them.

Moses was absent with God on the mountain when the people, unable to endure his necessary absence, demanded gods for themselves—gods they had already lost. Aaron was pressed into compliance and ordered the women's earrings thrown into the fire. They were about to forfeit in judgment the true ornaments of their ears: the very voices of God. A shrewd fire cast a calf's image for them, branding those who had hearts set on Egypt, where even a cow was consecrated among the other animals. As a result, three thousand men were slain by their own kin, because they had offended their nearest parent, God, thereby consecrating the origin and the penalty of their transgression. (Exodus 32:1-6)

In Numbers, when Israel encamped at Shittim, the men went whoring after the daughters of Moab, who invited them to their idols so that they would commit spiritual fornication as well. They ate the sacrifices of those polluted rites, then bowed down to the gods of the nation and were initiated into Baal-peor. On account of this idolatry, fornication's sister, twenty-three thousand Israelites fell by the swords of divine wrath. (Numbers 25:1-9)

After Joshua died, they abandoned the God of their fathers and served the idols Baal and Ashtoreth. The Lord burned with anger, handed them over to plunderers, and they were plundered and sold to enemies against whom they could no longer stand. Wherever they marched, the Lord's hand was against them for disaster, and they were severely crushed. (Judges 2:10-15) After this, God raised up Judges—whom we understand as censors—over them, but they would not obey even these. Whenever a Judge died, they reverted to corruption worse than their fathers, chasing after foreign gods, serving and worshiping them. So the Lord grew angry and declared: 'Because this nation has transgressed My covenant which I commanded their fathers, and has not obeyed My voice, I will no longer drive out before them any of the nations Joshua left when he died.' (Judges 2:10-15) Thus, throughout nearly all the annals of the Judges and the subsequent kings, with the strength of the surrounding nations held in reserve, He meted out His wrath to Israel through war, captivity, and the yoke of foreigners, every time they strayed far into idolatry.

latin: Nec putem disceptandum, an digne Deus prohibeat nomen et honorem suum mendacio addici, an digne quos ab errore superstitionis avulserit, rursus in Aegyptum regredi nolit; an digne a se non patitur absistere quos sibi allegit. Itaque nec illud exspectabit retractari a nobis, an observari voluerit disciplinam quam voluit instituere, et an merito ulciscatur desertam, quam voluit observatam: quando frustra instituisset, si observari eam noluisset; et frustra observari voluisset, si vindicare noluisset. Sequitur enim ut has definitiones Dei adversus superstitiones, tam evictas quam etiam vindicatas probem, quoniam ex his tota martyriorum ratio constabit. Aberat apud Deum in monte Moyses, cum populus tam necessariam absentiam ejus impatiens, deos sibi producere quaerit, quos potius ipse perdiderit. Urgetur Aaron, et jubet inaures foeminarum suarum in ignem conferri. Amissuri enim erant in judicium sibi vera ornamenta aurium, Dei voces. Sapiens ignis effigiem vituli defundit illis, suggillans illic cor habentes, ubi et thesaurum, apud Aegyptum scilicet inter caetera animalia bovis etiam cujusdam consecratricem; itaque tria millia hominum a parentibus proximis caesa, quia tam proximum parentem Deum offenderant, transgressionis et primordia et merita dedicaverunt. In Arithmis, cum divertisset Israel apud Sethim, abeunt libidinatum ad filias Moab, invitantur ad idola, ut et spiritu fornicarentur; edunt denique de pollutis eorum: dehinc et adorant deos gentis, et Beelphegor initiantur. Ob hanc quoque idololatriam, moechiae sororem, viginti tria millia domesticis obtruncata gladiis divinae irae litaverunt. Defuncto Jesu Nave, derelinquunt Deum patrum suorum, et serviunt idolis Baalim et Astartis; et iratus Dominus tradidit eos in manibus diripientium; et diripiebantur ab illis, et venundabantur inimicis, nec poterant omnino subsistere a facie inimicorum suorum; quocumque processerant, manus erat super illos in mala, et compressati sunt valde. Post quae instituit super illos Deus Critas, quos censores intelligimus, sed nec istis obaudire perseverarunt: ut quis Critarum obierat, illi ad delinquendum supra quam patres eorum, abeundo post deos alienorum et serviendo et adorando eos. Itaque Dominus iratus: Quoniam quidem, ait, transgressa est gens ista pactum meum, quod disposui patribus eorum, et non audierunt vocem meam, et ego non advertam ad auferendum virum a facie eorum ex nationibus quas relinquit decedens Jesu. Atque ita per omnes pene annales critarum et deinceps regum, reservatis gentium circumcolarum viribus, bello et captivitate et jugo allophylorum iram dispensavit Israel, quotienscumque ab illo maxime in idololatriam exorbitaverunt.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: If it is established from the beginning that this practice is forbidden by so many and such great precepts, never committed with impunity, and attested by so many and such great examples, and that no crime counts as more arrogant before God than this kind of transgression, we ought to grasp of our own accord the intention behind divine warnings and punishments. Those intentions were already backed by martyrdoms then — not only not to be doubted, but to be endured. Prohibiting idolatry made room for those martyrdoms; otherwise they would not have happened. And God certainly established his own authority, wishing to bring about the very things for which he had made room.

Now we are pricked by the will of God, and the scorpion doubles the blow, denying this will and accusing it — so as either to insinuate another God whose will this is not, or nonetheless to destroy our God whose will is of this kind, or altogether to deny the will of God if it cannot deny God himself. But we, who fight elsewhere about God and about the rest of the body of each heretical doctrine, now draw up fixed battle lines into a single kind of contest. We defend the will of no other God than the God of Israel — the will that made room for martyrdoms, both through precepts that always prohibited idolatry and through judgments that punished it.

For if an observed precept suffers violence, that will be, in a certain way, the observance of the precept: I suffer the very thing by which I can keep the precept — namely, whatever violence threatens me while I avoid idolatry. And the one who imposes the precept exacts obedience. Therefore he could not have been unwilling for those things to happen by which obedience is proved.

It is prescribed to me not to name any other God; not to fashion God, either by speaking or by hand, in any way; not to adore or venerate any other, in any way, except the One who so commands. I am also commanded to fear him, lest I be deserted by him, and to love him with all my substance, so that I may die for him. Fighting for this sacrament, I am provoked by enemies; I am their equal if I yield. Defending it, I fight in the line, I am wounded, I am struck down, I am killed. Who wished this outcome for his soldier, except the one who sealed him with such a sacrament?

latin: Hanc igitur si a primordio constat et prohibitam de tot tantisque praeceptis, et nunquam impune commissam, de tot tantisque documentis, nec ullum tam superbum crimen apud Deum deputari, quam hujusmodi transgressionem, ultro intelligere debemus divinarum et denuntiationum et executionum intentionem, jam tunc martyriis patrocinatam, non modo non dubitandis, verum etiam sustinendis, quibus scilicet locum fecerat prohibendo idololatriam: aliter enim martyria non evenirent; et utique auctoritatem suam praestruxerat, volens ea evenire quibus locum fecerat. Nunc enim de Dei voluntate compungimur, et ingeminat scorpius plagam, hanc negans, hanc accusans voluntatem, ut aut alium Deum insinuet, cujus haec non sit voluntas; aut nostrum nihilominus destruat, cujus talis sit voluntas; aut omnino neget voluntatem Dei, si ipsum negare non poterit. Nos autem de Deo alibi dimicantes, et de reliquo corpore haereticae cujusque doctrinae, nunc in unam speciem congressionis certas praeducimus lineas, non alterius Dei, quam Israelis, eam defendentes voluntatem, quae martyriis locum fecerit, tam ex praeceptis prohibitae semper, quam ex judiciis punitae idololatriae. Si enim praeceptum observatum vim patitur, hoc erit quodammodo observandi praeceptum, ut id patiar per quod potero observare praeceptum: vim scilicet quaecumque mihi imminet caventi ab idololatria. Et utique qui imponit praeceptum, extorquet obsequium. Non potuit ergo noluisse ea evenire, per quae constabit obsequium. Praescribitur mihi ne quem alium Deum dicam; ne, vel dicendo, non minus lingua quam manu Deum fingam; ne quem alium adorem, aut quoque modo venerer, praeter unicum illum qui ita mandat; quem et jubeor timere, ne ab eo deserar; et de omni substantia diligere, ut pro eo moriar. Huic sacramento militans ab hostibus provocor, par sum illis si manus dedero; hoc defendendo depugno in acie, vulneror, concidor, occidor. Quis hunc militi suo exitum voluit, nisi qui tali eum sacramento consignavit?

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: So you have my God's will: a remedy has been found for this affliction. Now let us consider another blow, concerning the quality of that will. It would take too long to prove my God is good; the Marcionites have already learned that from us. For now, it is enough to say 'God,' which forces the conclusion that He is good. Anyone who presumes God is evil cannot hold both positions: either he must deny the existence of the God he calls evil, or he must admit that the one he calls God is good. Therefore, the will of the One who is good is good—unless He is good, He is not God. The goodness of what God wills also proves this; I mean martyrdom, because only a good God wills what is good. I argue that martyrdom is good before the same God who prohibits and punishes idolatry. Martyrdom resists and opposes idolatry, but nothing evil can resist evil—only what is good can. We do not deny there is rivalry among evils and among goods, but this case is different. Martyrdom does not compete with idolatry over some common wickedness; it competes over its own grace, because it frees from idolatry. Who would not call good that which frees from evil? What is the opposition between idolatry and martyrdom if not death and life? Life is credited to martyrdom to the same degree that death is credited to idolatry. The man who calls life evil has death, which he calls good. This is the perversity of men: to reject what saves, accept what destroys, seek danger, avoid the cure, and finally desire death rather than healing. Many also shun medical help—fools, cowards, and the falsely modest. Medicine seems cruel with its scalpel, cautery, and burning mustard plasters, yet being cut, seared, and stretched is not evil because it brings useful pain. It is not rejected because it causes sorrow; because it necessarily causes sorrow, it is applied. The horror of the procedure is excused by its fruit. The patient who screams, groans, and bellows under the doctor's hands will afterward heap those same hands with praise, call them master artisans, and deny they were ever cruel. So martyrdoms also rage, but for salvation; God may cure through fires, swords, and every bitter thing for eternal life. You will marvel at the Doctor too: He mostly applies remedies whose qualities match the complaints—helping through perverse means, by the very things through which we suffer. He checks fevers by piling on greater heat, quenches burning by inducing thirst, gathers excess bile with bitter draughts, and recalls the flow of blood by opening a vein. Yet you would blame God, even a zealous God, if He chooses to contend with the cause and benefit by rivaling the injury: dissolving death by death, scattering killing by killing, shaking off torments by torments, evaporating punishments by punishments, conferring life by taking it, helping by wounding the flesh, saving by taking the soul. What you call perversity is reason; what you call cruelty is grace: thus the eternal God heals through temporary means. Praise your good God, however harsh He seems: you have fallen into His hands, but happily; He has also fallen into your afflictions. Man always strikes the bargain with the doctor first; in the end, he draws the danger of death upon himself. He had received from his Lord, as from a physician, a most useful discipline for living under the law (Genesis 2:16-17): he might eat of every tree, but abstain from only one, which the Doctor Himself knew was trouble. He listened to the voice he preferred, broke his fast, ate the forbidden fruit, and gorged on transgression until he grew raw in death—most worthy to perish utterly, because he chose it. But the Lord, sustaining the heat of the sin until the medicine was ready, gradually compounded remedies: all the disciplines of faith, even those rivaling vice—rescinding the word of death with the word of life, scraping the hearing of transgression clean with the hearing of devotion—so that even when the Doctor commands death, He excludes eternal death. Why does man now balk at suffering from the remedy, when he never balked at suffering from vice? Does it displease him to be killed for salvation, when it did not displease him to be killed for perdition? Will he gag on the antidote who swallowed poison?

latin: Habes igitur Dei mei voluntatem: occursum est huic plagae. In alium ictum consideremus, de voluntatis qualitate. Longum est ut Deum meum bonum ostendam, quod jam a nobis didicerunt Marcionitae. Deum interim sufficit dici, ut necesse sit bonum credi. Malum enim Deum qui praesumpserit, constare in utroque non poterit: aut Deum negare debebit, quem malum existimarit; aut bonum dicere, quem Deum pronuntiarit. Bona igitur erit et voluntas ejus, qui nisi bonus, non erit Deus. Probabit hoc etiam ipsius rei bonitas, quam Deus voluit; martyrii dico: quia bonum nonnisi bonus voluit. Bonum contendo martyrium apud eumdem Deum, a quo et prohibetur et punitur idololatria. Obnititur enim et adversatur idololatriae martyrium. Malo autem obniti et adversari nisi bonum non potest. Non quasi negemus esse aemulationem, tam malorum inter se, quam et bonorum. Sed alia conditio est hujus tituli. Martyrium enim non de communi aliqua malitia certat cum idololatria, sed de sua gratia; liberat enim ab idololatria. Quod a malo liberat, quis non bonum pronuntiabit? quid aliud est adversatio idololatriae atque martyrii, quam mortis et vitae? In tantum vita martyrio deputabitur, quantum mors idololatriae. Vitam qui malum dixerit, habet mortem quam bonum dicat. Est et haec perversitas hominum, salutaria excutere, exitiosa suscipere, periculosa quaerere, medica male vitare; mori denique citius, quam curari desiderare. Nam et medicinae praesidium plures refugiunt: plures enim stulti, plures timidi, et male verecundi. Et est plane quasi saevitia medicinae, de scalpello, deque cauterio, de sinapis incendio; non tamen secari, et inuri, et extendi, idcirco malum, quia dolores utiles affert: nec quia tantummodo contristat, recusabitur; sed quia necessario contristat, adhibebitur. Horrorem operis fructus excusat. Ululans denique ille, et gemens, et mugiens inter manus medici, postmodum easdem mercede cumulabit, artifices optimas praedicabit, et saevas jam negabit. Sic et martyria desaeviunt, sed in salutem; licebit et Deo in vitam aeternam per ignes et gladios et acerba quaeque curare. Sed medicum quidem miraberis etiam in illo, quod ferme pares adhibet qualitates medelarum adversus qualitates querelarum: cum quasi de perverso auxiliatur, per ea subveniens per quae laboratur. Nam et calores caloribus amplius onerando compescit, et ardores siti potius macerando restinguit, et fellis excessus amaris quibusque potiunculis colligit, et sanguinis fluxus defusa insuper venula revocat. Deum vero, et quidem zelotem, culpandum existimabis, si voluit certasse cum caussa, et injuriae aemulando prodesse, mortem morte dissolvere, occisionem occisione dispargere, tormentis tormenta discutere, supplicia suppliciis evaporare, vitam auferendo conferre, carnem laedendo juvare, animam eripiendo servare. Perversitas quam putas, ratio est; quod saevitiam existimas, gratia est: ita Deo de momentaneis aeterna medicante. Magnifica bono tuo Deum tetrum: incidisti in manus ejus, sed feliciter incidisti; incidit et ille in aegritudines tuas. Homo semper medico prior negotium facit: denique sibimetipse periculum mortis attraxit. Acceperat a Domino suo, ut a medico, satis utilem disciplinam secundum legem vivendi, ut omnia quidem ederet, ab una solummodo arbuscula temperaret, quam ipse medicus importunam interim noverat: audiit ille quem maluit, et abstinentiam rupit, edit illicitum, et transgressione saturatus, in mortem cruditavit, dignissimus bona fide in totum perire, qui voluit. Sed Dominus sustentata fervura delicti, donec tempore medicina temperaretur, paulatim remedia composuit, omnes fidei disciplinas, et ipsas aemulas vitio, verbum mortis verbo vitae rescindentes, auditum transgressionis auditu devotionis limantes, ita et cum mori praecipit medicus ille, veternum mortis excludit. Quid gravatur pati nunc homo ex remedio, quod non est tunc gravatus pati ex vitio? displicet occidi in salutem, cui non displicuit occidi in perditionem? nauseabit ad antidotum, qui hiavit ad venenum?

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Suppose God had offered us martyrdoms under the label of a contest, matches in which we would prove ourselves against an adversary, so that the very one from whom a person is gladly freed he might now steadily conquer; even then God's generosity would outweigh his severity. He wanted the human being ripped from the devil's jaws by faith to become the devil's conqueror by virtue, so that he would not merely escape but actually defeat the enemy. The One who loved us and called us to salvation also chose to invite us to glory, that we might rejoice in our liberation and exult in our crowning. Those brutal games—contentious, superstitious rites of the Greeks, of religions, of pleasures—which the world celebrates with such enthusiasm, even Africa has abandoned. Yet individual cities still harass Carthage with congratulations because she was awarded the Pythian games after the stadium's heyday had passed. From ancient times it was deemed supremely worthwhile to commit the arts to the stadium, to display the excellence of bodies and voices, with a prize as the measure, a spectacle as the judge, and pleasure as the verdict. In these contests there are no battles, yet wounds abound: blows shatter, kicks hammer, fists tear, whips lacerate. Still, no one ever reproaches the games' overseer, even though men decry violence and lawsuits for injury arise outside the arena; they only calculate how many bruises, how much blood, how many welts can be traded for crowns, glory, dowries, public privileges, civic stipends, images, statues, and the kind of eternal fame and resurrection of memory the world can supply. The boxer himself does not complain of pain, because he chooses it; the crown presses down his wounds, the palm obscures his blood; victory swells more than injury. Will you call that man injured whom you see rejoicing? Nor will the loser himself reproach the judge for his fall. Would God be ashamed to bring his arts and disciplines into the open, into this world's arena, into a spectacle for men and angels and all powers—to test flesh and soul for constancy and endurance, to award the palm to one, honor to another, citizenship to another, stipends to another, and also to reject some and dismiss the chastised in disgrace? You are effectively dictating to God the times, manners, and places in which he may judge his own household, as if a judge ought not to prejudge. What if God had not exposed faith to martyrdom under the name of a contest, but for its own advance? Would it not need some store of hope to draw its zeal and anchor its vow, the means by which it strives to ascend, since even earthly offices are ranked in grades? How else are there many dwellings with the Father, if not according to the variety of merits? How does one star differ from another in glory, if not by the diversity of its rays? (1 Corinthians 15:41). Moreover, if faith required some extension of sublimity and clarity, that benefit had to be one purchased by great labor, torture, torment, death. But consider the compensation: when flesh and soul are at stake—the two things dearer to a human being than anything else; one is the hand of God, the other the breath of God—these very things are ventured in the advance that belongs to them; these very things are spent, which bring gain; the same prices that are also rewards. God foresaw these frailties of the human condition, the adversary's snares, the deceptions of things, the world's nets, and that even after baptism faith would be endangered, that most would perish again after salvation—those who have worn out their wedding garment, who have not prepared oil for their lamps, who must be sought over mountains and hills and carried back on shoulders (Matthew 22:11-13; 25:1-13; Luke 15:4-5). Therefore he provided second comforts, final defenses, the struggle of martyrdom, and the baptism of blood, thereafter secure. Of its blessedness David says: "Blessed are those whose transgressions are forgiven, whose sins are covered. Blessed is the one whose sin the Lord does not count against them" (Psalm 32:1-2). For martyrs, indeed, nothing can be imputed, since life itself is laid down in that baptism. Thus love covers a multitude of sins (1 Peter 4:8)—the love of the one who loves God with all his strength, with which he wrestles in martyrdom, with his whole soul, which he lays down for God; the martyr is forged. Will you pronounce these remedies, counsels, judgments, and even spectacles to be the cruelty of God? Does God crave human blood? And yet I dare say: if man is the kingdom of God, if man is certain salvation, if man is also a second regeneration, no compensation is envied when the rationale of either grace or injury is shared.

latin: Sed si certaminis nomine Deus nobis martyria proposuisset, per quae cum adversario experiremur, ut a quo libenter homo elisus est, eum jam constanter elidat, hic quoque liberalitas magis, quam acerbitas Dei praeest. Evulsum enim hominem de diaboli gula per fidem, jam et inculcatorem ejus voluit efficere per virtutem; ne solummodo evasisset, verum etiam evicisset inimicum. Amavit, qui vocaverat in salutem, invitare et ad gloriam; ut gaudeamus liberati, exultemus etiam coronati. Agonas istos, contentiosa solemnia et superstitiosa certamina graecarum et religionum et voluptatum, quanta gratia saeculum celebret, etiam Africae liquit. Adhuc Carthaginem singulae civitates gratulando inquietant, donatam pythico agone post stadii senectutem. Ita ab aevo dignissimum creditum est stadiorum experimentum, committere artes, corporum et vocum praestantiam exprimere, praemio indice, spectaculo judice, sententia voluptate: qua nulla sunt praelia, non nulla vulnera, pugni quassant, calces arietant, cestus dilaniant, flagella dilacerant: nemo tamen agonis praesidem suggillaverit, quod homines violentiae objectat, injuriarum actiones extra stadium, sed quantum livores illi et cruores et vibices negotiantur intendet: coronas scilicet, et gloriam, et dotem, privilegia publica, stipendia civica, imagines, statuas, et qualem potest praestare saeculum de fama aeternitatem, de memoria resurrectionem. Pyctes ipse non queritur dolere se, nam vult, corona premit vulnera, palma sanguinem obscurat; plus victoria tumet quam injuria. Hunc tu laesum existimabis, quem vides laetum? Sed nec victus ipse de agonotheta casum suum exprobrabit. Deum dedecebit artes et disciplinas suas educere in medium, in hoc saeculi spatium, in spectaculum hominibus et angelis et universis potestatibus? carnem atque animam probare de constantia atque tolerantia? dare huic palmam, huic honorem, illi civitatem, illi stipendia? etiam quosdam reprobare, et castigatos cum ignominia summovere? Nimirum praescribes Deo, quibus temporibus, aut modis, aut locis de familia sua judicet, quasi non et praejudicare judici congruat. Quid nunc, si non certaminis nomine in martyria fidem exposuisset, sed et proprii profectus; nonne oportebat illam habere aliquem spei cumulum, cui studium suum cogeret, votumque suspenderet, quo eniteretur ascendere, cum terrena quoque officia in gradus aestuent? aut quomodo multae mansiones apud Patrem, si non pro varietate meritorum? quomodo et stella a stella distabit in gloria, nisi pro diversitate radiorum? Porro, et si fidei propterea congruebat sublimitatis et claritatis aliqua prolatio, tale quid esse oportuerat illud emolumenti, quod magno constaret labore, cruciatu, tormento, morte. Sed respice compensationem: cum caro et anima dependitur, quibus in homine carius nihil est; alterum manus Dei, alterum flatus; ipsa dependi in profectu, quorum est profectus; ipsa erogari, quae lucrifiant; eadem pretia, quae et merces. Prospexerat et has Deus imbecillitates conditionis humanae, adversarii insidias, rerum fallacias, saeculi retia, etiam post lavacrum periclitaturam fidem, perituros plerosque rursum post salutem, qui vestitum obsoletassent nuptialem, qui faculis oleum non praeparassent, qui requirendi per montes et saltus, et humeris essent reportandi. Posuit igitur secunda solatia, extrema praesidia, dimicationem martyrii, et lavacrum sanguinis exinde securum. De cujus felicitate David: Beati quorum dimissa sunt delicta, et quorum opertae sunt iniquitates. Beatus vir cui non imputaverit Deus delictum. Proprie enim martyribus nihil jam reputari potest, quibus in lavacro ipsa vita deponitur. Sic dilectio operit multitudinem delictorum, quae Deum scilicet diligens ex totis viribus suis, quibus in martyrio decertat, ex tota anima sua, quam pro Deo ponit, hominem martyrem excudit. Haec tu remedia, consilia, judicia, spectacula etiam Dei atrocitatem judicabis? sanguinem hominis Deus concupiscit? Et tamen ausim dicere, si et homo regnum Dei, si homo certam salutem, si et homo secundam regenerationem. Nulli compensatio invidiosa est, in qua aut gratiae, aut injuriae communis est ratio.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: My modest effort to set out the case for repentance—undertaken once, maintained forever—addresses everyone devoted to the Lord, all of them petitioners for salvation earned from God; yet it bears down hardest on the new converts. They have only just begun to steep their ears in divine sermons; they are still infants, fresh from their old life, groping about with undeveloped vision. True, they renounce their past and take up repentance, yet they neglect to shut themselves inside it. For the very desire for something from that past cuts them off short—just as fruit that has already begun to wither or turn bitter still flatters itself with a trace of its former sweetness. Moreover, every fault of hesitation and evasion toward repentance carries the presumption of baptism. Certain of unquestioned forgiveness, they steal the interim and issue themselves a license to sin, not instruction to avoid it. How foolish, how unjust: to skip repentance yet claim forgiveness—that is, to refuse the price and still reach for the merchandise. The Lord established that price for granting pardon; with this repentance-payment he offers to redeem impunity. If merchants test the coin before they strike a bargain, lest it be counterfeit, clipped, or adulterated, do we really believe the Lord submits repentance to prior testing before granting so great a reward as eternal life? But let us put off the truth of repentance for a moment. Do you suppose the corrected will be obvious once we are absolved? Not at all. While pardon still hangs in the balance, punishment looms; we do not yet merit release so that we may merit it when God threatens, not when he forgives. What servant, once freed, charges himself with his own thefts and escapes? What soldier, once discharged, still answers for his old offenses? The sinner must lament before forgiveness, because the time for repentance is a time of danger and fear. I do not deny that the divine benefit—the abolition of sins—is entirely secure for those initiated into the water; but reaching it demands effort. Who would grant even a single sprinkling of any water to a man of such faithless repentance? Stealthy assault and self-serving assertions come easily. But God guards his treasure and does not let the unworthy sneak in. What does he finally say? Nothing hidden will stay unrevealed. However much darkness you pile over your deeds, God is light. Some, however, imagine God is obliged to deliver his promise even to the unworthy, turning his liberality into a form of servitude. If he grants the sign of death out of necessity, he does it unwillingly; and who lets stand what he gave unwillingly? Do not many fall away afterward? Is that gift not taken from many? These are the infiltrators who, having assaulted the pledge of repentance, build a house doomed to collapse on sand. So let no one flatter himself just because he is counted among the novices, as if he may still sin now that he has come to know the Lord; let him fear and revere at the same time. But what does it profit you to have known, when you lie in the very things you were ignorant of before? What separates you from a perfect servant of God? Is Christ one thing to the baptized and another to the hearers? Is there another hope, another reward, another fear of judgment, another necessity of repentance? That washing is the seal of a faith which begins with and is commended by the faith of repentance. We are not washed so that we may cease to sin, since we have already been washed in heart. For this is the hearer’s first washing: a whole fear; from then on, as long as you sense the Lord, you possess sound faith, a conscience that has once embraced repentance. Yet if we stop sinning after the waters, we put on innocence by compulsion, not free will. Who then excels in goodness? To whom is evil not permitted, or displeasing? Who is commanded, and who delights, to be free of crime? So we do not turn our hands from theft unless prison’s harshness stops us; we do not restrain our eyes from lust unless bodyguards block us. If no one devoted to the Lord stops sinning unless bound by baptism, I cannot tell whether such a baptized man grieves more over having stopped sinning than he rejoices over having escaped. Therefore hearers ought to desire baptism, not presume it. He who desires honors; he who presumes is proud. In the one appears modesty; in the other, petulance. The one strives; the other neglects. The one wants to merit; the other promises himself the debt: the one receives; the other invades. Whom do you judge more worthy, if not the more corrected? Whom more corrected, if not the more fearful, and therefore the one who has performed true repentance? He still feared to sin, lest he fail to merit receiving. But the presumptuous man, secure in his self-made promise, could not fear; thus he did not fulfill repentance, because he lacked its instrument—fear. Presumption is a slice of shamelessness; it crowds the petitioner and despises the giver. Consequently it sometimes deceives. For it promises before the debt is due, and the one who must pay is always offended.

latin: Quicquid ergo mediocritas nostra ad poenitentiam semel capessendam et perpetuo continendam suggerere conata est, omnes quidem deditos Domino spectat, ut omnis salutis in promerendo Deo petitores, sed praecipue novitiolis istis imminet. Qui cum maxime incipiunt divinis sermonibus aures rigare, quique catuli infantiae adhuc recentis, nec perfectis luminibus incerta reptant; et dicunt quidem pristinis renuntiare, et poenitentiam assumunt, sed includere eam negligunt. Interpellat enim illos ad desiderandum ex pristinis aliquid, ipse finis desiderandi: velut poma cum jam in acorem vel amaritudinem senescere incipiunt, ex parte aliqua tamen adhuc ipsi gratiae suae adulantur. Omne praeterea cunctationis et tergiversationis erga poenitentiam vitium, praesumptio intinctionis importat. Certi enim indubitatae veniae delictorum, medium tempus interim furantur, et commeatum sibi faciunt delinquendi, quam eruditionem non delinquendi. Quam porro ineptum, quam iniquum, poenitentiam non adimplere, et veniam delictorum sustinere, hoc est, pretium non exhibere, ad mercem manum emittere! Hoc enim pretio Dominus veniam addicere instituit; hac poenitentiae compensatione redimendam proponit impunitatem. Si ergo qui venditant, prius nummum, quo paciscuntur, examinant, ne scalptus, neve rasus, ne adulter etiam: Dominum credimus poenitentiae probationem prius inire, tantam nobis mercedem perennis scilicet vitae concessurum? Sed differamus tantisper poenitentiae veritatem. Tunc opinor emendatos liquebit, cum absolvimur? Nullo pacto. Sed cum pendente venia, poena prospicitur, cum adhuc liberari non meremur ut possimus mereri cum Deus comminatur, non cum ignoscit. Quis enim servus, postquam libertate mutatus est, furta sua et fugas sibi imputat? Quis miles postquam castris suis emissus, pro notis suis satagit? Peccator ante veniam deflere se debet; quia tempus poenitentiae, id est, quod periculi et timoris. Neque ego renuo divinum beneficium, id est, abolitionem delictorum inituris aquam omnimodo salvum esse; sed ut eo pervenire contingat, elaborandum est. Quis enim tibi tam infidae poenitentiae viro asperginem unam cujuslibet aquae commodabit? furto quidem aggredi, et praepositum hujus rei asseverationibus tuis circumduci facile est. Sed Deus thesauro suo providet, nec sinit obrepere indignos. Quid denique ait? Nihil occultum, quod non revelabitur. Quantascumque tenebras factis tuis superstruxeris, Deus lumen est. Quidam autem sic opinantur, quasi Deus necesse habeat praestare etiam indignis quod spopondit: et liberalitatem ejus faciunt servitutem. Quod si necessitate nobis, symbolum mortis indulget ergo invitus facit: quis enim permittit permansurum id, quod tribuerit invitus? Non enim multi postea excidunt? non a multis donum illud aufertur? Hi sunt scilicet, qui obrepunt, qui poenitentiae fidem aggressi, super arenas domum ruituram collocant. Nemo ergo sibi aduletur, quia inter auditorum tirocinia deputatur, quasi eo etiam nunc sibi delinquere liceat Dominum simul cognoveris, timeas: simul inspexeris, reverearis. Caeterum quid te cognovisse interest, cum iisdem incubas, quibus retro ignarus? Quid autem te a perfecto servo Dei separat? An alius est intinctis Christus, alius audientibus? Num spes alia, vel merces, alia formido judicii, alia necessitas poenitentiae? Lavacrum illud obsignatio est fidei: quae fides a poenitentiae fide incipitur et commendatur. Non ideo abluimur, ut delinquere desinamus, quoniam jam corde loti sumus. Haec enim prima audientis intinctio est metus integer; exinde quoad Dominum senseris, fides sana, conscientia semel poenitentiam amplexata. Caeterum, si ab aquis peccare desistimus, necessitate, non sponte innocentiam induimus. Quis ergo in bonitate praecellens? cui non licet, aut cui displicet malo esse? qui jubetur, an qui delectatur a crimine vacare? Ergo nec a furto manus avertamus, nisi claustrorum duritia repugnet: nec oculos a stupri concupiscentiis refraenemus, nisi a custodibus corporum obstructi, si nemo Domino deditus delinquere desinet, nisi intinctione alligatus. Quod si qui ita senserit, nescio an intinctus magis contristetur, quod peccare desierit, quam laetetur, quod evaserit. Itaque audientes optare intinctionem, non praesumere oportet. Qui enim optat, honorat: qui praesumit, superbit. In illo verecundia, in isto petulantia apparet. Ille satagit, hic negligit. Ille mereri cupit, at hic, ut debitum, sibi repromittit: ille sumit, hic invadit. Quem censeas digniorem, nisi emendatiorem? quem emendatiorem, nisi timidiorem, et idcirco vera poenitentia functum? Timuit enim adhuc delinquere, ne non mereretur accipere. At ille praesumptor, cum sibi repromitteret, securus scilicet, timere non potuit: sic nec poenitentiam implevit, quia instrumento poenitentiae, id est, metu, caruit. Praesumptio inverecundiae portio est, instat petitorem, despicit datorem. Itaque decipit nonnunquam. Ante enim quam debeatur repromittit, quo semper is, qui est praestaturus, offenditur.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: If the scorpion, swinging his tail in the air, still reproach us with having a murderer for our God , I shall shudder at the altogether foul breath of blasphemy which comes stinking from his heretical mouth; but I will embrace even such a God , with assurance derived from reason, by which reason even He Himself has, in the person of His own Wisdom, by the lips of Solomon, proclaimed Himself to be more than a murderer: Wisdom ( Sophia ), says He has slain her own children. Sophia is Wisdom. She has certainly slain them wisely if only into life, and reasonably if only into glory . Of murder by a parent, oh the clever form! Oh the dexterity of crime! Oh the proof of cruelty, which has slain for this reason, that he whom it may have slain may not die! And therefore what follows?

Wisdom is praised in hymns , in the places of egress; for the death of martyrs also is praised in song. Wisdom behaves with firmness in the streets, for with good results does she murder her own sons. Nay, on the top of the walls she speaks with assurance, when indeed, according to Esaias, this one calls out, I am God's; and this one shouts, In the name of Jacob; and another writes, In the name of Israel . Isaiah 44:5 O good mother! I myself also wish to be put among the number of her sons, that I may be slain by her; I wish to be slain, that I may become a son. But does she merely murder her sons, or also torture them? For I hear God also, in another passage, say, I will burn them as gold is burned, and will try them as silver is tried.

Zechariah 13:9 Certainly by the means of torture which fires and punishments supply, by the testing martyrdoms of faith . The apostle also knows what kind of God he has ascribed to us, when he writes: If God spared not His own Son, but gave Him up for us, how did He not with Him also give us all things? Romans 8:32 You see how divine Wisdom has murdered even her own proper, first-born and only Son, who is certainly about to live, nay, to bring back the others also into life. I can say with the Wisdom of God ; It is Christ who gave Himself up for our offenses. Romans 4:25 Already has Wisdom butchered herself also. The character of words depends not on the sound only, but on the meaning also, and they must be heard not merely by ears, but also by minds.

He who does not understand, believes God to be cruel; although for him also who does not understand, an announcement has been made to restrain his harshness in understanding otherwise than aright . For who, says the apostle , has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been His counsellor, to teach Him? Or who has pointed out to Him the way of understanding? Romans 11:34 But, indeed, the world has held it lawful for Diana of the Scythians, or Mercury of the Gauls, or Saturn of the Africans, to be appeased by human sacrifices ; and in Latium to this day Jupiter has human blood given him to taste in the midst of the city; and no one makes it a matter of discussion, or imagines that it does not occur for some reason, or that it occurs by the will of his God , without having value.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: We press a single point, and this alone is our challenge: are martyrdoms divine commands? Recognize that, and you will trust the commands by reason, because God never commands anything without reason. After all, the death of His faithful ones is honored in His sight, as David sings (Psalm 116:15). I do not take this for the common debt owed by all; that death is just, yes, but ignominious, the wages of transgression and deserved condemnation. The death that is added to it, though — the death born of religious witness and the battle of confession, for justice and for a sacrament — that is another matter. As Isaiah says: "See how the righteous perishes, and no one takes it to heart; the devout are taken away, and no one understands. From the face of injustice the righteous perishes, and his burial will be in peace" (Isaiah 57:1-2). Here you have both the preaching and the reward of martyrs.

From the very beginning, justice has suffered violence. The moment God began to be worshiped, religion drew envy's aim: the man who pleased God was murdered, and by his own brother at that — so that impiety, having tasted blood at home, would more readily hunt the blood of strangers. In the end, not only the just but the prophets as well. David was hounded, Elijah driven into flight, Jeremiah stoned, Isaiah sawn in two, Zachariah slaughtered between altar and sanctuary, stamping the stones with perpetual stains of his blood (Jeremiah). The very climax of the Law and the Prophets — not a prophet but an angel — was cut down by a contemptuous slaughter for the fee of a psalm-singing girl. And certainly those who were driven by the Spirit of God were directed by Him into martyrdoms, so that they might also suffer what they had preached.

So too the three brothers. When the dedication of the royal image pressed the city with its duty, they did not ignore what faith — which alone had not been taken captive in them — demanded: to die rather than serve idolatry. They remembered Jeremiah writing to them as that captivity loomed: "And now you will see the golden, silver, and wooden gods of the Babylonians carried on shoulders, striking fear into the nations. Take care, therefore, that you do not become like the foreigners, and be seized with fear when you see the crowds worshiping before and behind them; but say in your hearts: 'You, Lord, we must worship'" (Jeremiah). And so they spoke, their confidence conceived from God, when they shook off the king's conditional threats with the strength of their spirit: "We have no need to answer you on this. The God we worship is able to deliver us from the fiery furnace and from your hand; and then it will be clear to you that we will neither serve your god nor worship the golden image you have set up" (Daniel 3:16-18). Oh, a martyrdom perfected without suffering! They suffered enough, they were scorched enough — those whom God shielded, lest His power seem a lie.

Nor was Daniel spared the pattern. A suppliant of God alone, he was denounced and demanded by the Chaldeans; the lions' accustomed ferocity would have devoured him at once, had Darius's worthy confidence in God been allowed to fail. Moreover, it was necessary for every preacher and worshiper of God who, provoked to idolatry, refused obedience, to suffer — in keeping with that same logic by which the truth had to be commended to those present then and to posterity afterward, for which their passion would stand as the truth's defense; because no one would choose to be killed unless he possessed the truth. Such things from the beginning — both commandments and examples — prove that faith is indebted to martyrdom.

latin: Unum igitur gradum insistimus, et in hoc solum provocamus, an praecepta sint a Deo martyria, ut credas ratione praecepta, si praecepta cognoveris, quia nihil Deus non ratione praeceperit. Siquidem honorata est apud illum mors religiosorum ipsius, ut canit David; non opinor ista communis et omnium debitum: atqui justa, etiam ignominiosa est ex elogio transgressionis et merito damnationis; sed illa quae in ipso aditur ex testimonio religionis, et praelio confessionis, pro justitia et sacramento; sicut Esaia: Videte, inquit, quomodo perit justus, et nemo excipit corde; et viri justi auferuntur, et nemo animadvertit: a facie enim injustitiae perit justus, et erit honor sepultura ejus. Habes hic quoque et praedicationem et remunerationem martyriorum. A primordio enim justitia vim patitur. Statim ut coli Deus coepit, invidiam religio sortita est: qui Deo placuerat, occiditur, et quidem a fratre; quo proclivius impietas alienum sanguinem sectaretur, a suo auspicata est. Denique, non modo justorum; verum etiam et prophetarum. David exagitatur, Elias fugatur, Jeremias lapidatur, Esaias secatur, Zacharias inter altare et aedem trucidatur, perennes cruoris sui maculas silicibus adsignans. Ipse clausula Legis et Prophetarum; nec prophetes, sed angelus dictus, contumeliosa caede truncatur in puellae psalticae lucar. Et utique qui spiritu Dei agebantur, ab ipso in martyria dirigebantur, ut et jam patiendo quae et praedicassent. Proinde et trina fraternitas, cum dedicatio imaginis regiae urbem urgeret officio, non ignoraverunt quid fides, quae sola in illis captiva non fuerat, exigeret; moriendum scilicet adversus idololatriam. Meminerant enim et Jeremiae scribentis ad eos, quibus illa captivitas imminebat: Et nunc videbitis deos Babyloniorum aureos et argenteos et ligneos portari super humeros, ostentantes nationibus timorem. Cavete igitur ne et vos consimiles sitis Allophylis, et timore capiamini, dum aspicitis turbas adorantes retro eos et ante; sed dicite in animo vestro: Te, Domine, adorare debemus. Itaque dixerunt a Deo concepta fiducia, quando vigore animi conditionales minas regis excutiunt: Non habemus necessitatem respondendi huic tuo imperio. Est enim Deus noster quem colimus, potens eruere nos de fornace ignis, et ex manibus tuis; et tunc manifestum fiet tibi, quod neque idolo tuo famulabimur, nec imaginem tuam auream, quam stauisti, adorabimus. O martyrium et sine passione perfectum! Satis passi, satis exusti sunt, quos propterea Deus texit, ne potestatem ejus mentiri viderentur. Nam et Danielem nullius praeter Dei supplicem, et idcirco a Chaldaeis delatum ac depostulatum, statim utique conclusa et usitata feritas leonum devorasset, si Darii digna praesumptio de Deo falli debuisset. Caeterum, pati oportebat omnem Dei praedicatorem atque cultorem qui ad idololatriam provocatus negasset obsequium, secundum illius quoque rationis statum, qua et praesentibus tunc et posteris deinceps commendari veritatem oportebat, pro qua fidem diceret passio ipsorum defensorum ejus; quia nemo voluisset occidi, nisi compos veritatis. Talia a primordio et praecepta et exempla debitricem martyrii fidem ostendunt.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: If the old order has its own sacrament, we must examine the Christian innovation—unless we are prepared to admit another God, and thus a rival discipline, whose wisdom does not know how to slaughter its own sons. In Christ, the divinity, the will, and the school are clearly different: either there are no martyrdoms at all, or they must be understood differently by the One who urges no one into such danger, who promises nothing to those who suffer for Him, because He does not want them to suffer. And so, laying out the principles of His teaching: "Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness' sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven" (Matt. 5:10–12). That promise is absolute, addressed to everyone; then He narrows it to the Apostles themselves: "Blessed are you when they revile you, persecute you, and speak every evil against you on my account; rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven, for so they persecuted the prophets before you" (Matt. 5:11–12). He was thereby prophesying that they, too, would be killed, following the pattern of the prophets. Even if He had destined this conditional persecution solely for the Apostles at that moment, He would still have had in view—through them, with the whole sacrament, the propagation of the Name, and the transmission of the Holy Spirit to us—the discipline of enduring persecution for the heirs of the disciples, the fruits of the apostolic seed. For He speaks again to the Apostles: "Behold, I send you out as sheep in the midst of wolves" (Matt. 10:16), and "Beware of men; for they will hand you over to councils and flog you in their synagogues, and you will be dragged before governors and kings for my sake, as a testimony to them and to the nations" (Matt. 10:17–18). But when He adds, "Brother will deliver brother to death, and a father his child, and children will rise against parents and have them put to death" (Matt. 10:21), He plainly pronounces this wickedness upon others—a treachery we do not find among the Apostles. None of them suffered a brother or a father as a betrayer, yet many of our own have already done so.

latin: Superest, ne antiquitas suum quoque habuerit sacramentum, novitatem christianam recensere, quasi et de Deo aliam, ac proinde disciplina quoque aemulam, cujus sophia filios suos jugulare non norit. Plane alia in Christo et divinitas et voluntas et schola, martyria aut nulla in totum, aut aliter intelligenda mandarit, qui neminem ad hujusmodi discrimen hortetur, qui pro eo passis nihil repromittat, quia pati eos nolit. Et ideo praeceptorum principia deducens: Beati, inquit, qui persecutionem patiuntur ob justitiam, quoniam illorum est regnum coelorum. Hoc quidem absolute ad omnes, dehinc proprie ad Apostolos ipsos: Beati eritis cum vos dedecoraverint, et persecuti fuerint, et dixerint adversus vos omnia mala propter me; gaudete et exultate, quoniam merces vestra plurima in coelo: sic enim faciebant et prophetis patres eorum. Ut etiam prophetaret quod et ipsi occidi haberent ad exemplum prophetarum. Quanquam et si omnem hanc persecutionem conditionalem in solos tunc Apostolos destinasset, utique per illos cum toto sacramento, cum propagine nominis, cum traduce Spiritus Sancti in nos quoque spectasset etiam persecutionis obeundae disciplina, ut in haereditarios discipulos, et apostolici seminis frutices. Nam et rursus ad Apostolos dirigit: Ecce ego mitto vos tanquam oves in medio luporum; et: Cavete ab hominibus; tradent enim vos in consessus, et in synagogis suis flagellabunt vos, et ad praesides et reges perducemini, mei caussa, in testimonium illis et nationibus, etc. Cum autem subjicit: Tradet autem frater fratrem, et pater filium in mortem, et insurgent filii in parentes, et mortificabunt eos; manifeste iniquitatem istam in caeteros pronuntiavit, quam in Apostolis non invenimus. Nemo enim eorum aut fratrem aut patrem passus est traditorem, quod plerique jam nostri.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: I have said as much as my limited ability allows about everything that constitutes the religion of Baptism; now I will move on, as best I can, to its remaining aspects, touching on a few minor questions. Baptism, announced by John, already faced a question posed by the Lord himself to the Pharisees: was that Baptism heavenly or earthly? They could not give a consistent answer, because they did not understand, because they did not believe. For our part, we can only gauge it with as much understanding as we have faith; we judge that Baptism was indeed divine, but by command, not by power. We read that John was sent by the Lord to that office, yet his condition remained human (John 3:31). He displayed nothing heavenly; rather, he served heavenly things, appointed to administer repentance, which lies within human power. Finally, the teachers of the law and the Pharisees, who refused to believe, also refused to undergo repentance. If repentance is human, then the Baptism attached to it must share that same condition; otherwise, it would have conferred both the Holy Spirit and the remission of sins, had it been heavenly. But it forgives no sin and grants no Spirit—God alone does that. Even the Lord himself declared that the Spirit would not descend unless he first ascended to the Father. What the Lord was not yet bestowing, a servant could certainly not supply. We see this confirmed afterward in the Acts of the Apostles: those who had received John's Baptism had not received the Holy Spirit; they had not even heard of him. Therefore, it was not heavenly, because it did not exhibit heavenly gifts. The very thing that was heavenly in John—the spirit of prophecy—failed completely after the full transfer of the Spirit to the Lord, so much so that John, who had predicted the Coming One and identified him, later sent to ask whether he himself was the one. Thus, the Baptism of repentance was administered as a candidate for the remission and sanctification in Christ that would follow. When he preached a Baptism of repentance for the remission of sins, he announced a remission still future. Repentance precedes; remission follows. That is what it means to prepare the way: the one who prepares does not himself complete the work, but arranges for another to complete it. John himself confesses that his gifts are not heavenly, but Christ's, saying: "He who is from the earth speaks from the earth; he who comes from above is above all" (John 3:31). He baptized only in repentance; the One coming soon would baptize in Spirit and fire. Clearly, true and steadfast faith in the water brings baptism for salvation; counterfeit and weak faith brings baptism in fire for judgment (Acts 19:1-6).

latin: Diximus, quantum mediocritati nostrae licuit, de universis quae Baptismi religionem struunt; nunc ad reliquum statum ejus, aeque ut potero, progrediar de quaestiunculis quibusdam. Baptismus ab Joanne denuntiatus jam tunc habuit quaestionem ab ipso quidem Domino propositam Pharisaeis, coelestisne is Baptismus esset, an vero terrenus? De quo illi non valuerunt constanter respondere, utpote non intelligentes, quia non credentes. Nos porro quantula fide sumus, tantulo et intellectu possumus aestimare, divinum quidem eum Baptismum fuisse, mandatu tamen, non et potestate, quod et Joannem a Domino missum legimus in hoc munus caeterum humanum conditione. Nihil enim coeleste praestabat, sed coelestibus praeministrabat, poenitentiae scilicet praepositus, quae est in hominis potestate. Denique legis doctores et Pharisaei, qui credere noluerunt, nec poenitentiam egere. Quod si poenitentia humanum est, et Baptismus ipsius ejusdem conditionis fuerit necesse est; aut daret et Spiritum Sanctum et remissionem delictorum, si coelestis fuisset. Sed neque peccatum dimittit, neque Spiritum indulget, nisi Deus solus. Etiam ipse Dominus, nisi ipse prius ascenderet ad Patrem, aliter negavit, Spiritum descensurum. Id quod Dominus nondum conferebat, servus utique praestare non posset. Adeo postea in Actis apostolorum invenimus, quoniam qui Joannis Baptismum habebant, non accepissent Spiritum sanctum, quem ne auditu quidem noverant: ergo non erat coeleste, quod coelestia non exhibebat: cum ipsum quod coeleste in Joanne fuerat, spiritus prophetiae, post totius spiritus in Dominum translationem usque adeo defecerit, ut quem praedicaverat, quem advenientem designaverat, postmodum, an ipse esset miserit sciscitatum. Agebatur itaque Baptismus poenitentiae, quasi canditatus remissionis et sanctificationis in Christo subsecuturae. Nam quod praedicabat Baptismum poenitentiae in remissionem delictorum, in futuram remissionem enuntiatum est. Siquidem poenitentia antecedit, remissio subsequitur, et hoc est viam praeparare: qui autem praeparat, non idem ipse perficit, sed alii perficiendum procurat. Ipse profitetur sua non esse coelestia, sed Christi, dicendo: Qui de terra est, de terra loquitur: qui de supernis venit, super omnes est. Item, in sola poenitentia tinguere; venturum mox, qui tingueret in spiritu et igni. Scilicet, quia vera et stabilis aquae fides qua tinguitur in salutem; simulata autem et infirma, igni tinguitur in judicium.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Since the rule states that no one attains salvation without Baptism, grounded on the Lord's own pronouncement — "Unless someone is born of water, he will not have life" (John 3:5) — certain people raise scrupulous, or rather reckless, objections: how can this rule apply to the Apostles, whom we do not find baptized in the Lord except for Paul? Because Paul alone among them has put on Christ's Baptism, either the verdict on the danger facing the others who lack Christ's water must be prejudged so the rule stands, or the rule must be rescinded if salvation is also granted to the unbaptized. I have heard such things, with the Lord as my witness, so that no one thinks me so lost as to voluntarily stir up with my pen's lust what causes scruples for others. Now I will answer, as best I can, those who deny the Apostles were baptized. If they had undergone John's human baptism and desired the Lord's, since the Lord Himself defined one Baptism by telling Peter, who resisted being washed, "He who has been washed once has no need to be washed again" — which He would not have said to someone never baptized at all — this is the proof brought against those who deny the Apostles even John's baptism, aiming to destroy the sacrament of water. Can anyone believe that the very persons then preparing the Lord's way, that is, John's baptism, destined to open the Lord's way throughout the whole world, did not undergo it? The Lord Himself, who owed no debt of penitence, was baptized; was it not necessary for sinners? What then? Were others baptized? Yes, but not the companions of Christ — rather the rivals of faith, the teachers of the law, and the Pharisees. Hence it is also suggested that when those opposing the Lord refused baptism, those who followed Him were baptized and did not share their rivals' mindset, especially when the Lord to whom they adhered extolled John with the testimony: "No one among those born of women is greater than John the Baptist." Others crudely force the issue, claiming the Apostles then fulfilled Baptism's role when they were sprinkled and covered by waves in the boat, and that Peter was sufficiently immersed when he walked on the sea. But in my opinion, it is one thing to be sprinkled or overtaken by the sea's violence, another to be baptized by the discipline of religion. Moreover, that boat prefigured the Church, which is troubled in the sea, that is, the world, by waves, that is, persecutions and temptations, while the Lord is asleep, as it were, through patience, until, aroused by the prayers of the Saints in the last times, He restrains the world and gives tranquility to His own. Now, whether they were baptized somehow or remained unbaptized, it is nevertheless too rash to judge the Apostles' salvation, because they could have been granted the privilege of Baptism by the prerogative of their first calling and subsequent intimate familiarity with Him. For they followed Him who promised salvation to every believer, saying: "Your faith has saved you," and: "Your sins are forgiven," to the believer, indeed, even if not baptized. If the Apostles lacked this, I do not know what their faith was; at one word of the Lord, the tax collector rose and left his post; he deserted his father, his boat, and the trade by which he made his living; he despised his father's funeral: he fulfilled that greatest commandment of the Lord, "Whoever prefers father or mother to me is not worthy of me," before he even heard it.
