excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: The sacrifice acceptable to God is the unregretted separation of soul from body and its passions, and this constitutes true devotion to the living God. It is therefore not without reason that Socrates calls philosophy a study of death; for the philosopher neither brings sight into his thinking nor allows himself to be drawn by any other sense, but encounters reality with a pure mind and so pursues true philosophy. Pythagoras intends the same thing by the five-year silence he prescribes to his acquaintances, so that, turning away from sensory things, they may contemplate the divine with a bare intellect. The greatest of the Greeks have philosophized in this manner, following Moses; for he commands that the whole burnt offerings be flayed and divided into parts (Leviticus 1:9), since the cognitive soul, once stripped naked of its material covering and having shed all passions born of empty and false assumptions and stripped off fleshly desires, must be dedicated to the light. Most people, however, clothe themselves in mortality like snails and curl around their own excesses like hedgehogs, and they attribute to the blessed and immortal God the very qualities they find in themselves. This escapes their notice, even when they are near us: God has given us countless gifts of which He Himself has no share—being unborn, He has no need of birth; being self-sufficient, He has no need of nourishment; being unchanging, He has no need of growth; being immortal and ageless, He has no need of a good old age or a good death. Therefore no one should suppose that hands, feet, mouth, eyes, entrances, exits, organs, and threats are passions of God, as they are spoken of among the Hebrews; rather, certain of these names are to be understood allegorically in a holier sense, which we will clarify as the discussion proceeds. Wisdom is the panacea for all things, as Callimachus writes in his epigrams, and Bacchylides says in his Paeans, 'One man becomes wise from another, both in the past and in the present.' For it is not easy to find the gates of unspoken words. Isocrates asks in his Panathenaic Oration, 'Whom do I call educated?' and answers: first, those who handle well the things that meet them each day and possess a good reputation for judging the times so as to aim for the most part at what is beneficial; second, those who conduct themselves toward their associates with propriety and justice, bearing the unpleasantness and heaviness of others easily and lightly, and presenting themselves as lightly and moderately as possible to their companions; third, those who master their pleasures and are not utterly defeated by misfortunes, but behave manfully in them and live worthily of the nature they share; fourth, and most important, those who are not corrupted by good fortune, nor carried out of themselves, nor made arrogant, but remain steadfast in the discipline of sound judgment. He concludes by saying that those who possess a well-ordered soul not merely in one of these respects but in all of them are wise, perfect men who possess every virtue.

greek: Θυσία δὲ ἡ τῷ θεῷ δεκτὴ σώματός τε καὶ τῶν τούτου παθῶν ἀμετανόητος χωρισμός. ἡ ἀληθὴς τῷ ὄντι θεοσέβεια αὕτη. καὶ μή τι εἰκότως μελέτη θανάτου διὰ τοῦτο εἴρηται τῷ Σωκράτει ἡ φιλοσοφία· ὁ γὰρ μήτε τὴν ὄψιν παρατιθέμενος ἐν τῷ διανοεῖσθαι μήτε τινὰ τῶν ἄλλων αἰσθήσεων ἐφελκόμενος, ἀλλ’ αὐτῷ καθαρῷ τῷ νῷ τοῖς πράγμασιν ἐντυγχάνων τὴν ἀληθῆ φιλοσοφίαν μέτεισιν. τοῦτο ἄρα βούλεται καὶ τῷ Πυθαγόρᾳ ἡ τῆς πενταετίας σιωπή, ἣν τοῖς γνωρίμοις παρεγγυᾷ, ὡς δὴ ἀποστραφέντες τῶν αἰσθητῶν ψιλῷ τῷ νῷ τὸ θεῖον ἐποπτεύοιεν. παρὰ Μωυσέως τοιαῦτα φιλοσοφήσαντες οἱ τῶν Ἑλλήνων ἄκροι. προστάσσει γὰρ τὰ ὁλοκαυτώματα δείραντας εἰς μέλη διανεῖμαι, ἐπειδὴ γυμνὴν τῆς ὑλικῆς δορᾶς γενομένην τὴν γνωστικὴν ψυχὴν ἄνευ τῆς σωματικῆς φλυαρίας καὶ τῶν παθῶν πάντων, ὅσα περιποιοῦσιν αἱ κεναὶ καὶ ψευδεῖς ὑπολήψεις, ἀποδυσαμένην τὰς σαρκικὰς ἐπιθυμίας, τῷ φωτὶ καθιερωθῆναι ἀνάγκη. οἱ δὲ πλεῖστοι τῶν ἀνθρώπων τὸ θνητὸν ἐνδυόμενοι καθάπερ οἱ κοχλίαι καὶ περὶ τὰς αὑτῶν ἀκρασίας ὥσπερ οἱ ἐχῖνοι σφαιρηδὸν εἱλούμενοι περὶ τοῦ μακαρίου καὶ ἀφθάρτου θεοῦ τοιαῦτα οἷα καὶ περὶ αὑτῶν δοξάζουσιν. λέληθεν δ’ αὐτούς, κἂν πλησίον ἡμῶν τύχωσιν, ὡς μυρία ὅσα δεδώρηται ἡμῖν ὁ θεός, ὧν αὐτὸς ἀμέτοχος, γένεσιν μὲν ἀγένητος ὤν, τροφὴν δὲ ἀνενδεὴς ὤν, καὶ αὔξησιν ἐν ἰσότητι ὤν, εὐγηρίαν τε καὶ εὐθανασίαν ἀθάνατός τε καὶ ἀγήρως ὑπάρχων. διὸ καὶ χεῖρας καὶ πόδας καὶ στόμα καὶ ὀφθαλμοὺς καὶ εἰσόδους καὶ ἐξόδους καὶ ὀργὰς καὶ ἀπειλὰς μὴ πάθη θεοῦ τις ὑπολάβῃ παρὰ Ἑβραίοις λέγεσθαι, μηδαμῶς, ἀλληγορεῖσθαι δέ τινα ἐκ τούτων τῶν ὀνομάτων ὁσιώτερον, ἃ δὴ καὶ προϊόντος τοῦ λόγου κατὰ τὸν οἰκεῖον καιρὸν διασαφήσομεν. ἦ πανακὲς πάντων φάρμακον ἁ σοφία, Καλλίμαχος ἐν τοῖς ἐπιγράμμασι γράφει· ἕτερος (δὲ) ἐξ ἑτέρου σοφὸς τό τε πάλαι τό τε νῦν, φησὶ Βακχυλίδης ἐν τοῖς Παιᾶσιν· οὐδὲ γὰρ ῥᾷστον ἀρρήτων ἐπέων πύλας ἐξευρεῖν· καλῶς ἄρα Ἰσοκράτης ἐν τῷ Παναθηναϊκῷ τίνας οὖν καλῶ πεπαιδευμένους; προθεὶς ἐπιφέρει· πρῶτον μὲν τοὺς καλῶς χρωμένους τοῖς πράγμασι τοῖς κατὰ τὴν ἡμέραν ἑκάστην προσπίπτουσι καὶ τὴν δόξαν ἐπιτυχῆ τῶν καιρῶν ἔχοντας καὶ δυναμένην ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ στοχάζεσθαι τοῦ συμφέροντος· ἔπειτα τοὺς πρεπόντως καὶ δικαίως ὁμιλοῦντας ἀεὶ τοῖς πλησιάζουσι καὶ τὰς μὲν τῶν ἄλλων ἀηδίας καὶ βαρύτητας εὐκόλως καὶ ῥᾳδίως φέροντας, σφᾶς δ’ αὐτοὺς ὡς δυνατὸν ἐλαφροτάτους καὶ μετριωτάτους τοῖς ξυνοῦσι παρέχοντας· ἔτι δὲ τοὺς τῶν μὲν ἡδονῶν κρατοῦντας, τῶν δὲ συμφορῶν μὴ λίαν ἡττωμένους, ἀλλ’ ἀνδρωδῶς ἐν αὐταῖς ἀναστρεφομένους καὶ τῆς φύσεως ἀξίως ἧς μετέχοντες τυγχάνομεν· τέταρτον, ὅπερ μέγιστόν ἐστι, τοὺς μὴ διαφθειρομένους ὑπὸ τῶν εὐπραγιῶν μηδ’ ἐξισταμένους αὑτῶν μηδὲ ὑπερηφάνους γινομένους, ἀλλ’ ἐμμένοντας τῇ τάξει τῶν εὖ φρονούντων. εἶτα ἐπιφέρει τὸν κολοφῶνα τοῦ λόγου· τοὺς δὲ μὴ μόνον πρὸς ἓν τούτων, ἀλλὰ πρὸς ἅπαντα ταῦτα τὴν ἕξιν τῆς ψυχῆς εὐάρμοστον ἔχοντας, τούτους φημὶ καὶ φρονίμους εἶναι καὶ τελείους ἄνδρας καὶ πάσας ἔχειν τὰς ἀρετάς.

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: He never recalls those who have sinned against him; he simply forgives them. That is why he can pray justly, saying, "Forgive us, for we also forgive" — because forgiving is one of the very things God wills: to desire nothing, to hate no one, since all humanity is the work of a single divine will. And our Savior, wanting the gnostic to be "perfect as the heavenly Father" (Matt. 5:48) — that is, Himself — says, "Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord" (Ps. 34:11). He does not intend the gnostic still to need help mediated through angels, but to become worthy of receiving aid directly from Himself. And is the gnostic to have a guard through obedience? Such a person demands this from the Lord; he does not merely ask. Even on behalf of needy brothers, the gnostic will not petition for a surplus of wealth to distribute, but will pray to become himself the provision of whatever they lack. For the gnostic gives his prayer to those in need, and through that prayer supplies their want unknowingly and without pride.

Therefore poverty, sickness, and similar trials are often brought as instruction, for the correction of past failures and for the return to a right path in the future. The gnostic, who possesses the distinctive gift of knowledge, seeks relief from these afflictions not from vainglory but simply because he is a gnostic; and so he himself works the good, becoming an instrument of God's goodness. The traditions report that the apostle Matthew said of each situation: "If a neighbor of the elect sins, the elect has sinned; for if he had conducted himself as the Word dictates, his neighbor would have been restrained from sinning by the warning of his life." What then shall we say of the gnostic himself? "Do you not know that you are a temple of God?" (1 Cor. 3:16), says the apostle. The gnostic is therefore divine and already holy, bearing God and borne by God. Scripture immediately presents sin as something alien, handing over those who have fallen to the aliens, and saying, "Do not look with desire upon an alien woman" (cf. Prov. 6:25); it declares sin to be utterly alien and contrary to the nature of the temple of God. The temple is both great, as the Church, and small, as the person who guards the seed of Abraham. Hence the one who has God resting in him will not desire anything else. At once he leaves behind every hindrance and, rising above all the matter that distracts him, cuts through the heavens by means of knowledge. Passing through the spiritual substances and every rule and authority, he touches the highest thrones, straining toward that alone which he has known. Having blended the dove with the serpent, he lives perfectly and with a clear conscience, weaving faith with hope toward the expectation of what is to come.

For he is aware of the gift he has received, having become worthy to obtain it and having been transferred from slavery into adoption. Walking in step with knowledge, he fulfills the works worthy of grace, displaying the deeds; for works follow knowledge as the shadow follows the body. Consequently he is not disturbed by anything that happens, nor does he suspect any event that occurs for his benefit within the divine economy; he is not even ashamed to die, conscious that he will appear before the authorities with a clear conscience, having cleansed every stain from his soul. Knowing full well that it will be far better for him after his departure, he never prefers the pleasant or the immediately advantageous over the economy, but trains himself through the commandments so that he may be well-pleasing to the Lord in all things and commended even by the world. Since all things stand fast upon the one Almighty God, he says, "The Son of God came to his own, and his own did not receive him" (John 1:11). Therefore, in his use of worldly things he not only gives thanks and marvels at creation, but by using them as he ought he is himself commended. For his goal is to advance through gnostic activity according to the commandments into contemplation. From this point onward, harvesting the provisions for contemplation through knowledge and embracing the magnitude of knowledge with greatness of soul, he presses on toward the holy reward of transference. For he has heard the psalm saying, "Walk about Zion, go around her, number her towers" (Ps. 48:12–13); this means, I think, that those who have received the Word in a lofty way will become lofty as towers and will stand firm in both faith and knowledge.

greek: Οὐδέποτε τῶν εἰς αὐτὸν ἁμαρτησάντων μέμνηται, ἀλλὰ ἀφίησι. διὸ καὶ δικαίως εὔχεται, »ἄφες ἡμῖν« λέγων· »καὶ γὰρ ἡμεῖς ἀφίεμεν·« ἓν γάρ ἐστι καὶ τοῦτο ὧν ὁ θεὸς βούλεται. μηδενὸς ἐπιθυμεῖν. μηδένα μισεῖν· ἑνὸς γὰρ θελήματος ἔργον οἱ πάντες ἄνθρωποι. καὶ μή τι τὸν γνωστικὸν »τέλειον« εἶναι βουλόμενος ὁ σωτὴρ ἡμῶν »ὡς τὸν οὐράνιον πατέρα«. τουτέστιν ἑαυτόν. ὁ λέγων »δεῦτε. τέκνα. ἀκούσατέ μου φόβον κυρίου«, οὐ τῆς δι᾿ ἀγγέλων βοηθείας ἐπιδεῆ ἔτι εἶναι βούλεται τοῦτον, παρ᾿ ἑαυτοῦ δὲ ἄξιον γενόμενον λαμβάνειν. καὶ τὴν φρουρὰν ἔχειν παρ᾿ ἑαυτοῦ διὰ τῆς εὐπειθείας; ὁ τοιοῦτος ἀπαιτεῖ παρὰ κυρίου, οὐχὶ δὲ καὶ αἰτεῖ. καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν πενομένων ἀδελφῶν οὐκ αὐτὸς αἰτήσεται ὁ γνωστικὸς [οὐ] χρημάτων περιουσίαν εἰς μετάδοσιν, ἐκείνοις δὲ ὧν δέονται χορηγίαν εὔξεται γενέσθαι. δίδωσι γὰρ οὕτως καὶ τὴν εὐχὴν τοῖς δεομένοις ὁ γνωστικὸς καὶ τὸ διὰ τῆς εὐχῆς ἀγνώστως ἅμα καὶ ἀτύφως παρέχεται. πενία μὲν οὖν πολλάκις καὶ νόσος καὶ τοιαῦται πεῖραι ἐπὶ νουθεσίᾳ προσφέρονται καὶ πρὸς διόρθωσιν τῶν παρεληλυθότων καὶ πρὸς ἐπιστροφὴν τῶν μελλόντων. ὁ τοιοῦτος τὸν ἐπικουφισμὸν τούτοις αἰτούμενος. ἅτε τὸ ἐξαίρετον τῆς γνώσεως ἔχων, οὐ διὰ κενοδοξίαν, ἀλλὰ δι᾿ αὐτὸ τὸ εἶναι γνωστικός, αὐτὸς ἐργάζεται τὴν εὐποιίαν. ὄργανον γενόμενος τῆς τοῦ θεοῦ ἀγαθότητος. Λέγουσι δὲ ἐν ταῖς παραδόσεσι Ματθίαν τὸν ἀπόστολον παρ᾿ ἕκαστα εἰρηκέναι ὅτι »ἐὰν ἐκλεκτοῦ γείτων ἁμαρτήσῃ, ἥμαρτεν ὁ ἐκλεκτός· εἰ γὰρ οὕτως ἑαυτὸν ἦγεν, ὡς ὁ λόγος ὑπαγορεύει, κατῃδέσθη ἂν αὐτοῦ τὸν βίον καὶ ὁ γείτων εἰς τὸ μὴ ἁμαρτεῖν«. τί τοίνυν περὶ αὐτοῦ τοῦ γνωστικοῦ φήσαιμεν ἄν; »ἢ οὐκ οἴδατε«, φησὶν ὁ ἀπόστολος. »ὅτι ναός ἐστε τοῦ θεοῦ;« θεῖος ἄρα ὁ γνωστικὸς καὶ ἤδη ἅγιος, θεοφορῶν καὶ θεοφορούμενος. αὐτίκα τὸ ἁμαρτῆσαι ἀλλότριον παριστᾶσα ἡ γραφὴ τοὺς μὲν παραπεσόντας τοῖς ἀλλοφύλοις πιπράσκει· »μὴ ἐμβλέψῃς« δὲ »πρὸς ἐπιθυμίαν ἀλλοτρίᾳ γυναικὶ« λέγουσα. ἄντικρυς ἀλλότριον καὶ παρὰ φύσιν τοῦ ναοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν λέγει. ναὸς δέ ἐστιν ὃ μὲν μέγας, ὡς ἡ ἐκκλησία, ὃ δὲ μικρός. ὡς ὁ ἄνθρωπος ὁ τὸ σπέρμα σῴζων τὸ Ἀβραάμ. οὐκ ἄρα ἐπιθυμήσει τινὸς ἑτέρου ὁ ἔχων ἀναπαυόμενον τὸν θεόν. αὐτίκα πάντα τὰ ἐμποδὼν καταλιπὼν καὶ πᾶσαν τὴν περισπῶσαν αὐτὸν ὕλην ὑπερηφανήσας τέμνει διὰ τῆς ἐπιστήμης τὸν οὐρανόν. καὶ διελθὼν τὰς πνευματικὰς οὐσίας καὶ πᾶσαν ἀρχὴν καὶ ἐξουσίαν ἅπτεται τῶν θρόνων τῶν ἄκρων, ἐπ᾿ ἐκεῖνο μόνον ἱέμενος, [ἐφ᾿] ὃ ἔγνω μόνον. μείξας οὖν τῇ περιστερᾷ τὸν ὄφιν τελείως ἅμα καὶ εὐσυνειδήτως βιοῖ, πίστιν ἐλπίδι κεράσας πρὸς τὴν τοῦ μέλλοντος ἀπεκδοχήν. αἴσθεται γὰρ τῆς δωρεᾶς ἧς ἔλαβεν ἄξιος γενόμενος τοῦ τυχεῖν, καὶ μετατεθεὶς ἐκ δουλείας εἰς υἱοθεσίαν. [ἀν] ἀκόλουθα τῇ ἐπιστήμῃ [μήτε μὴ] (»γνοὺς τὸν θεὸν [μᾶλλον δὲ] γνωσθείς τε πρὸς αὐτοῦ«) ἐπιτελεῖ, πρὸς ἀξίαν τῆς χάριτος ἐνδεικνύμενος τὰ ἐνεργήματα. ἕπεται γὰρ τὰ ἔργα τῇ γνώσει ὡς τῷ σώματι ἡ σκιά. Ἐπ᾿ οὐδενὶ τοίνυν εἰκότως ταράσσεται τῶν συμβαινόντων οὐδὲ ὑποπτεύει τῶν κατὰ τὴν οἰκονομίαν ἐπὶ τῷ συμφέροντι γινομένων οὐδὲν οὐδὲ αἰσχύνεται ἀποθανεῖν, εὐσυνείδητος ὢν ταῖς ἐξουσίαις ὀφθῆναι, πάντας ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν τοὺς τῆς ψυχῆς ἀποκεκαθαρμένος σπίλους, ὅ γε εὖ μάλα ἐπιστάμενος ἄμεινον αὐτῷ μετὰ τὴν ἔξοδον γενήσεσθαι. ὅθεν οὐδέποτε τὸ ἡδὺ καὶ τὸ συμφέρον προκρίνει τῆς οἰκονομίας, γυμνάζων ἑαυτὸν διὰ τῶν ἐντολῶν, ἵνα καὶ πρὸς τὸν κύριον εὐάρεστος ἐν πᾶσι γένηται καὶ πρὸς τὸν κόσμον ἐπαινετός. ἐπεὶ τὰ πάντα ἐφ᾿ ἑνὸς τοῦ παντοκράτορος θεοῦ ἵσταται. »εἰς τὰ ἴδια«. φησίν, »ἦλθεν ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ οἱ ἴδιοι αὐτὸν οὐκ ἐδέξαντο.« διὸ καὶ κατὰ τὴν τῶν κοσμικῶν χρῆσιν οὐ μόνον εὐχαριστεῖ καὶ θαυμάζει τὴν κτίσιν, ἀλλὰ καὶ χρώμενος ὡς προσῆκεν ἐπαινεῖται. ἐπεὶ τὸ τέλος αὐτῷ δι᾿ ἐνεργείας γνωστικῆς τῆς κατὰ τὰς ἐντολὰς εἰς θεωρίαν περαιοῦται. ἐνθένδε ἤδη, δι᾿ ἐπιστήμης τὰ ἐφόδια τῆς θεωρίας καρπούμενος μεγαλοφρόνως τε τὸ τῆς γνώσεως ἀναδεξάμενος μέγεθος, πρόεισιν ἐπὶ τὴν ἁγίαν τῆς μεταθέσεως ἀμοιβήν. ἀκήκοεν γὰρ τοῦ ψαλμοῦ λέγοντος· »κυκλώσατε Σιὼν καὶ περιλάβετε αὐτήν, διηγήσασθε ἐν τοῖς πύργοις αὐτῆς« αἰνίσσεται γάρ. οἶμαι. τοὺς ὑψηλῶς προσδεξαμένους τὸν λόγον ὑψηλοὺς ὡς πύργους ἔσεσθαι καὶ βεβαίως ἔν τε τῇ πίστει καὶ τῇ γνώσει στήσεσθαι.

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: And so the *apatheia* that belongs to us, as it were, by way of the gnostic advances through love "to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature" and reaches its goal, becoming assimilated to God and truly "equal to angels" (Eph 4:13). Many other scriptural testimonies could be brought forward, but I think it better to forgo that ambition because of the length of the discourse, leaving those who wish to labor and toil over the doctrines by a selection from the Scriptures to do so. I will, however, recall one passage in brief so as not to leave the place unremarked. For the divine apostle says in the first epistle to the Corinthians, "Does any of you dare, having a matter against another, to be judged before the unrighteous and not before the saints? Or do you not know that the saints will judge the world?" and what follows (1 Cor 6:1). Since the passage is very large, we will present the apostle's thought by synchronizing with the opportune words of the apostolic writings, as it were translating the phrase in brief, according to which he describes the perfection of the gnostic. For he does not establish the gnostic only on the ground of being wronged rather than wronging, but also teaches him to be forgetful of evils, not permitting him to pray against the one who wronged him. For he knows that the Lord commanded "to pray for enemies" (Matt 5:44). So then, the phrase "to be judged before the unrighteous" means that the wronged person wishes nothing other than to repay and to retaliate, which is equally to do wrong himself. But the phrase "to be judged before the saints" indicates that some wish to have the excess returned to those who wronged them by prayer, and these are better than the former ones, yet not yet *apathetic*, unless they become completely forgetful of evils, having prayed according to the Lord's teaching and for their enemies. It is good, therefore, for them to acquire sound minds from repentance, having partaken of faith. For even if the truth seems to acquire enemies who are jealous, it does not hate anyone. For "God causes his sun to shine on the righteous and the unrighteous" (Matt 5:45), and he sent the Lord upon the righteous and the unrighteous. The one who forces himself to be assimilated to God, through much forgetfulness of evils, "forgiving seventy times seven" (Matt 18:22) — that is, throughout the whole life and throughout the whole cosmic cycle, signified by the number seventy — shows kindness to everyone, even if someone wrongs the gnostic all the time he lives in the flesh. For he does not think it worthy to entrust judgment to others only, but also to ask from those who judge for the forgiveness of sins against him, and rightly so; for if the injury is only what is outside and concerns the body, even if it proceeds to death.

greek: καὶ δὴ τῆς κατὰ τὸν γνωστικὸν ἡμῖν ὡς εἰπεῖν ἀπαθείας, καθ᾿ ἣν ἡ τελείωσις τοῦ πιστοῦ δι᾿ ἀγάπης »εἰς ἄνδρα τέλειον. εἰς μέτρον ἡλικίας« προβαίνουσα ἀφικνεῖται, ἐξομοιουμένη θεῷ, »ἰσάγγελος« ἀληθῶς γενομένη. πολλὰ μὲν καὶ ἄλλα ἐκ γραφῆς μαρτύρια ἔπεισι παρατίθεσθαι. ἄμεινον δὲ οἶμαι ὑπερθέσθαι τὴν τοιαύτην φιλοτιμίαν διὰ τὸ μῆκος τοῦ λόγου, τοῖς πονεῖν ἐθέλουσι καὶ προσεκπονεῖν τὰ δόγματα κατ᾿ ἐκλογὴν τῶν γραφῶν ἐπιτρέψαντα. μιᾶς δ᾿ οὖν διὰ βραχυτάτων ἐπιμνησθήσομαι, ὡς μὴ ἀνεπισημείωτον παραλιπεῖν τὸν τόπον. λέγει γὰρ ἐν τῇ προτέρᾳ [τῆς] πρὸς Κορινθίους ἐπιστολῇ ὁ θεῖος ἀπόστολος· »τολμᾷ τις ὑμῶν πρᾶγμα ἔχων πρὸς τὸν ἕτερον κρίνεσθαι ἐπὶ τῶν ἀδίκων καὶ οὐχὶ ἐπὶ τῶν ἁγίων; ἢ οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι ἅγιοι τὸν κόσμον κρινοῦσι;« καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς. μεγίστης δ᾿ οὔσης τῆς περικοπῆς. ταῖς ἐπικαίροις τῶν ἀποστολικῶν συγχρώμενοι λέξεσι, διὰ βραχυτάτων ἐξ ἐπιδρομῆς οἷον μεταφράζοντες τὴν ῥῆσιν, τὴν διάνοιαν τοῦ ῥητοῦ τοῦ ἀποστόλου παραστήσομεν. καθ᾿ ἣν τοῦ γνωστικοῦ τὴν τελειότητα ὑπογράφει. οὐ γὰρ ἐπὶ τοῦ ἀδικεῖσθαι μᾶλλον ἢ ἀδικεῖν ἵστησι τὸν γνωστικὸν μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀμνησίκακον εἶναι διδάσκει, μηδὲ εὔχεσθαι κατὰ τοῦ ἀδικήσαντος ἐπιτρέπων· οἶδεν γὰρ καὶ τὸν κύριον ἄντικρυς »εὔχεσθαι ὑπὲρ τῶν ἐχθρῶν« παραγγείλαντα. τὸ μὲν οὖν »ἐπὶ τῶν ἀδίκων κρίνεσθαι« τὸν ἠδικημένον φάσκει οὐδὲν ἀλλ᾿ ἢ ἀνταποδοῦναι βούλεσθαι δοκεῖν καὶ ἀνταδικῆσαι δεύτερον ἐθέλειν, ὅπερ ὁμοίως ἐστὶν ἀδικῆσαι καὶ αὐτόν. τὸ δὲ »ἐπὶ τῶν ἁγίων κρίνεσθαι« ἐθέλειν τινὰς λέγειν ἐμφαίνει τοὺς δι᾿ εὐχῆς τοῖς ἀδικήσασιν ἀνταποδοθῆναι τὴν πλεονεξίαν αἰτουμένους, καὶ εἶναι μὲν τῶν προτέρων τοὺς δευτέρους ἀμείνους, οὐδέπω δὲ ἀπαθεῖς, ἢν μὴ ἀμνησίκακοι τέλεον γενόμενοι κατὰ τὴν τοῦ κυρίου διδασκαλίαν προσεύξωνται καὶ ὑπὲρ τῶν ἐχθρῶν. Καλὸν οὖν καὶ φρένας καλὰς ἐκ μετανοίας αὐτοὺς τῆς εἰς τὴν πίστιν μεταλαβεῖν. εἰ γὰρ καὶ ἐχθροὺς ἡ ἀλήθεια τοὺς παραζηλοῦντας κεκτῆσθαι δοκεῖ, ἀλλ᾿ οὔ τί γε αὐτὴ διεχθρεύεταί τινι. »ὅ« τε γὰρ »θεὸς ἐπὶ δικαίους καὶ ἀδίκους τὸν αὑτοῦ ἐπιλάμπει ἥλιον« καὶ τὸν κύριόν γε αὐτὸν ἐπὶ δικαίους ἔπεμψεν καὶ ἀδίκους, ὅ τε ἐξομοιοῦσθαι βιαζόμενος θεῷ, διὰ τῆς πολλῆς ἀμνησικακίας »ἀφεὶς ἑβδομηκοντάκις ἑπτά« (οἶον κατὰ πάντα τὸν βίον καὶ καθ᾿ ὅλην τὴν κοσμικὴν περιήλυσιν ἑβδομάσιν ἀριθμουμέναις σημαινομένην), παντί τῳ χρηστεύεται, εἰ καί τις τὸν πάντα τοῦτον ἐν σαρκὶ βιοὺς χρόνον ἀδικεῖ τὸν γνωστικόν. οὐ γὰρ τὴν κρίσιν μόνην ἄλλοις ἐπιτρέπειν ἀξιοῖ τὸν σπουδαῖον τῶν ἠδικηκότων αὐτόν, ἀλλὰ καὶ παρ᾿ ἐκείνων αἰτεῖσθαι τῶν κριτῶν βούλεται τὸν δίκαιον τὴν ἄφεσιν τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν τοῖς εἰς αὐτὸν πεπλημμεληκόσι, καὶ εἰκότως· εἴ γε τὸ ἐκτὸς μόνον καὶ τὸ περὶ σῶμα, κἂν μέχρι θανάτου προβαίνῃ.

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: The Gnostic therefore examines the closest likeness — the mind of the teacher. That teacher, when he understood, both commanded and advised the prudent and self-controlled; the Gnostic grasps this mind exactly as the teacher himself wished it to be grasped. Taking hold privately of the grand and noble concept, he teaches worthily on the rooftops those who are able to be built up highly, and he begins beforehand the activity of the things said according to the model of the polity. For he commanded powerful things, and it is necessary for the royal and Christian man to be truly archaic and hegemonic, since we were not ordered to rule only the external beasts, but also the wild passions within ourselves. Accordingly, by precise knowledge of the bad life and the good life, the Gnostic is saved, understanding and acting more than the scribes and Pharisees.

"Stretch out and guide and reign," David writes, "because of truth and gentleness and righteousness, and your right hand will guide you wonderfully," that is, the Lord (Psalm 119:5). Who then is wise and will understand these things? Who is intelligent and will know them? Because the ways of the Lord are straight, says the prophet, showing that only the Gnostic can understand and clarify the things spoken secretly by the Spirit. And the one who understands will be silent at that very time, the Scripture says — clearly, in the presence of the unworthy — because the Lord says, "The one who has ears to hear, let him hear," not saying that hearing and understanding belong to everyone (Matthew 11:15). Immediately David writes, "Dark water in clouds of air"; from the radiance before him the clouds passed, hail and coals of fire, teaching that the holy words are hidden. And so, to the Gnostics, visible and radiant things are sent down from God like harmless hail, but to the many they are dark things like coals of fire that have been extinguished, which if someone does not ignite and rekindle, will neither blaze up nor give light.

greek: Ὁ γνωστικὸς ἄρα τὴν προσεχεστέραν ἀναμάσσεται ὁμοιότητα, τὴν διάνοιαν τὴν τοῦ διδασκάλου, ἥντινα ἐκεῖνος νοῶν ἐνετείλατό τε καὶ συνεβούλευσε τοῖς φρονίμοις καὶ σώφροσι, ταύτην συνιείς, ὡς ὁ διδάξας ἐβούλετο, καὶ ἰδίᾳ τὴν νόησιν ἀναλαβὼν τὴν μεγαλοπρεπῆ, διδάξας μὲν ἀξιολόγως ἐπὶ τῶν δωμάτων τοὺς ὑψηλῶς οἰκοδομεῖσθαι δυναμένους, προκατάρξας δὲ τῆς τῶν λεγομένων ἐνεργείας κατὰ τὸ ὑπόδειγμα τῆς πολιτείας· δυνατὰ γὰρ ἐνετείλατο, καὶ δεῖ τῷ ὄντι ἀρχικὸν εἶναι καὶ ἡγεμονικὸν τὸν βασιλικόν τε καὶ Χριστιανόν, ἐπεὶ μὴ τῶν ἔξω μόνον θηρίων κατακυριεύειν ἐτάγημεν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν ἐν ἡμῖν αὐτοῖς ἀγρίων παθῶν. κατ’ ἐπίστασιν οὖν, ὡς ἔοικεν, τοῦ κακοῦ καὶ ἀγαθοῦ βίου σῴζεται ὁ γνωστικός, πλέον τῶν γραμματέων καὶ Φαρισαίων συνιείς τε καὶ ἐνεργῶν. ἔντεινον καὶ κατευοδοῦ καὶ βασίλευε, ὁ Δαβὶδ γράφει, ἕνεκεν ἀληθείας καὶ πραότητος καὶ δικαιοσύνης, καὶ ὁδηγήσει σε θαυμαστῶς ἡ δεξιά σου, τουτέστιν ὁ κύριος. τίς οὖν σοφὸς καὶ συνήσει ταῦτα; συνετὸς καὶ γνώσεται αὐτά; διότι εὐθεῖαι αἱ ὁδοὶ τοῦ κυρίου, φησὶν ὁ προφήτης, δηλῶν μόνον δύνασθαι τὸν γνωστικὸν τὰ ἐπικεκρυμμένως πρὸς τοῦ πνεύματος εἰρημένα νοήσειν τε καὶ διασαφήσειν· καὶ ὁ συνίων ἐν τῷ καιρῷ ἐκείνῳ ἐκείνῳ σιωπήσεται, λέγει ἡ γραφή, δηλονότι πρὸς τοὺς ἀναξίους ἐξειπεῖν, ὅτι φησὶν ὁ κύριος· ὁ ἔχων ὦτα ἀκούειν ἀκουέτω, οὐ πάντων εἶναι τὸ ἀκούειν καὶ συνιέναι λέγων. αὐτίκα ὁ Δαβὶδ σκοτεινὸν ὕδωρ ἐν νεφέλαις ἀέρων γράφει· ἀπὸ τῆς τηλαυγήσεως ἐνώπιον αὐτοῦ αἱ νεφέλαι διῆλθον, χάλαζα καὶ ἄνθρακες πυρός, ἐπικεκρυμμένους τοὺς ἁγίους λόγους εἶναι διδάσκων. καὶ δὴ τοῖς μὲν γνωστικοῖς διειδεῖς καὶ τηλαυγεῖς καθάπερ χάλαζαν ἀβλαβῆ καταπέμπεσθαι θεόθεν μηνύει, σκοτεινοὺς δὲ τοῖς πολλοῖς καθάπερ τοὺς ἐκ πυρὸς ἀπεσβεσμένους ἄνθρακας, οὓς εἰ μή τις ἀνάψαι καὶ ἀναζωπυρήσαι, οὐκ ἐκφλεγήσονται οὐδ’ ἐμφωτισθήσονται.

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: Let the Decalogue be set before us as an example, by way of a brief digression, for the sake of clear knowledge. That the Ten is sacred need not be stated at this point. But if the written tablets are a work of God, they will be found to reveal a natural creation; for the finger of God is understood as the power of God, through which the creation of heaven and earth is completed, and both tablets will be recognized as symbols of the two realms (Exodus 31:18; Deuteronomy 9:10). The writing and shaping of God, inscribed on the tablet, constitutes the creation of the world. The Decalogue, in its heavenly image, contains the sun and moon, stars, clouds, light, spirit, water, air, darkness, and fire. This is the natural Decalogue of heaven. The earthly image, by contrast, contains humans, cattle, reptiles, wild beasts, and among aquatic creatures, fish and sea monsters; likewise among birds, both the flesh-eating and those that feed by day; and among plants, both the fruit-bearing and the unfruitful. This is the natural Decalogue of earth. The ark that encloses these things would be the knowledge and wisdom of things divine and human. Perhaps these two tablets represent the prophecy of two covenants. They were therefore renewed mystically, as ignorance and sin abounded together. It appears that the commandments are written twice, by two spirits, for the ruling part and the subject part, since the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh. There is also a certain tenfold structure within the human person himself: the five senses, the faculty of speech, the seminal faculty, and this—eighth—is the spiritual faculty according to formation; ninth is the ruling faculty of the soul; and tenth is the characteristic mark of the Holy Spirit, which comes through faith. Beyond these, the legislation seems to command ten human parts: sight, hearing, smell, touch, taste, and the two pairs of organs that serve them—hands and feet; for this is the formation of the human. The soul is then inserted, and the ruling part is added, by which we reason; this is not born at the casting of the seed, so that the number ten is complete even without it, and through these the whole activity of the human person is fulfilled. For the human, coming directly into being in due order, receives the beginning of life from the passive elements. We therefore affirm that the rational and ruling part is the cause of the animal's constitution, but also of the irrational part being ensouled and becoming a part of it. The bodily spirit, then, receives the vital power, which encompasses the nutritive, augmentative, and generally motive functions; it is swift-moving, traversing all the senses and the rest of the body, and suffers first impact through the body. The ruling part, however, possesses the power of choice, about which lies inquiry, learning, and knowledge. But since the reference of all things is gathered into one, the ruling part is constituted, and through it the human lives and lives in a certain way.

greek: Ὑπόδειγμα δ’ ἡμῖν κατὰ παραδρομὴν ἐκκείσθω εἰς σαφήνειαν γνωστικὴν ἡ δεκάλογος. καὶ ὅτι μὲν ἱερὰ ἡ δεκάς, παρέλκει λέγειν τὰ νῦν. εἰ δὲ αἱ πλάκες αἱ γεγραμμέναι ἔργον θεοῦ, φυσικὴν ἐμφαίνουσαι δημιουργίαν εὑρεθήσονται· δάκτυλος γὰρ θεοῦ δύναμις νοεῖται θεοῦ, δἰ ἧς ἡ κτίσις τελειοῦται οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς, ὧν ἀμφοῖν αἱ πλάκες νοηθήσονται σύμβολα. θεοῦ μὲν γὰρ γραφὴ καὶ εἰδοποιία ἐναποκειμένη τῇ πλακὶ δημιουργία τοῦ κόσμου τυγχάνει. ἡ δεκάλογος δὲ κατὰ μὲν οὐράνιον εἰκόνα περιέχει ἥλιον καὶ σελήνην, ἄστρα, νέφη, φῶς, πνεῦμα, ὕδωρ, ἀέρα, σκότος, πῦρ. αὕτη φυσικὴ δεκάλογος οὐρανοῦ. ἡ δὲ τῆς γῆς εἰκὼν περιέχει ἀνθρώπους, κτήνη, ἑρπετά, θηρία καὶ τῶν ἐνύδρων ἰχθύας καὶ κήτη, τῶν τε αὖ πτηνῶν ὁμοίως τά τε σαρκοβόρα καὶ τὰ ἡμέρῳ χρώμενα τροφῇ, φυτῶν τε ὡσαύτως τὰ καρποφόρα καὶ ἄκαρπα. αὕτη φυσικὴ δεκάλογος γῆς. καὶ ἡ κιβωτὸς δὲ ἡ ταῦτα περιειληφυῖα ἡ τῶν θείων τε καὶ ἀνθρωπίνων γνῶσις εἴη ἂν καὶ σοφία. τάχα δ’ ἃν εἶεν αἱ δύο πλάκες αὗται δισσῶν προφητεία διαθηκῶν. ἀνεκαινίσθησαν οὖν μυστικῶς, πλεοναζούσης ἀγνοίας ἅμα καὶ ἁμαρτίας. δισσῶς, ὡς ἔοικεν, γράφονται δισσοῖς πνεύμασιν ἐντολαί, τῷ τε ἡγεμονικῷ τῷ τε ὑποκειμένῳ, ἐπεὶ ἡ σὰρξ ἐπιθυμεῖ κατὰ τοῦ πνεύματος καὶ τὸ πνεῦμα κατὰ τῆς σαρκός. ἔστι δὲ καὶ δεκάς τις περὶ τὸν ἄνθρωπον αὐτόν, τά τε αἰσθητήρια πέντε καὶ τὸ φωνητικὸν καὶ τὸ σπερματικὸν καὶ τοῦτο δὴ ὄγδοον τὸ κατὰ τὴν πλάσιν πνευματικόν, ἔνατον δὲ τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν τῆς ψυχῆς καὶ δέκατον τὸ διὰ τῆς πίστεως προσγινόμενον ἁγίου πνεύματος χαρακτηριστικὸν ἰδίωμα. ἔτι πρὸς τούτοις δέκα τισὶν ἀνθρωπείοις μέρεσι προστάσσειν ἡ νομοθεσία φαίνεται, τῇ τε ὁράσει καὶ ἀκοῇ καὶ τῇ ὀσφρήσει ἁφῇ τε καὶ γεύσει καὶ τοῖς τούτων ὑπουργοῖς ὀργάνοις δισσοῖς οὖσι, χερσί τε καὶ ποσίν· αὕτη γὰρ ἡ πλάσις τοῦ ἀνθρώπου. ἐπεισκρίνεται δὲ ἡ ψυχὴ καὶ προσεισκρίνεται τὸ ἡγεμονικόν, ᾧ διαλογιζόμεθα, οὐ κατὰ τὴν τοῦ σπέρματος καταβολὴν γεννώμενον, ὡς συνάγεσθαι καὶ ἄνευ τούτου τὸν δέκατον ἀριθμόν, δἰ ὧν ἡ πᾶσα ἐνέργεια τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐπιτελεῖται. τῇ τάξει γὰρ εὐθέως γενόμενος. ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἀπὸ τῶν παθητικῶν τὴν ἀρχὴν τοῦ ζῆν λαμβάνει. τὸ λογιστικὸν τοίνυν καὶ ἡγεμονικὸν αἴτιον εἶναί φαμεν τῆς συστάσεως τῷ ζῴῳ, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῦ τὸ ἄλογον μέρος ἐψυχῶσθαί τε καὶ μόριον αὐτῆς εἶναι. αὐτίκα τὴν μὲν ζωτικὴν δύναμιν, ᾗ ἐμπεριέχεται τὸ θρεπτικόν τε καὶ αὐξητικὸν καὶ καθ’ ὅλου κινητικόν, τὸ πνεῦμα εἴληχεν τὸ σαρκικόν, ὀξυκίνητον ὃν καὶ πάντῃ διά τε τῶν αἰσθήσεων καὶ τοῦ λοιποῦ σώματος πορευόμενόν τε καὶ πρωτοπαθοῦν διὰ σώματος· τὴν προαιρετικὴν δὲ τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν ἔχει δύναμιν, περὶ ἣν ἡ ζήτησις καὶ ἡ μάθησις καὶ ἡ γνῶσις. ἀλλὰ γὰρ ἡ πάντων ἀναφορὰ εἰς ἓν συντέτακται τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν καὶ δἰ ἐκεῖνο ζῇ τε ὁ ἄνθρωπος καί πως ζῇ.

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: We will take up the question of how the philosophers' doctrines were observed by the Hebrews a little later, but first, as is fitting, we must speak of the times of Moses. Through those times it will be shown beyond doubt that the philosophy of the Hebrews is the most ancient of all wisdom. Tatian has already treated these matters precisely in his *Against the Greeks*, and Cassian has done so in the first of his *Exegetical Works*; nevertheless the present memoir requires that we too run through what has been said on the subject. Apion the grammarian, surnamed Plistonicus, in the fourth book of his *Egyptian History*—though he writes with marked hostility toward the Hebrews, being himself an Egyptian by birth and the author of a treatise against the Jews—mentions Amosis, king of the Egyptians, and the events of his reign, and cites Ptolemy of Mendes as his witness. Ptolemy's words are these: "Amosis, having become king in the time of the Argive Inachus, dug up Avaris," as Ptolemy of Mendes recorded in his *Chronicles*. This Ptolemy was a priest who set forth the deeds of the Egyptian kings in three complete books, and he states that under Amosis, king of Egypt, the Jews made their exodus from Egypt under the leadership of Moses. From this it follows that Moses flourished in the time of Inachus. The most ancient of the Greek traditions are the Argolic, which begin with Inachus, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus teaches in his *Chronicles*. Of these, the Attic line that springs from Cecrops—who was two-natured and autochthonous, to use Tatian's exact words—is forty generations younger; the Arcadian line from Pelasgus is nine generations younger, and Pelasgus himself is also said to be autochthonous. The Phthiotic line from Deucalion is two generations younger than the Arcadian. Reckoning from Inachus down to the Trojan War, twenty or a few more generations are counted, amounting, so to speak, to four hundred years. But if the Assyrian records are far older than the Greek, as Ctesias asserts, then the exodus of Moses from Egypt under the Egyptian Amosis and the Argive Inachus falls in the 402nd year of the Assyrian empire and the 32nd year of the eighth dynasty of Belochus. In Greece, during the time of Phoroneus, who succeeded Inachus, there occurred the flood of Ogygus, the kingdom in Sicyon—first under Aegialeus, then Eurypus, then Telchin—and the kingdom of Crete in Crete.

greek: Καὶ περὶ μὲν τοῦ παρ’ Ἑβραίων τὰ τῶν φιλοσόφων ἐσκευωρῆσθαι δόγματα μικρὸν ὕστερον διαληψόμεθα, πρότερον δέ, ὅπερ ἀκόλουθον ἦν, περὶ τῶν κατὰ Μωυσέα χρόνων ἤδη λεκτέον, δἰ ὧν δειχθήσεται ἀναμφηρίστως πάσης σοφίας ἀρχαιοτάτη ἡ κατὰ Ἑβραίους φιλοσοφία. εἴρηται μὲν οὖν περὶ τούτων ἀκριβῶς Τατιανῷ ἐν τῷ Πρὸς Ἕλληνας, εἴρηται δὲ καὶ Κασσιανῷ ἐν τῷ πρώτῳ τῶν Ἐξηγητικῶν· ἀπαιτεῖ δὲ ὅμως τὸ ὑπόμνημα καὶ ἡμᾶς ἐπιδραμεῖν τὰ κατὰ τὸν τόπον εἰρημένα. Ἀπίων τοίνυν ὁ γραμματικός, ὁ Πλειστονίκης ἐπικληθείς, ἐν τῇ τετάρτῃ τῶν Αἰγυπτιακῶν ἱστοριῶν, καίτοι φιλαπεχθημόνως πρὸς Ἑβραίους διακείμενος, ἅτε Αἰγύπτιος τὸ γένος, ὡς καὶ κατὰ Ἰουδαίων συντάξασθαι βιβλίον, Ἀμώσιος τοῦ Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέως μεμνημένος καὶ τῶν κατ’ αὐτὸν πράξεων, μάρτυρα παρατίθεται Πτολεμαῖον τὸν Μενδήσιον. καὶ τὰ τῆς λέξεως αὐτοῦ ὧδε ἔχει· κατέσκαψε δὲ τὴν Ἀουαρίαν Ἄμωσις κατὰ τὸν Ἀργεῖον γενόμενος Ἴναχον, ὡς ἐν τοῖς Χρόνοις ἀνέγραφεν ὁ Μενδήσιος Πτολεμαῖος. ὁ δὲ Πτολεμαῖος οὗτος ἱερεὺς μὲν ἦν, τὰς δὲ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέων πράξεις ἐν τρισὶν ὅλαις ἐκθέμενος βίβλοις κατὰ Ἄμωσίν φησιν Αἰγύπτου βασιλέα Μωυσέως ἡγουμένου γεγονέναι Ἰουδαίοις τὴν ἐξ Αἰγύπτου πορείαν, ἐξ ὧν συνῶπται κατὰ Ἴναχον ἠκμακέναι τὸν Μωσέα. παλαίτατα δὲ τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν τὰ Ἀργολικά, τὰ ἀπὸ Ἰνάχου λέγω, ὡς Διονύσιος ὁ Ἁλικαρνασσεὺς ἐν τοῖς Χρόνοις διδάσκει, τούτων δὲ † τεσσαράκοντα μὲν γενεαῖς νεώτερα τὰ Ἀττικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Κέκροπος τοῦ διφυοῦς δὴ καὶ αὐτόχθονος, ὥς φησι κατὰ λέξιν ὁ Τατιανός, ἐννέα δὲ τὰ Ἀρκαδικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Πελασγοῦ· λέγεται δὲ καὶ οὗτος αὐτόχθων. τούτων δὲ ἄλλαιν δυοῖν νεώτερα τὰ Φθιωτικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Δευκαλίωνος. εἰς δὲ τὸν χρόνον τῶν Τρωϊκῶν ἀπὸ Ἰνάχου γενεαὶ μὲν εἴκοσι ἢ μιᾷ πλείους διαριθμοῦνται, ἔτη δέ, ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν, τετρακόσια καὶ πρόσω. εἰ δὲ τὰ Ἀσσυρίων πολλοῖς ἔτεσι πρεσβύτερα τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν ἀφ’ ὧν Κτησίας λέγει, φανήσεται τῷ δευτέρῳ καὶ τετρακοσιοστῷ ἔτει τῆς Ἀσσυρίων ἀρχῆς, τῆς δὲ Βηλούχου τοῦ ὀγδόου δυναστείας τῷ δευτέρῳ καὶ τριακοστῷ ἡ Μωυσέως κατὰ Ἄμωσιν τὸν Αἰγύπτιον καὶ κατὰ Ἴναχον τὸν Ἀργεῖον ἐξ Αἰγύπτου κίνησις. ἦν δὲ κατὰ τὴν Ἑλλάδα κατὰ μὲν Φορωνέα τὸν μετὰ Ἴναχον ὁ ἐπὶ Ὠγύγου κατακλυσμὸς καὶ ἡ ἐν Σικυῶνι βασιλεία, πρώτου μὲν Αἰγιαλέως, εἶτα Εὔρωπος, εἶτα Τελχῖνος, καὶ ἡ Κρητὸς ἐν Κρήτῃ.

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: We have ample means of encountering those who are given to carping. For we are not termed children and infants with reference to the childish and contemptible character of our education, as those who are inflated on account of knowledge have calumniously alleged. Straightway, on our regeneration, we attained that perfection after which we aspired. For we were illuminated, which is to know God. He is not then imperfect who knows what is perfect. And do not reprehend me when I profess to know God ; for so it was deemed right to speak to the Word, and He is free. For at the moment of the Lord's baptism there sounded a voice from heaven, as a testimony to the Beloved, You are My beloved Son , today have I begotten You. Let us then ask the wise, Is Christ, begotten today, already perfect, or — what were most monstrous — imperfect?

If the latter, there is some addition He requires yet to make. But for Him to make any addition to His knowledge is absurd, since He is God . For none can be superior to the Word, or the teacher of the only Teacher. Will they not then own, though reluctant, that the perfect Word born of the perfect Father was begotten in perfection, according to œconomic fore-ordination? And if He was perfect, why was He, the perfect one, baptized ? It was necessary, they say, to fulfil the profession that pertained to humanity. Most excellent. Well, I assert, simultaneously with His baptism by John, He becomes perfect? Manifestly. He did not then learn anything more from him? Certainly not. But He is perfected by the washing — of baptism — alone, and is sanctified by the descent of the Spirit? Such is the case.

The same also takes place in our case, whose exemplar Christ became. Being baptized , we are illuminated; illuminated, we become sons; being made sons, we are made perfect; being made perfect, we are made immortal . I, says He, have said that you are gods, and all sons of the Highest. This work is variously called grace , and illumination, and perfection, and washing: washing, by which we cleanse away our sins ; grace , by which the penalties accruing to transgressions are remitted; and illumination, by which that holy light of salvation is beheld, that is, by which we see God clearly. Now we call that perfect which wants nothing. For what is yet wanting to him who knows God? For it were truly monstrous that that which is not complete should be called a gift (or act) of God's grace . Being perfect, He consequently bestows perfect gifts.

As at His command all things were made, so on His bare wishing to bestow grace , ensues the perfecting of His grace . For the future of time is anticipated by the power of His volition. Further release from evils is the beginning of salvation . We then alone, who first have touched the confines of life, are already perfect; and we already live who are separated from death. Salvation, accordingly, is the following of Christ: For that which is in Him is life. John 1:4 Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that hears My words, and believes in Him that sent Me, has eternal life, and comes not into condemnation, but has passed from death to life. John 5:24 Thus believing alone, and regeneration, is perfection in life; for God is never weak.

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: To go through every prophetic and legal passage spoken in riddles, which we call allegories, would be a long task; for nearly all Scripture is ordained in this way. I think, however, that a few examples will suffice to show one who has a mind what is at hand. The covering of the old Hebrew temple, with its seven surrounding courts, immediately confesses the symbol of the covenant stretching from heaven to earth through various symbols of the visible world. The veil and the curtain, embroidered with hyacinth, purple, scarlet, and fine linen, signified that the nature of the elements contains the revelation of God. Purple comes from water, fine linen from the earth; hyacinth, being dark, resembles the air, just as scarlet resembles fire. In the space between the veil and the curtain, where priests were allowed to enter, stood an altar of incense — a symbol of the earth placed in the middle of this world, from which the offerings of incense arise. That place is also midway between the inner sanctuary, where only the high priest could enter on appointed days, and the outer court open to all Hebrews; therefore they say it symbolizes what lies between heaven and earth, while others say it represents the intelligible and the sensible worlds. The veil served as a barrier to the people's unbelief, stretched across five pillars that kept those in the courtyard out. In this very way, the five loaves are mystically broken by the Savior and multiplied for the crowd of listeners. For many attend only to sensible things as if they alone existed. "Gather, then, and examine carefully," says Plato, "lest any of the uninitiated hear." These are the people who think nothing exists except what they can grasp with their hands, refusing to accept actions, generations, and all invisible realities as part of true being; for they incline only to the five senses. The understanding of God is inaccessible to hearing and to those of like kind. From this the Son is called the face of the Father, having become flesh endowed with five senses, the Word who interprets the Father's distinctive character. "If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit. We walk by faith, not by sight," the good Apostle says (2 Corinthians 5:7). Inside the veil, then, a priestly ministry is hidden, and it holds those who labor in it far more strictly than those outside. Again, the curtain at the entrance to the holy of holies rests on four pillars — a holy sign of the four ancient covenants — and also of the mystical four-letter name that was guarded by those alone to whom the inner sanctuary was accessible. It is called Iaoue, which translates as "He who is" and "He who will be." And indeed, even among the Greeks the name "God" contains a tetrad of letters. But into the intelligible world only the Lord enters, having become high priest; passing through the passions into the knowledge of the ineffable, he goes beyond every name known by voice.

greek: Μακρὸν δ’ ἂν εἴη πάντα ἐπεξιέναι τὰ προφητικὰ καὶ τὰ νομικὰ τὰ δἰ αἰνιγμάτων εἰρημένα ἐπιλεγομένους. σχεδὸν γὰρ ἡ πᾶσα ὧδέ πως θεσπίζεται γραφή. ἀπόχρη δ’, οἶμαι, τῷ γε νοῦν κεκτημένῳ εἰς ἔνδειξιν τοῦ προκειμένου ὀλίγα τινὰ ἐκτεθέντα παραδείγματα. αὐτίκα ὁμολογεῖ τὴν ἐπίκρυψιν ἡ περὶ τὸν νεὼν τὸν παλαιὸν τῶν ἑπτὰ περιβόλων πρός τι ἀναφορὰ παρ’ Ἑβραίοις ἱστορουμένη ἥ τε κατὰ τὸν ποδήρη διασκευή, διὰ ποικίλων τῶν πρὸς τὰ φαινόμενα συμβόλων τὴν ἀπ’ οὐρανοῦ μέχρι γῆς αἰνισσομένη συνθήκην. τό τε κάλυμμα καὶ παραπέτασμα ὑακίνθῳ καὶ πορφύρᾳ κόκκῳ τε καὶ βύσσῳ πεποίκιλτο, ᾐνίττετο δ’ ἄρα, ὡς ἡ τῶν στοιχείων φύσις περιέχει τὴν ἀποκάλυψιν τοῦ θεοῦ· ἐξ ὕδατος μὲν γὰρ ἡ πορφύρα, βύσσος δὲ ἐκ γῆς, ὑάκινθός τε ὡμοίωται ἀέρι ζοφώδης ὤν, ὥσπερ ὁ κόκκος τῷ πυρί. ἀνὰ μέσον δὲ τοῦ καλύμματος καὶ τοῦ παραπετάσματος, ἔνθα τοῖς ἱερεῦσιν ἐξῆν εἰσιέναι, θυμιατήριον τε ἔκειτο σύμβολον τῆς ἐν μέσῳ τῷ κόσμῳ τῷδε κειμένης γῆς, ἐξ ἧς αἱ ἀναθυμιάσεις. μέσος δὲ καὶ ὁ τόπος ἐκεῖνος τοῦ τε ἐντὸς τοῦ καταπετάσματος, ἔνθα μόνῳ τῷ ἀρχιερεῖ ἐπετέτραπτο ῥηταῖς εἰσιέναι ἡμέραις, καὶ τῆς ἔξωθεν περικειμένης αὐλαίας τῆς πᾶσιν ἀνειμένης Ἑβραίοις· διὸ μεσαίτατον οὐρανοῦ φασι καὶ γῆς· ἄλλοι δὲ κόσμου τοῦ νοητοῦ καὶ τοῦ αἰσθητοῦ λέγουσιν εἶναι σύμβολον. τὸ μὲν οὖν κάλυμμα κώλυμα λαϊκῆς ἀπιστίας ἐπίπροσθε τῶν πέντε τετάνυστο κιόνων, εἶργον τοὺς ἐν τῷ περιβόλῳ. ταύτῃ τοι μυστικώτατα πέντε ἄρτοι πρὸς τοῦ σωτῆρος κατακλῶνται καὶ πληθύνουσι τῷ ὄχλῳ τῶν ἀκροωμένων. πολὺς γὰρ ὁ τοῖς αἰσθητοῖς ὡς μόνοις οὖσι προσανέχων. ἄθρει δὴ περισκοπῶν, φησὶν ὁ Πλάτων, μή τις τῶν ἀμυήτων ἐπακούῃ. εἰσὶ δὲ οὗτοι οἱ οὐδὲν ἄλλο οἰόμενοι εἶναι ἢ οὗ ἂν ἀπρὶξ τοῖν χειροῖν λαβέσθαι δύναιντο, πράξεις δὲ καὶ γενέσεις καὶ πᾶν τὸ ἀόρατον οὐκ ἀποδεχόμενοι ὡς ἐν οὐσίας μέρει· τοιοῦτοι γὰρ οἱ τῇ πεντάδι τῶν αἰσθήσεων προσανέχοντες μόνῃ. ἄβατον δὲ ἀκοαῖς καὶ τοῖς ὁμογενέσιν ἡ νόησις τοῦ θεοῦ. ἐντεῦθεν πρόσωπον εἴρηται τοῦ πατρὸς ὁ υἱός, αἰσθήσεων πεντάδι σαρκοφόρος γενόμενος, ὁ λόγος ὁ τοῦ πατρῴου μηνυτὴς ἰδιώματος. εἰ δὲ ζῶμεν πνεύματι, πνεύματι καὶ στοιχῶμεν. διὰ πίστεως περιπατοῦμεν, οὐ διὰ εἴδους. ὁ καλὸς ἀπόστολος λέγει. ἔνδον μὲν οὖν τοῦ καλύμματος ἱερατικὴ κέκρυπται διακονία καὶ τοὺς ἐν αὐτῇ πονουμένους πολὺ τῶν ἔξω εἴργει. πάλιν τὸ παραπέτασμα τῆς εἰς τὰ ἅγια τῶν ἁγίων παρόδου, κίονες τέτταρες αὐτόθι, ἁγίας μήνυμα τετράδος διαθηκῶν παλαιῶν, ἀτὰρ καὶ τὸ τετράγραμμον ὄνομα τὸ μυστικόν, ὃ περιέκειντο οἷς μόνοις τὸ ἄδυτον βάσιμον ἦν· λέγεται δὲ Ἰαουε, ὃ μεθερμηνεύεται ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἐσόμενος. καὶ μὴν καὶ καθ’ Ἕλληνας θεὸς τὸ ὄνομα τετράδα περιέχει γραμμάτων. εἰς δὲ τὸν νοητὸν κόσμον μόνος ὁ κύριος ἀρχιερεὺς γενόμενος εἴσεισι, διὰ τῶν παθῶν εἰς τὴν τοῦ ἀρρήτου γνῶσιν παρεισδυόμενος, ὑπὲρ πᾶν ὄνομα ἐξαναχωρῶν, ὃ φωνῇ γνωρίζεται.

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: We are commanded to revere and honor the Word, having been convinced that He is both our Savior and Leader, and that through Him we come to the Father. We must do this not only on particular days, as some people do, but continuously throughout our entire lives and in every possible way. Scripture says of the chosen race, 'Seven times a day I have praised you,' justifying this practice by the commandment (Psalms 119:164). Consequently, the spiritual person requires neither a designated place nor a special temple, nor appointed festivals and days. Instead, he honors God in every place and at all times, whether he happens to be alone or in the company of those who have believed in the same way. This honor consists in giving thanks for the knowledge and the way of life God has granted.

Consider this: if the presence of a good man always molds the one who meets him toward what is better through shame and respect, how much more will the person who is continually present with God through knowledge, life, and unceasing thanksgiving become better in every respect—in deeds, words, and disposition? The spiritual person is convinced that God is present everywhere; he does not suppose that God is confined to specific locations. Were he to think otherwise, he might imagine himself without God at some moment and behave improperly, both night and day.

Therefore, conducting our whole life as a festival, persuaded that God is present everywhere, we farm while praising and sail while hymning. We conduct ourselves skillfully according to the demands of our higher citizenship. The spiritual person draws especially near to God, maintaining a demeanor that is both dignified and cheerful in all things. He is dignified because of his orientation toward the divine; he is cheerful because he reckons up the human goods God has given us.

The prophet displays the excellence of knowledge in this prayer: 'Teach me goodness and discipline and knowledge,' thereby advancing the ruling faculty of perfection step by step (Psalms 119:66). This, then, is truly the royal person; this is the holy priest of God. Even now, the most rational of the barbarians preserve the priestly office, linking it to the kingdom. Such a person never surrenders himself to the mob rule of the theaters, nor does he even dream of the things said, done, and seen there for the sake of dissolute pleasure. He does not pursue those visual pleasures, nor the varied delights of the other senses—such as costly incense that beguiles the sense of smell, or rich foods and diverse wines that lure the sense of taste, or elaborate, fragrant hairstyles that soften the soul through sensation.

Rather, he consistently directs the dignified enjoyment of all things toward God. For every meal, drink, and anointing, he offers firstfruits to the Giver of all, acknowledging the gift and the use of what has been granted to him through the Word.

greek: Σέβειν δὲ δεῖν ἐγκελευόμεθα καὶ τιμᾶν τὸν [αὐτὸν καὶ] λόγον, σωτῆρά τε αὐτὸν καὶ ἡγεμόνα εἶναι πεισθέντες, καὶ δι᾿ αὐτοῦ τὸν πατέρα, οὐκ ἐν ἐξαιρέτοις ἡμέραις, ὥσπερ ἄλλοι τινές, ἀλλὰ συνεχῶς τὸν ὅλον βίον τοῦτο πράττοντες καὶ κατὰ πάντα τρόπον. ἀμέλει »τὸ γένος τὸ ἐκλεκτὸν« »ἑπτάκις τῆς ἡμέρας ᾔνεσά σοι« φησί, κατ᾿ ἐντολὴν δικαιούμενον. ὅθεν οὔτε ὡρισμένον τόπον * οὔτε ἐξαίρετον ἱερὸν οὐδὲ μὴν ἑορτάς τινας καὶ ἡμέρας ἀποτεταγμένας, ἀλλὰ τὸν πάντα βίον ὁ γνωστικὸς ἐν παντὶ τόπῳ, κἂν καθ᾿ ἑαυτὸν μόνος ὢν τυγχάνῃ καὶ ὅπου τινὰς ἂν τῶν ὁμοίως πεπιστευκότων ἔχῃ, τιμᾷ τὸν θεόν, τουτέστιν χάριν ὁμολογεῖ τῆς γνώσεως καὶ τῆς πολιτείας. εἰ δὲ ἡ παρουσία τινὸς ἀνδρὸς ἀγαθοῦ διὰ τὴν ἐντροπὴν καὶ τὴν αἰδῶ πρὸς τὸ κρεῖττον ἀεὶ σχηματίζει τὸν ἐντυγχάνοντα, πῶς οὐ μᾶλλον ὁ συμπαρὼν ἀεὶ διὰ τῆς γνώσεως καὶ τοῦ βίου καὶ τῆς εὐχαριστίας ἀδιαλείπτως τῷ θεῷ οὐκ εὐλόγως ἂν ἑαυτοῦ παρ᾿ ἕκαστα κρείττων εἴη εἰς πάντα καὶ τὰ ἔργα καὶ τοὺς λόγους καὶ τὴν διάθεσιν; τοιοῦτος ὁ πάντῃ παρεῖναι τὸν θεὸν πεπεισμένος, οὐχὶ δὲ ἐν τόποις τισὶν ὡρισμένοις κατακεκλεισμένον ὑπολαβών, ἵνα δὴ χωρὶς αὐτοῦ ποτε οἰηθεὶς εἶναι καὶ νύκτωρ καὶ μεθ᾿ ἡμέραν ἀκολασταίνῃ. πάντα τοίνυν τὸν βίον ἑορτὴν ἄγοντες, πάντῃ πάντοθεν παρεῖναι τὸν θεὸν πεπεισμένοι, γεωργοῦμεν αἰνοῦντες, πλέομεν ὑμνοῦντες. κατὰ τὴν ἄλλην πολιτείαν ἐντέχνως ἀναστρεφόμεθα. προσεχέστερον δὲ ὁ γνωστικὸς οἰκειοῦται θεῷ σεμνὸς ὢν ἅμα καὶ ἱλαρὸς ἐν πᾶσι. σεμνὸς μὲν διὰ τὴν ἐπὶ τὸ θεῖον ἐπιστροφήν. ἱλαρὸς δὲ διὰ τὸν ἐπιλογισμὸν τῶν ἀνθρωπείων ἀγαθῶν ὧν ἔδωκεν ἡμῖν ὁ θεός. Φαίνεται δὲ τὸ ἔξοχον τῆς γνώσεως ὁ προφήτης ὧδε παριστάς· »χρηστότητα καὶ παιδείαν καὶ γνῶσιν δίδαξόν με·« κατ᾿ ἐπανάβασιν αὐξήσας τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν τῆς τελειότητος. οὗτος ἄρα ὄντως ὁ βασιλικὸς ἄνθρωπος, οὗτος ἱερεὺς ὅσιος τοῦ θεοῦ. ὅπερ ἔτι καὶ νῦν παρὰ τοῖς λογιωτάτοις τῶν βαρβάρων σῴζεται τὸ ἱερατικὸν γένος εἰς βασιλείαν προσαγόντων. οὗτος οὖν οὐδαμῇ μὲν ἑαυτὸν εἰς ὀχλοκρασίαν τὴν τῶν θεάτρων δεσπότιν ἐνδίδωσιν. τὰ λεγόμενα δὲ καὶ πραττόμενα καὶ ὁρώμενα ἡδονῆς ἀσώτου χάριν οὐδὲ ὄναρ προσίεται· οὔτ᾿ οὖν ταύτας τὰς ἡδονὰς τῆς θέας οὔτε τὰς διὰ τῶν ἄλλων ἀπολαυσμάτων ποικιλίας, οἷον θυμιαμάτων πολυτέλειαν τὴν ὄσφρησιν γοητεύουσαν ἢ βρωμάτων συγκαττύσεις καὶ τὰς ἐξ οἴνων διαφόρων ἀπολαύσεις δελεαζούσας τὴν γεῦσιν, οὐδὲ τὰς πολυανθεῖς καὶ εὐώδεις πλοκὰς ἐκθηλυνούσας δι᾿ αἰσθήσεως τὴν ψυχήν· πάντων δὲ τὴν σεμνὴν ἀπόλαυσιν ἐπὶ τὸν θεὸν ἀναγαγὼν ἀεὶ καὶ τῆς βρώσεως καὶ τοῦ πόματος καὶ τοῦ χρίσματος τῷ δοτῆρι τῶν ὅλων ἀπάρχεται, χάριν ὁμολογῶν καὶ [διὰ] τῆς δωρεᾶς καὶ τῆς χρήσεως διὰ λόγου τοῦ δοθέντος αὐτῷ.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: I shall not be sorry to bestow attention on the shorter epistles also. Even in brief works there is much pungency. The Jews had slain their prophets . 1 Thessalonians 2:15 I may ask, What has this to do with the apostle of the rival god, one so amiable withal, who could hardly be said to condemn even the failings of his own people; and who, moreover, has himself some hand in making away with the same prophets whom he is destroying? What injury did Israel commit against him in slaying those whom he too has reprobated, since he was the first to pass a hostile sentence on them? But Israel sinned against their own God. He upbraided their iniquity to whom the injured God pertains; and certainly he is anything but the adversary of the injured Deity .

Else he would not have burdened them with the charge of killing even the Lord, in the words, Who both killed the Lord Jesus and their own prophets , although (the pronoun) their own be an addition of the heretics . Now, what was there so very acrimonious in their killing Christ the proclaimer of the new god, after they had put to death also the prophets of their own god? The fact, however, of their having slain the Lord and His servants, is put as a case of climax.

Now, if it were the Christ of one god and the prophets of another god whom they slew, he would certainly have placed the impious crimes on the same level, instead of mentioning them in the way of a climax; but they did not admit of being put on the same level: the climax, therefore, was only possible by the sin having been in fact committed against one and the same Lord in the two respective circumstances. To one and the same Lord, then, belonged Christ and the prophets . What that sanctification of ours is, which he declares to be the will of God , you may discover from the opposite conduct which he forbids. That we should abstain from fornication, not from marriage; that every one should know how to possess his vessel in honour . 1 Thessalonians 4:3-4 In what way? Not in the lust of concupiscence, even as the Gentiles .

1 Thessalonians 4:5 Concupiscence, however, is not ascribed to marriage even among the Gentiles , but to extravagant, unnatural, and enormous sins . The law of nature is opposed to luxury as well as to grossness and uncleanness; it does not forbid connubial intercourse, but concupiscence; and it takes care of our vessel by the honourable estate of matrimony. This passage (of the apostle) I would treat in such a way as to maintain the superiority of the other and higher sanctity , preferring continence and virginity to marriage, but by no means prohibiting the latter. For my hostility is directed against those who are for destroying the God of marriage, not those who follow after chastity .

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: What sort of exit awaits that one, cast out? 'He'll be seized by the Creator's fire,' they say. Has he no element, no provision for this very purpose—something to release his own sinners without cruelty, so he doesn't have to hand them over to the Creator? So what does the Creator do then? I'll tell you: he'll prepare a sulphurous Gehenna for them, fit for his blasphemers—unless, perhaps, the zealous God spares those who desert his adversary. Oh, a God perverse in every way, irrational everywhere, empty in all things, and therefore not existing at all! I see no status, no condition, no nature, no order of his holding together—nor even the sacrament of his faith. For what reason is baptism even required among them? If it's for the remission of sins, how will he appear to forgive sins when he doesn't appear to retain them, since if he retained them, he would judge? If it's for release from death, how will he release from death someone he never bound to death? He would have condemned them if he had bound them from the beginning. If it's for the regeneration of man, how will he regenerate someone he never generated? Repetition doesn't suit one from whom nothing was ever made once. If it's for the bestowal of the Holy Spirit, how will he confer the Spirit who never first imparted a soul? Because the Spirit will somehow supply what the soul lacks. So he seals a man who was never sealed by him, washes a man who was never defiled by him. And in all this, does he immerse the whole sacrament of salvation in the flesh that arises from salvation? Not even a peasant waters ground that won't yield fruit—unless he's as empty as Marcion's God. So then, when he imposes such tremendous sanctity, without burden or glory, on the weakest or most unworthy flesh, what does he burden the weak flesh with, or adorn the unworthy flesh with? What does he not reward with salvation, since he burdens or adorns it? What does he cheat of the wage of work, not repaying the flesh with salvation? And what does he let the honor of sanctity die in it?

latin: Exitus autem illi abiecto quis? \'ab igni\', inquiunt, \'creatoris deprehendetur\'. adeone nullum habet elemeutum uel in hanc causam prouisum, quo peccatores suos uel sine saeuitia releget, ne illos dedat creatori? quid tunc creator? credo. sulphuratiorem eis gehennam praeparabit, ut blasphemis suis scilicet; nisi quod deus zelotes fortassean desertoribus aduersarii sui parcat. o deum usquequaque peruersum, ubique inrationalem, in omnibus uanum, atque ita neminem! cuius non statum, non condicionem, non naturam, non ullum ordinem uideo consistere, iam nec ipsum fidei eius sacramentum. cui enim rei baptisma quoque apud eum exigitur? si remissio delictorum est, quomodo uidebitur delicta dimittere qui non uidebitur retinere, quia, si retineret, iudicaret? si absolutio mortis est, quomodo absoluet a morte qui non deuinxit ad mortem? damnasset enim, si a primordio deuinxisset. si regeneratio est hominis, quomodo regenerat qui non generauit? iteratio enim non competit ei, a quo quid nec semel factum est. si consecutio est spiritus sancti, quomodo spiritum adtribuet qui animam non prius contulit? quia suffectura est quodammodo spiritus animae. signat igitur hominem numquam apud se resignatum, lauat hominem numquam apud se coinquinatum. et in hoc totum salutis sacramentum carnem mergit exortem salutis? nec rusticus terram rigabit fructum non relaturam. nisi tam uanus quam deus Marcionis. proinde. cum tantam sine sarcinam siue gloriam infirmissimae aut indignissimae carni imponit sanctitatem, quid aut onerat infirmam aut exornat indignam? quid non salute remunerat quam onerat uel exornat? quid fraudat mercedem operis, non rependens carni salutem? quid et honorem sanctitatis in illa mori patitur?

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: All this shows whose God's wisdom Paul speaks of among the mature: the God who stripped the wise of their wisdom, nullified the experts' prudence, and drove the world's wisdom mad, choosing its foolish elements and arranging them for salvation. He says this wisdom lay hidden in secret among the foolish, the insignificant, and the dishonored, veiled under figures, allegories, and riddles, only to be unveiled later in Christ. The Creator set Christ as a light to the nations and promised through Isaiah to disclose invisible, hidden treasures (Isaiah). It is simply incredible that a God who has done absolutely nothing — nothing in which anything could be thought hidden — should have hidden something. If such a God existed, He could not remain hidden, let alone His mysteries. The Creator, by contrast, is well known, and so are His mysteries, openly active in Israel, though cloaked in symbolic forms where God's wisdom took delight. This wisdom is to be declared among the mature at the proper time, having been purposed in God's plan before the ages. Whose ages, if not the Creator's? If the ages are structured by times, and times are composed of days, months, and years, and days, months, and years are marked by the sun, moon, and stars that the Creator set in place — 'and they will be for signs of months and years' — then the ages belong to the Creator, and whatever is said to have been purposed before the ages belongs to no one else but the One whose ages they are. Let Marcion prove the ages of his own god; let him produce the world itself in which ages are reckoned, a vessel of time, and the signs or mechanisms that govern them. If he demonstrates nothing, I return to my point: why did the Creator purpose our glory before the ages? One might suppose He purposed it before the ages to reveal it when the age dawned. But He does this only after nearly all the Creator's ages have already run their course. He purposed it in vain before the ages, and not so much within the ages what He would reveal almost after the ages. For it is not in the nature of the One who delays in revealing to have rushed in purposing.

latin: Igitur per haec omnia ostendit, cuius dei sapientiam loquatur inter perfectos, eius scilicet, qui sapientiam sapientium abstulerit et prudentiam prudentium inritam fecerit, qui infatuauerit sapientia mundi, stulta eligens eius et disponens in salutem. hanc dicit sapientiam in occulto fuisse, quae fuerit in stultis et in pusillis et (in) inhonestis, quae latuerit etiam sub figuris, allegoriis et aenigmatibus. reuelanda postmodum in Christo, posito in lumen nationum a creatore promittente per Esaiae uocem patefacturum se thesauros inuisibiles et occultos. nam ut absconderit aliquid is deus, qui nihil egit omnino, in quod aliquid abscondisse existimaretur, satis incredibile. ipse si esset, latere non posset, nedum aliqua eius sacramenta. creator autem tam ipse notus quam et sacramenta eius, palam scilicet decurrentia apud Israhel, sed de significantiis obumbrata, in quibus sapientia dei delitiscebat. inter perfectos narranda suo in tempore, proposita uero in proposito dei ante saecula. cuius et saecula, nisi creatoris? si enim et saecula temporibus structa sunt, tempora autem diebus et mensibus et annis compinguntur, dies porro et menses et anni solibus et lunis et sideribus creatoris signantur in hoc ab eo positis, — et erunt enim, inquit, in signa mensium et annorum — apparet et saecula creatoris esse et omne, quod ante saecula propositum dicatur, non alterius esse, quam cuius et saecula. aut probet dei sui saecula Marcion; ostendat et mundum ipsum, in quo saecula deputentur, uas quodammodo temporum, et signa aliqua uel organa eorum. si nihil demonstrat, reuertor, ut et illud dicam: cur autem ante saecula creatoris proposuit gloriam nostram? posset uideri eam ante saecula proposuisse, quam introductione saeculi reuelasset. at cum id facit paene iam totis saeculis creatoris prodactis, uane ante saecula proposuit et non magis intra saecula quod reuelaturus erat paene post saecula. non enim eius est festinasse in proponendo, cuius est retardasse in reuelando.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius (for such is Marcion's proposition) he came down to the Galilean city of Capernaum, of course meaning from the heaven of the Creator, to which he had previously descended from his own. What then had been his course, for him to be described as first descending from his own heaven to the Creator's? For why should I abstain from censuring those parts of the statement which do not satisfy the requirement of an ordinary narrative, but always end in a falsehood ? To be sure, our censure has been once for all expressed in the question, which we have already suggested: Whether, when descending through the Creator's domain, and indeed in hostility to him, he could possibly have been admitted by him, and by him been transmitted to the earth, which was equally his territory?

Now, however, I want also to know the remainder of his course down, assuming that he came down. For we must not be too nice in inquiring whether it is supposed that he was seen in any place. To come into view indicates a sudden unexpected glance, which for a moment fixed the eye upon the object that passed before the view, without staying. But when it happens that a descent has been effected, it is apparent, and comes under the notice of the eyes. Moreover, it takes account of fact , and thus obliges one to examine in what condition with what preparation, with how much violence or moderation, and further, at what time of the day or night, the descent was made; who, again, saw the descent, who reported it, who seriously avouched the fact, which certainly was not easy to be believed , even after the asseveration.

It is, in short, too bad that Romulus should have had in Proculus an avoucher of his ascent to heaven, when the Christ of (this) god could not find any one to announce his descent from heaven; just as if the ascent of the one and the descent of the other were not effected on one and the same ladder of falsehood ! Then, what had he to do with Galilee , if he did not belong to the Creator by whom that region was destined (for His Christ) when about to enter on His ministry? As Isaiah says: Drink in this first, and be prompt, O region of Zabulon and land of Nephthalim, and you others who (inhabit) the sea-coast, and that of Jordan, Galilee of the nations , you people who sit in darkness, behold a great light; upon you, who inhabit (that) land, sitting in the shadow of death, the light has arisen.

It is, however, well that Marcion's god does claim to be the enlightener of the nations , that so he might have the better reason for coming down from heaven; only, if it must needs be, he should rather have made Pontus his place of descent than Galilee . But since both the place and the work of illumination according to the prophecy are compatible with Christ, we begin to discern that He is the subject of the prophecy , which shows that at the very outset of His ministry , He came not to destroy the law and the prophets , but rather to fulfil them; Matthew 5:17 for Marcion has erased the passage as an interpolation. It will, however, be vain for him to deny that Christ uttered in word what He immediately did partially indeed. For the prophecy about place He at once fulfilled. From heaven straight to the synagogue .

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Christ is the head of the man. But who is Christ? Is He not the author of the man? 'Head' implies authority, and authority belongs to no one but the author. So of which man is He the head? Certainly the one Paul goes on to discuss: the man ought not to be veiled, because he is the image of God. If he is the image of the Creator — who, looking at His own Word about to make man, said, 'Let us make man in our image and likeness' (Gen 1:26) — how can I have any other head than the One whose image I am? When I am the Creator's image, there is no room in me for another head. But then why must the woman have a symbol of authority on her head? If it is because she was made from the man and for the man according to the Creator's institution, then the Apostle also enforced His discipline, deriving the reasons for that discipline from His institution. Paul adds: 'because of the angels.' Which angels? That is, whose angels? If they are the apostate angels of the Creator, then rightly so, so that the face which scandalized them might bear a mark of humility and the veiling of beauty. But if they belong to another God, what is there to fear, when not even the Marcionites themselves desire women? We have often shown that the Apostle ranks heresies among evils as an evil, and that those who flee heresies as an evil are to be approved. Accordingly, we have already proven in the Gospel the truth of the Lord's body and blood in the sacrament of bread and cup against Marcion's phantom, and also that every mention of judgment belongs to the Creator as the judging God — a point treated almost throughout the whole work. Now concerning spiritual gifts. I say these things, too, which were promised in Christ by the Creator, under that rule — most just, I think — that no one's manifestation is to be believed except His whose promise has been proven. Isaiah declared: 'A shoot will spring from the stump of Jesse, a branch from his roots will bear fruit, and the Spirit of the Lord will rest on Him — the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of the Lord' (Isa 11:1-2). He then lists the Spirit's species: wisdom, intelligence, counsel, strength, knowledge, piety, and the Spirit of the fear of God filling Him. Isaiah portrays Christ as the flower rising from the shoot that comes from the root of Jesse — that is, from the virgin of David's line, Jesse's son — in whom Christ was to possess the whole substance of the Spirit, not as something added later to One who was always the Spirit of God even before the flesh. Otherwise you might argue the prophecy refers to a Christ who, as mere man from David's stock, would only later receive the Spirit of His God. Rather, from the moment He blossomed in the flesh taken from David's line, every operation of spiritual grace was to rest in Him, be dispensed, and reach its completion as far as the Jews were concerned — just as the facts prove: from that time on, nothing breathed the Creator's Spirit among them, once the wise architect, prudent counselor, and prophet had been taken from Judea, so that 'the Law and the Prophets were until John.' Now see how He also foretold the charisms that would come after Christ was received into heaven: 'He ascended on high,' that is, into heaven; 'He led captivity captive,' that is, death or human bondage; 'He gave gifts to the sons of men' — the gifts we call charisms. He says 'sons of men' elegantly, not 'men' indiscriminately, pointing us to the true sons of men, the Apostles. For in the Gospel He says: 'I have begotten you,' and 'My sons, whom I am begetting again.' And already now that promise of the Spirit is fulfilled, spoken through Joel: 'In the last days I will pour out My Spirit on all flesh; your sons and daughters will prophesy, and on My servants and handmaids I will pour out My Spirit' (Joel 2:28-29). And certainly, if the Creator promised the grace of His Spirit for the last days, but Christ, the dispenser of spiritual things, appeared in the last days — as the Apostle says: 'When the time had fully come, God sent His Son,' and again: 'The time is already gathered up' — it follows that this grace of the Spirit belongs to Christ the Preacher, in the preaching of the last times. Finally, compare the Apostle's list with Isaiah's. Paul says: 'To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom' — and immediately Isaiah sets the Spirit of wisdom; 'to another a word of knowledge' — here is the Spirit of intelligence and counsel; 'to another faith by the same Spirit' — here is the Spirit of piety and fear of God; 'to another gifts of healing, to another workings of miracles' — here is the Spirit of strength; 'to another prophecy, to another distinguishing of spirits, to another kinds of tongues, to another interpretation of tongues' — here is the Spirit of knowledge. See the Apostle conspiring with the prophet both in distributing the one Spirit and in specifying the gifts. I can say: the same One who adapted the unity of diverse charisms to the many members of our body shows Himself Lord of both the human body and the Holy Spirit — who did not want the merits of charisms to reside in the Spirit, any more than He placed them in the human body, and who also taught the Apostle to prefer love above all charisms by the principal commandment that Christ Himself endorsed: 'You shall love the Lord with all your heart, with all your strength, and with all your soul, and your neighbor as yourself.' And when Paul recalls something written in the Law — that the Creator would speak in other tongues and through other lips — he confirms the charism of tongues by that very recollection; nor can the Creator's charism appear alien here, confirmed as it is by the preaching. Likewise, prescribing silence for women in the church, lest they speak merely for the sake of learning — though He has already shown they also have the right to prophesy, when He requires a veil on a prophesying woman — He takes the authority for the woman's subjection from the Law, which, as I have said once, he ought not to have known except to destroy it. But now that we turn from spiritual things, the facts themselves must prove which of us rashly claims his God, and whether this can be opposed to our side. If the Creator promised in His Christ, not yet revealed, destined only for the Jews, that He would have His operations in His Christ and His people in His time, then let Marcion produce the gifts of his god: some prophets who spoke not from human sense but from God's Spirit, who foretold the future and exposed the heart's secrets; let him produce a psalm, a vision, a spiritual prayer — at least in ecstasy, that is, madness — if any interpretation of tongues has been added; let him also prove that a woman has prophesied among his people, from those holier women of his. I say: if all these things are more easily produced by me and certainly align with the Creator's rules, dispositions, and disciplines, then without doubt the Christ, the Spirit, and the Apostle belong to my God. Anyone who wishes may demand my profession.
